21113a7a19:ceb8f0e6118ab179.title: Jlateh Vincent Jappah, on the job market--a remarkable candidate
21113a7a19:ceb8f0e6118ab179.author: Al Roth (noreply@blogger.com)
21113a7a19:ceb8f0e6118ab179.summary: Not for the first time, I have a remarkable student on the job market this year, Jlateh Vincent Jappah . Born in Liberia and now a US citizen, Vincent is on an unusual intellectual and academic journey. He is presently finishing his PhD in Health Policy here at Stanford, and has also taken a full load of graduate courses in the Economics department. He is also a physician, with an MD from a Russian medical school. I am co-supervising his dissertation with my colleague Caroline Hoxby. His main project is on the impact of incentives on blood donation in Sub-Saharan Africa. His results are dramatic. Per-diem cash payments, e.g. for transportation, are far more effective and much less expensive than telephone credits or meals for eliciting safe blood donation. If he sounds really special, it's because he is. I'll be happy to correspond with anyone interested in pursuing him on this year's job market.

21113a7a19:2ee7f4f10d726586.title: Human organ trafficking and missing persons in China, PNAS
21113a7a19:2ee7f4f10d726586.author: Al Roth (noreply@blogger.com)
21113a7a19:2ee7f4f10d726586.summary: Here's a study, recently published in PNAS, that tries to very indirectly infer the rate of illegal organ trafficking in China. It's sure to be controversial. X. Wang, Human organ trafficking and missing persons in China , Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 123 (44) e2608464123, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2608464123 (2026). "Abstract The persistent shortage of human organs for transplantation has long been a global challenge. The prospect of substantial profit creates strong incentives for illegal organ trafficking, including murder for organ harvesting, yet empirical evidence remains scarce. This study addresses this gap by exploiting a unique quasi-natural experiment created by China’s organ policy reform. From 1984 to 2014, executed prisoners were the primary source of transplant organs in China. In 2015, the Chinese government abolished the use of organs from executed prisoners, sharply exacerbating the organ shortage. Following this policy change, the number of missing persons rose notably nationwide. Employing difference-in-differences and triple-difference strategies, we show that, compared to cases unrelated to organ trafficking (e.g., voluntary disappearances), the number and incidence of involuntary missing persons plausibly related to organ trafficking increased significantly after 2015. The effects are especially pronounced among individuals with mental illness and in regions with higher transplant demand and greater transplant capacity. Although we do not directly observe organ trafficking, the spatial, temporal, and demographic patterns we document are consistent with the hypothesis that increased organ scarcity intensified incentives for illicit organ procurement. More broadly, the findings suggest that severe organ shortages may generate unintended and highly harmful consequences, even in a low-crime setting such as China. These results underscore the importance of accounting for behavioral responses and illicit-market incentives when designing…

21113a7a19:ee0ff3f10b82afff.author: Al Roth (noreply@blogger.com)
21113a7a19:ee0ff3f10b82afff.summary: I'm just back from an unexpectedly grueling trip, and hope to resume semi-daily blogging. This story caught my eye: basketball has been an inner city game in the U.S., in part because basketball courts can be set up very inexpensively in urban parks, and not so expensively in gyms. So inner city kids are disproportionately represented among the most talented players. But who those kids are has changed over time. The WSJ has the story: When Jews Ruled the Basketball Court. Six players on the New York Knicks’ inaugural roster were Jewish. By Michael Freund "It was Nov. 1, 1946, and Ossie Schectman of the New York Knicks took a bounce pass and scored on a two-handed underhand layup. Schectman, the son of Russian Jewish immigrants, had just scored the first basket in NBA history. ... "Six members of the Knicks’ original roster, including Schectman, were Jewish. That was no coincidence. For much of the early 20th century, basketball was widely regarded as a Jewish game. "The reason can be traced to the immigrant neighborhoods of New York and Philadelphia. Millions of Jews arrived from Eastern Europe beginning in the 1880s, often settling in neighborhoods with little open space and scant money to spend on recreation. Baseball required a field and equipment. Basketball needed little more than a ball, a hoop and a schoolyard. "

21113a7a19:4a1e5a37dfce9f4e.title: Market design and water conservation in the the Great Salt Lake
21113a7a19:4a1e5a37dfce9f4e.author: Al Roth (noreply@blogger.com)
21113a7a19:4a1e5a37dfce9f4e.summary: Silvia Console Battilana, who co-founded Auctionomics along with Paul Milgrom, writes in Forbes about the prospects for market design efforts to help conserve Utah's Great Salt Lake. How Market Design Could Help Save Utah’s Great Salt Lake by By Silvia Console Battilana "the Great Salt Lake is drying up. "To save the lake while protecting water users, business leaders can adopt a little-known but powerful economic tool: market design. When water levels drop, the consequences immediately hit commercial supply chains and local commerce. Market-based incentives give businesses a way to reward upstream water conservation, bringing more water to the lake without hurting regional growth. The invisible hand of the market could identify the least expensive conservation, compensate participating water users and restore the Great Salt Lake. ... "The shrinking of the Great Salt Lake has many causes, and there is no silver-bullet fix. But any solution to refill the lake will likely involve conservation within Utah. Seventy-one percent of the water diverted from the lake’s basin is allocated to agriculture. If those commercial users could make more efficient use of water, more would reach the lake. The catch is that many conservation practices, like water-friendly infrastructure and precision irrigation, are expensive. Under Utah’s traditional “use-it-or-lose-it” water rights system, users have little financial reason to conserve. Without modern economic incentives, asking businesses and farms to voluntarily cut back simply isn’t realistic. Even if water users could be forced to cut back, it’s not clear who should cut back, or by how much. The costs of water conservation aren’t the same across users, and they can be very hard to estimate. Market design can address both of these challenges. Crucially, markets don’t force particular actions or behaviors. Instead, well-designed markets create an incentive for farms and communities to cut back on water and be rewarded for their…

Poetic justice: A review of moral economics by Alvin E. Roth Michael A. Rees "Alvin E. Roth describes poetic justice as the Virginia state flag flying at half-mast in 2020 in honor of Bernie Cohen, who argued the US Supreme Court case Loving v. Virginia that made interracial marriage legal. Turns out Mildred and Richard Loving were convicted of interracial marriage in 1967, arrested by police at 2 AM at home in their bed, and sentenced to 1 year in prison but suspended on the condition that they leave Virginia for 25 years. Reading what the Virginia Court of Appeals judge wrote, side by side with what the US Supreme Court wrote, is, by itself, worth the price of the book. "Those of us in the field of transplantation have felt—and will continue to feel—the impact of repugnance. In moral economics, Alvin E. Roth takes us on a grand tour of how repugnance shapes transactions across a wide spectrum of human activities. Take uterus transplantation, pioneered in Sweden, a country where repugnance to surrogacy has made it illegal. You can transplant a uterus into a woman with infertility in Sweden, but do not you dare use a surrogate’s uterus in her own body to help you achieve a baby! Alvin E. Roth defines repugnance as a morally contested market that some people would like to participate in, but others think should be outlawed. He goes on to call a transaction repugnant if “all parties to the transaction want to engage in it, and others think they shouldn’t be allowed to for moral or religious reasons, even though those others can’t detect that the transaction has taken place unless someone tells them.”1 I found it fascinating to walk through all the ways in which repugnance has shaped the world in which we live. "The book starts with a clear example of a transaction that many people want to engage in: sex. Of course, I knew about the repugnance…

We assessed predefined desensitization failure or anticipated failure with the intended donor, compared immunologic compatibility between intended and exchange donors, and recorded perioperative desensitization, graft function, delayed graft function (DGF), and biopsy-proven acute rejection (BPAR). 21113a7a19:a7d807e7d8608906.title: The once and future market for prostitution in Rhode Island
21113a7a19:a7d807e7d8608906.author: Al Roth (noreply@blogger.com)
21113a7a19:a7d807e7d8608906.summary: Kim Krawiec , the great legal scholar of repugnant transactions, has written that rare (almost never seen) book review that extends the empirical study of an important, well-studied social science event, namely Rhode Island's experience of legal prostitution. It provides an illuminating followup to the germinal paper by Cunningham and Shah. (Prostitution in R.I. is one of the controversial markets covered in Moral Economics , and I believe Krawiec's book review is headed for a forthcoming symposium on the book in Œconomia ­­.) The Smallest State's Big Experiment by Kimberly D. Krawiec October 09, 2026 Abstract Rhode Island’s accidental decriminalization of prostitution in 1980 is typically told as the story of a legal change that went unnoticed for more than two decades. This review of Alvin Roth’s latest book, Moral Economics, challenges that standard account and explores its implications for Roth’s argument that markets need social support to flourish. Drawing on court records, contemporaneous news reports, arrest statistics, and legislative proceedings, I show that the statutory change was noticed almost immediately. Prostitution-related arrests continued, not because police and prosecutors were ignorantly arresting and charging sex workers and clients under a statute that no longer existed, but because the legal system adapted using tools – primarily the loitering prohibition that survived the 1980 rewrite – that have long been used to police behavior and individuals considered repugnant. After a 2003 judicial ruling closed an important enforcement avenue against indoor sex work and vaulted the market into the open, a coalition formed around trafficking concerns that eventually paved the way for recriminalization in 2009. Rhode Island’s accidental experiment with decriminalized sex work provided neither the deliberately designed regulatory framework nor the political backing that could build the type of social support that Roth insists (correctly, in my view)…

BMC Med Ethics (2026). https://doi.org/10.1186/s12910-026-01590-5 "Background Organ donation after euthanasia (ODE) is an evolving, patient-initiated procedure in the Netherlands. While it gives meaning to donors at the end-of-life, it introduces complex ethical and practical challenges for healthcare professionals. This study aims to describe the clinical characteristics and donation outcomes of the first 100 ODE procedures in the Netherlands, while outlining the practical and ethical dilemmas encountered. Methods A retrospective analysis was performed on prospectively collected data from the first 100 ODE procedures conducted between September 2012 and February 2023. To gain deeper insight into practical experiences and ethical themes, these data were discussed with organ donation coordinators and intensivists involved in the procedures. The analysis focused on clinical characteristics and donation outcomes, as on ethical and practical challenges. Results Neurodegenerative disorders were the primary underlying cause of suffering (52%), followed by psychiatric conditions (31%). The first 100 procedures resulted in 408 transplanted organs. Most procedures were performed in intensive care units, with general practitioners performing euthanasia. Key ethical and practical challenges included the tension between clinical protocols (e.g., fasting) and patient comfort, the medicalisation of the dying process through invasive monitoring, and the logistical barriers of starting ODE from home (ODEH). 2f5fdda6a0:07a1b8850d9ac432.title: Careers in Finance
2f5fdda6a0:07a1b8850d9ac432.author: Scognamiglio, Annalisa
2f5fdda6a0:07a1b8850d9ac432.summary: Past research has documented a substantial finance wage premium. We examine whether this premium reflects differences in lifetime career opportunities. Using resume data, we reconstruct career trajectories in finance and nonfinance sectors and build synthetic measures of career attractiveness that account for compensation levels, growth, and risk. We find that asset management and investment banking provide a sizable risk-adjusted career premium relative to banking, insurance, and other sectors. This premium has declined across cohorts, particularly relative to high tech. Labor-market entry patterns respond to these premia: potential entrants treat finance and high-tech careers as substitutes when choosing where to start.

2f5fdda6a0:638ae45ef0c67b5e.title: Political Affiliation and Media Distrust: Evidence from Stock Market Investors
2f5fdda6a0:638ae45ef0c67b5e.author: Massa, Massimo
2f5fdda6a0:638ae45ef0c67b5e.summary: Does distrust in politically affiliated media induce a bias in investor beliefs? We study the acquisition of Dow Jones & Co. by News Corporation in 2007 as a shock to the political affiliation of Dow Jones outlets. Following the acquisition, the prices of Republican- (Democrat-) aligned stocks become less sensitive to favorable (unfavorable) Dow Jones Newswires (DJNW) sentiment, consistent with the market attaching less credibility to a politically affiliated source. There is, however, no evidence of change in DJNW sentiment, coverage, or language about Republican/Democrat stocks, suggesting a loss of stock price informativeness. Consistent with this view, a portfolio exploiting the attenuated reaction to DJNW news earns abnormal returns following 2007.

2f5fdda6a0:a7908c944a06eff7.title: Optimal Retirement Saving and Dissaving
2f5fdda6a0:a7908c944a06eff7.author: Munk, Claus
2f5fdda6a0:a7908c944a06eff7.summary: Applying a rich model of individuals’ life-cycle utility maximization, I comprehensively evaluate retirement saving plans. Across a range of individual characteristics, access to basic plans with constant expected payouts and no or full annuitization leads to individual utility gains of up to 5.07% of initial wealth and lifetime income ($43,800 in present value terms), and almost all individuals prefer full annuitization and a target-date fund investment strategy. With flexible plans allowing for partial annuitization and non-constant expected payouts, utility gains go up to 5.81%, and most individuals prefer a high degree of annuitization and expected payouts being increasing through retirement.

2f5fdda6a0:11279647bd188980.title: Household Finance at the Origin: Home Ownership as a Cultural Heritage from Agriculture
2f5fdda6a0:11279647bd188980.author: Vuillemey, Guillaume
2f5fdda6a0:11279647bd188980.summary: I show that home ownership decisions across countries and individuals are shaped by a cultural heritage from agriculture. For centuries, dominant assets in preindustrial economies were either land or cattle. Consequently, the type of farming prevailing locally shaped preferences and beliefs about the relative value of immovable and movable assets. This cultural heritage had long-lasting consequences. Today, individuals originating from societies with a history of crop agriculture—where the dominant asset was land—are more likely to be homeowners. For identification, I rely both on home ownership decisions of second-generation immigrants in the United States and on an instrument.

04be1a0d28:52c0582ec530de7b.title: How Will the 340B Rebate Model Pilot Affect Covered Entity Finances? -- by Charles J. Courtemanche
04be1a0d28:52c0582ec530de7b.summary: The Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) plans to implement a pilot switching 340B from an upfront discount model to a rebate model for drugs in the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program (MDPNP). This study uses calibration methods to predict the impact of the rebate model pilot (RMP) on covered entities’ net revenues from the 340B program. I examine possible losses from averted duplicate discounts; denial of valid claims; manufacturers using data to exert influence; liquidity-related expenses; and administrative and staffing costs. I also project the effects of switching the entire 340B program to a rebate model. I project net revenue losses from the RMP of $1.5 billion. Expansion to all of 340B would increase the predicted losses to $22.8 billion, cutting net revenues from the program by 32%. The majority of losses will come from administrative and staffing costs, which do not benefit manufacturers, implying a net negative effect of switching to a rebate model. Covered entity losses from the RMP will be limited by the pilot only applying to a small percentage of 340B sales as well as restrictions HRSA’s guidance places on manufacturers. If the rebate model expands to all of 340B or if the restrictions are inadequately enforced, the losses will grow substantially.

04be1a0d28:53f7320f9ef409fd.title: Horizontal Equity of Taxation: Citizen Beliefs and Policy Preferences -- by Pierre Bachas, Christopher A. Hoy, Anders Jensen, Mahvish Shaukat
04be1a0d28:53f7320f9ef409fd.summary: Taxes are harder to enforce on the self-employed than on wage earners, creating horizontal inequities among taxpayers with similar incomes. Using tax microsimulation and household survey data from 29 developing countries, we show that horizontal inequities in actual tax systems are comparable in magnitude to vertical equity and are exacerbated by progressive reforms that fall disproportionately on wage earners. We then conduct surveys and randomized information experiments in Pakistan to study public perceptions of these inequities. Although providing information raises fairness concerns, it does not increase support for reforms reducing it, revealing an important political constraint to improving tax equity.

04be1a0d28:45437ae8bc8db92b.title: Monetary policy in a Phelps–Winter Economy -- by Bruce C. Greenwald, Joseph E. Stiglitz
04be1a0d28:45437ae8bc8db92b.summary: We use the Phelps-Winter customer market—providing a better theory of price determination for large parts of the economy than the standard model—to show that raising interest rates induces higher prices, as firms value current profits more, and are more willing to lose customers for short-term gains. These inflationary effects can be significant in relevant ranges of interest rates; they exist in the short run even when interest rate hikes succeed in cutting aggregate demand; and that they are amplified by policy uncertainty and the uncertainty about the effects of interest rate changes, both of which have increased as conventional policy has demonstrably failed badly to keep inflation at the 2% target. Empirical studies confirm this low level of ineffectiveness of raising interest rates in reducing inflation. The weakening effectiveness of monetary policy was predicted by our earlier work on banks and the supply of credit, as a result of the elimination of interest prohibition on deposits; and further suggested by work on the structural transformation of the economy, as customer markets become more important.

04be1a0d28:c18f8fddc6f2fba2.title: Measuring the Impact of Impact Measurement -- by Emanuele Colonnelli, Timothy McQuade, Natalia Rigol, Benjamin N. Roth
04be1a0d28:c18f8fddc6f2fba2.summary: Impact measurement is central to impact investing and social entrepreneurship, yet little is known about whether firms benefit privately from measuring impact. We conduct the first randomized controlled trial of an impact measurement intervention among high-growth social enterprises in India. Treated firms exhibit nearly twice as much revenue growth and raise nearly twice as much capital as control firms. In a companion experiment with early-stage investors, we find that investors respond strongly to quantified impact metrics but not to generic qualitative impact statements. Together, our results show that impact measurement can shape firm growth and capital allocation.

04be1a0d28:2028e1483f8d9a60.title: Gambling for Goals -- by Costas Arkolakis, Spencer Y. Kwon, Dominic Russel, Claire Shi, Hyunjoo Yang
04be1a0d28:2028e1483f8d9a60.summary: Young adults in advanced economies have grown more pessimistic about their economic prospects in recent years. At the same time, gambling-like financial activities have proliferated. We link these trends through a Friedman-Savage (1948) motive: when life goals such as homeownership or marriage seem out of reach, individuals turn to financial gambles. We test this theory using an original survey combined with millions of linked records from Korea’s leading credit bureau, telecom provider, and credit card issuer. Consistent with the theory, individuals who place greater importance on hard-to-reach goals take more risk, and the form of risk they take varies systematically with their distance from those goals. Within individuals, cryptocurrency app usage rises during unemployment and falls after winning the right to purchase price-regulated housing through a lottery. A calibration shows how hard-to-reach goals lead households to act more aggressively on their beliefs, amplifying the consequences of overoptimism.

04be1a0d28:a21f925ecc6a5980.title: Investment and Governance: Through The Lens of Sustainability -- by Jitendra Aswani, Roberto Rigobon
04be1a0d28:a21f925ecc6a5980.summary: Using 3,944 sustainable bond issuances by public firms from 2013 to 2022, we examine the causal effect of sustainable investment on governance adoption. A heteroskedasticity-based identification strategy reveals that a 1% increase in sustainable debt (by total debt) raises the likelihood of sustainable governance adoption by 9.2%. Such adoption improves environmental performance by 16% (structural estimates). These effects are confined to non-financial firms; for financial firms, governance adoption alone is in-sufficient, as sustainable loan borrowers environmental performance does not improve. Firms with stronger environmental performance are less likely to adopt sustainable governance. Results are robust to alternative definitions and extensive specification checks.

04be1a0d28:5868f90932c43e67.title: Last-Mile Delivery and the Future of Aid -- by Erika Deserranno, Andrea Guariso, Nancy Qian
04be1a0d28:5868f90932c43e67.summary: Foreign aid seeks to provide basic services, such as health care and education, to poor and vulnerable populations. Its effectiveness depends on last-mile delivery: whether those services reach the people who need them. This article reviews evidence on two key aspects of last-mile delivery. The first concerns the growing role of non-state providers, especially NGOs, and its implication for state’s capacity to deliver services and coordinate across providers. The second concerns the selection, motivation, and management of frontline workers who provide the services directly to beneficiaries. We argue that decisions about aid allocation and withdrawal should account for the but can quickly erode. need to preserve last-mile delivery capacity, which takes time and resources to build.

04be1a0d28:3f907ace2cfa10a5.title: Irregular Demand: The Anti-Compromise Effect in the Field -- by Nicola Gennaioli, John A. List, Matthias Rodemeier, Gregory K. Sun
04be1a0d28:3f907ace2cfa10a5.summary: Neoclassical demand obeys regularity: adding a good can only draw demand away from existing goods. In a natural field experiment with Lyft covering 7.2 million riders and 47 million choices, we randomize the presence and price of a premium ride. Contrary to regularity, the premium ride raises demand for the cheapest incumbent and for not buying. The effect grows with the premium price and with repeated exposure, and persists in sessions where the premium ride is not displayed. Rational inference and inattention cannot account for these facts. A model in which a surprisingly high price, cued on the app and retrieved from memory, draws attention to prices explains them.

04be1a0d28:1d115b8a596a62b5.title: The Labor Market Impact of Temporary High-Skill Immigration Programs -- by George J. Borjas
04be1a0d28:1d115b8a596a62b5.summary: In 2019, about 1.2 million foreign workers were employed through temporary high-skill programs, including H-1B and OPT. This paper identifies likely temporary workers in the American Community Survey and measures their supply by education and field of degree. Natives in the most exposed skill groups experienced slower earnings growth and a relative decline in full-time year-round work. Many temporary workers stay after their status ends, but surveys cannot identify these stayers. A model of temporary inflows and stayers shows that, under specified conditions, the coefficient from an IV regression of native outcomes on the number of current temporary workers embodies a stayer multiplier, capturing the effects of both those workers and earlier stayers. Multiplying the coefficient by the observed increase in temporary workers recovers the programs’ full effect without data on stayers. The estimates imply that natives with science and engineering degrees earn about 3.5 percent less, and those with master’s degrees in computing or electrical and computer engineering about 16 percent less. Production complementarities raise average wages by about 1.4 percent, offsetting only part of those losses. Absent externalities, the programs mainly redistribute earnings.

04be1a0d28:e5fbdf95126a385b.title: Education and Gender Voting Polarization: The Effect of Compulsory Schooling on Sex-Based Preferences for the Democratic and Republican Parties -- by Philip DeCicca, Harry Krashinsky, Erik T. Nesson
04be1a0d28:e5fbdf95126a385b.summary: One of the most notable developments in U.S. electoral politics over the last 40 years is the increasing divide between men and women voters. While men and women had roughly equivalent levels of support for both the Democratic and Republican parties in 1980, more recent surveys have revealed a roughly 10 to 15-percentage-point gap in preference for the Democratic party among women relative to men. We explain this result by using a variety of econometric strategies to establish a novel connection between compulsory schooling laws (CSLs), educational attainment, and diverging political preferences by sex. First, we show that the timing of this divergence is coincident with recent changes in CSLs, and that this divergence is almost entirely due to changes in sex-related preferences for the Democratic party in states where there exists a much stronger effect of CSLs on average educational attainment -- very little change in sex-related preferences for the Democratic party is present in other states. Furthermore, in states with more-impactful CSLs, changes in CSLs and their associated increased educational attainment explain almost all of the diverging support for political parties and differences in opinion over major policy issues by sex, such as gun control and abortion. Altogether, these new facts present an original explanation that relies upon the effect of education to explain the evolution of gender political preferences in the U.S. over the last 40 years.

04be1a0d28:95196ce38c735e0b.title: An Odd Approximation of Inflation for State Dependent Pricing Models -- by Luca Gagliardone, Mark Gertler, Simone Lenzu, Joris Tielens, Al-Mahdi Ebsim
04be1a0d28:95196ce38c735e0b.summary: We derive an aggregate state-space representation of state-dependent pricing models with random menu costs and strategic complementarities. The representation, derived from first principles, replaces the cross-sectional distribution of price gaps with a finite set of its moments (the first three), while preserving the key economic forces of state-dependent pricing--movements in the frequency of price adjustment and selection. Along the impulse response, inflation is an odd (cubic) polynomial in the average price gap. Embedded in a general equilibrium setting, the model can be solved by perturbation, filtered, and estimated with standard DSGE tools, and it matches well the global solution across shock sizes. Applied to the 2021--22 inflation surge in the United States and the euro area, it shows that much of the variation that linear models would attribute to cost-push shocks is in fact endogenous amplification through the frequency of price changes and selection.

04be1a0d28:25c59f4baac52bd9.title: fereg: Fast High-Dimensional Fixed-Effects Regressions in Stata -- by Johannes F. Schmieder
04be1a0d28:25c59f4baac52bd9.summary: Regressions with many fixed effects are central to applied research, but fitting them to large datasets can be slow. In this article, I present the commands fereg and feppml, which fit linear and Poisson pseudo-maximum-likelihood regressions with high-dimensional fixed effects. Both commands use familiar Stata syntax and pass the computation to a compiled plugin. The plugin chooses among projection, Krylov, and multigrid solvers according to the structure of the fixed effects, checks every result before posting it, and runs on several processor cores. The commands support multiple and interacted fixed effects, group-specific slopes, regression weights, robust and multiway clustered standard errors, saved fixed effects, and prediction. Two simulated examples illustrate their use. In simulated designs with up to ten million observations and default stopping settings, fereg was 6–204 times faster than reghdfe and feppml 11–103 times faster than ppmlhdfe. The commands were also faster than fixest (R) and PyFixest (Python) in all 53 simulated configurations and than the Julia packages FixedEffectModels.jl and GLFixedEffectModels.jl in 52 of 53, with geometric-mean time ratios between 3.0 and 7.7. On administrative data with 1.2 million workers and 117,000 firms, fereg and feppml were at least 3.4 times faster than every other command at every number of cores.

04be1a0d28:0e5d7289195e823e.title: Decoding Success: Phonics-based Instruction and Student Achievement -- by Alex Hollingsworth, Alberto Ortega, Nikolaos Zirogiannis
04be1a0d28:0e5d7289195e823e.summary: Reading is a foundational skill, yet fewer than one in three US fourth graders read at a proficient level. How best to teach reading and improve educational attainment has been an active policy debate for decades. Recently, phonics-based approaches have surged in popularity, even though the largest attempt to put similar methods into classrooms was previously abandoned out of concerns that the program was ineffective. This paper studies Reading First, a nearly $1 billion per year federal program established under No Child Left Behind that promoted phonics-based instruction in K-3 classrooms. Exploiting administrative data from Texas and program eligibility formulas, we estimate effects via difference-in-differences and instrumental variables specifications. We find that eligibility increased third-grade reading test scores by 0.1 standard deviations and that effects persisted through at least the eighth grade. An analysis of digitized exam questions shows that treated students outperformed peers on questions that required basic decoding skills and those with more words, a benefit that also drove improvements in math scores. We follow exposed cohorts into early adulthood, finding that the program increased on-time high school graduation, college enrollment, four-year college completion, and adult earnings at age 25.

04be1a0d28:0dd22e716fe8fb33.title: Economics of Mental Health -- by Janet Currie, N. Meltem Daysal
04be1a0d28:0dd22e716fe8fb33.summary: This chapter provides an overview of the rapidly evolving economics literature on mental health, focusing on research published since 2015. This literature has grown substantially, reflecting the increased recognition of the prevalence and economic costs of mental illness, declining stigma, and the growing availability of data on mental health. In addition to the economic costs of mental illness, the review focuses on four broad classes of determinants of mental health: endowments, economic resources, education, and trauma. We also examine the determinants and effects of mental health treatment. Finally, we discuss how certain features of mental illness, including its episodic and recurrent nature, pose challenges for the canonical health capital model.

04be1a0d28:625737a3552f8ea3.title: The Effects of Years of Health Insurance on the Health of Older Adults -- by Yu Liu, Kevin Callison, Robert Kaestner
04be1a0d28:625737a3552f8ea3.summary: Whether longer exposure to health insurance improves health remains an open empirical question. This study examines the health effects of an additional year of health insurance coverage by exploiting differential changes in coverage pre-to-post implementation of the Affordable Care Act (ACA) for those who were and were not insured prior to the ACA. Using longitudinal data from the Health and Retirement Study (HRS), we instrument for insurance duration using baseline uninsured status interacted with the post-ACA period. We find that the ACA increased insurance coverage by approximately one additional year among previously uninsured respondents relative to those insured at baseline. Instrumental-variable estimates provide no statistically significant evidence of improvements in self-rated health, depressive symptoms, or hypertension over a four-year follow-up period. These findings are robust across alternative specifications. Overall, results provide little evidence that longer insurance coverage translates into measurable short-term health improvements, while leaving open the possibility of modest or longer-term benefits.

04be1a0d28:8e24f860b22b6082.title: Impacts of AI in Higher Education: A Panel Survey of Undergraduates -- by Bruce Sacerdote, Mason Parris-Bacon
04be1a0d28:8e24f860b22b6082.summary: We report findings from the first wave of a survey of undergraduates including separate samples of Dartmouth students, graduating high school seniors, and U.S. college students more broadly. Students report extensive use of AI both for tasks which are likely harmful to learning and tasks which are likely helpful to learning. Students report much higher peer misuse of AI relative to reports of own misuse. Ninety-two percent of students agree or strongly agree that use of AI is harmful to writing. Use of graded out-of-class assignments has become increasingly unfair due to cheating with AI. But students see the value of using AI to answer conceptual questions in real time, create practice quizzes and study guides and to enable meaningful and efficient progress on research projects. Eighty-four percent of Dartmouth respondents report that AI is changing the nature of jobs in their desired (future) field as opposed to eliminating jobs. AI’s perceived value and harms vary widely by academic discipline suggesting that use, rules, and approaches must also vary greatly based on the discipline and context. Students are largely self-taught in AI but have strong demand for incorporating AI effectively in the curriculum.

04be1a0d28:a4cb3d9a6269aaf2.title: The Last Arbitrage? Capital Flows, Development, and Infrastructure as an Asset Class -- by Anusha Chari, Monroe Gamble, Peter Blair Henry
04be1a0d28:a4cb3d9a6269aaf2.summary: Lucas (1990) asked why capital does not flow from rich to poor countries. When poor countries opened their stock markets to foreign investors in the late 1980s, it did: rich-country capital arbitraged away the excess return on emerging-market equity and created a new asset class. Infrastructure may offer the last such arbitrage. The median social return on paved roads in poor countries was 3.7 times the return on U.S. capital at the time of liberalization, but investors capture only the share of social returns that contracts, user fees, and political risk allow, a constraint we call the private foreign hurdle. Confidential IFC data show that its infrastructure equity portfolio outperformed the S&P 500 by 2 percentage points per year, even though only 41 percent of individual investments in the portfolio did so. This suggests that strong risk-adjusted portfolio returns can mask substantial project-specific uncertainty. Despite high social returns, transportation accounted for just 9 IFC infrastructure project investments versus 157 in power and telecommunications. This raises the question of whether private investors can appropriate enough of the social returns on infrastructure to make these investments. Moreover, investors cannot learn from returns they cannot see. Disclosure of historical equity returns is therefore necessary, but not sufficient, to efficiently mobilize more private capital for infrastructure. Because the benefits of disclosure accrue to the market, not to any one firm, multilateral development banks, working with an independent research partner, are best placed to provide it.

04be1a0d28:166120eb92b1cac2.title: The Role of Parental Beliefs and Public Policies in Financing Higher Education: An Experimental Study -- by Francesco Agostinelli, Guglielmo Briscese, Giovanni M. Topa
04be1a0d28:166120eb92b1cac2.summary: Parents who want to financially support their child’s pursuit of higher education must save against assumptions about what college will cost and how it will be funded. This study examines how parental beliefs and future borrowing costs shape college saving decisions. Through a survey experiment with an embedded financial planning tool, we elicit parental beliefs about the future costs of college and their expectations of different funding sources, including financial aid and student loans. We find that nearly all parents want to cover some of the future costs of college, but many may fall short in their savings due to underestimating future expenses and overestimating available financial aid. A corrective information intervention encourages most parents to recalibrate their saving target. However, when a substantial gap between expected and actual costs is combined with a salient high repayment burden for their child, we find a discouragement effect that diminishes both their willingness to save and their aspirations for their child’s educational attainment. We calibrate a model of parental saving with learning about college costs, which reproduces both the absence of an average response to borrowing costs and the shift of children away from college attendance, and use it to price the welfare cost of misperception. Parents with higher financial literacy hold better-calibrated beliefs and respond more to correction. We discuss policy implications for outreach activities to support informed financial planning for college education.

04be1a0d28:dc7cffc28ef7b5d2.title: Aging and Structural Change: Cost Disease in the Care Sector -- by Nick Pretnar, Finn Kydland, Tonya Y. Kydland
04be1a0d28:dc7cffc28ef7b5d2.summary: For most of the service sector, market productivity growth has pulled production out of the home. We show that formal nursing care is an exception because its productivity growth has been negative. A two-sector general equilibrium overlapping generations model with informal care attributes the rise in formal care's relative price to this decline, not demography. Care/non-care complementarity dominates formal/informal complementarity. As formal prices rise, elders substitute non-care consumption for formal care, shifting care onto informal caregivers. Population aging need not slow growth if non-care productivity rises or entering cohorts grow and its effects are offset by declining care needs.

04be1a0d28:209b88246bd3ef4f.title: The Health Effects of Eating Red Meat: A Natural Experiment in Alpha-Gal Syndrome -- by Vishal Patel, Christopher M. Worsham, Michael Liu-Hass, Anupam Jena
04be1a0d28:209b88246bd3ef4f.summary: Observational associations between red meat consumption and cardiometabolic disease are confounded by diet and other health behaviors. Alpha-gal syndrome, a tick-borne allergy to mammalian meat, leads to an abrupt and involuntary cessation of red meat consumption. Using national electronic health records, we compared changes in weight and cardiometabolic health over two years before and after newly detected alpha-gal syndrome with those in patients with other tick-borne diseases, who were also bitten and sought care but whose diagnoses carry no dietary restriction. Relative to this comparison group, diagnosis of alpha-gal syndrome led to a sustained 0.8 kg (95% CI, 0.6 to 1.0) reduction in body weight that increased with the degree of sensitization, as well as small reductions in triglycerides, glycated hemoglobin, glucose, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol. Not eating red meat appears to yield modest but measurable cardiometabolic benefits.

04be1a0d28:1221fa29d932fb83.title: Crime on ICE: Local Police Behavior and Immigration Enforcement in the United States -- by John J. Donohue, Tai Markman, Eric A. Baldwin
04be1a0d28:1221fa29d932fb83.summary: A growing number of local police departments now hold authority to enforce federal immigration law, a role traditionally reserved for federal officers. Despite claims that this authority enhances public safety, empirical evidence remains limited. Using FBI Uniform Crime Report data from 2000–2024, we exploit staggered adoption across U.S. jurisdictions to estimate causal effects on policing. We find that this enforcement authority increases arrests for low-level, discretionary offenses by approximately 7%, with no corresponding decreases in offense rates or serious crime. These results suggest that such agreements realign police priorities toward discretionary enforcement without measurable public safety benefits.

04be1a0d28:733366800fb463d8.title: Federal Eminent Domain and Interstate Energy Infrastructure: Evidence from History -- by Zachary Liscow, Joseph S. Shapiro, Heidi L. Williams
04be1a0d28:733366800fb463d8.summary: We analyze a historical episode to generate evidence on how federal eminent domain authority affected construction of energy transportation infrastructure. The 1947 amendment to the Natural Gas Act gave federally approved interstate natural gas pipelines the power to acquire rights of way by eminent domain when negotiations with landowners failed. We compare construction of interstate gas pipelines with construction of oil pipelines and of within-state gas pipelines, neither of which was directly affected by the reform, using newly digitized historical government records and trade press listings. After 1947, annual additions to interstate gas pipeline mileage rose nearly sixfold while oil pipeline growth held steady, and the gain in interstate mileage was nearly five times the gain for within-state pipelines. Both comparisons suggest that the amendment substantially increased interstate gas pipeline construction. We discuss what this historical evidence implies for current congressional proposals to provide federal eminent domain authority for interstate electricity transmission.

04be1a0d28:cdc1885f3da737f0.title: Crash Injuries and Fatalities in the United States Following Standardization of Automatic Emergency Braking -- by Vishal Patel, Christopher M. Worsham, Michael Liu-Hass, Thomas Tsai, Anupam Jena
04be1a0d28:cdc1885f3da737f0.summary: Whether vehicle safety technologies reduce crash injuries and fatalities is relevant to consumers and regulators, but rigorous real world evidence is limited because drivers who choose optional features differ from those who do not. As a natural experiment, we leveraged the staggered implementation of automatic emergency braking as standard rather than optional equipment on 39 vehicle models between 2017 and 2022. Across the United States, the percentage of crash injuries from rear-end collisions caused by the vehicle fell from 13.9% to 8.0% at the first standard model year, and the percentage of crash fatalities fell from 6.0% to 4.7%. Neither fell in models that never standardized the technology, and crash types it was not designed to prevent were unaffected. Automatic emergency braking reduces crash injuries and fatalities.

04be1a0d28:63450647a1e71c00.title: Childhood Learning and Adult Earnings in Four LMIC Cohorts -- by Jishnu Das, Yash Dhuldhoya, Marta Favara, Amory Gethin, Alan Sánchez, Abhijeet Singh
04be1a0d28:63450647a1e71c00.summary: Researchers and policymakers in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) have customarily relied on indirect evidence to justify investments in learning, either by linking test scores to economic growth or by connecting adult cognitive assessments to earnings. This reliance on indirect evidence largely stems from the scarcity of longitudinal data linking school-age learning to adult earnings. We address this gap by using data from Ethiopia, India, Pakistan, and Peru to estimate associations between foundational learning (FL), measured by test scores around age 12, and human capital and earnings in young adulthood. In Peru, India, and Pakistan, a one-standard-deviation increase in FL is associated with an 8-13 log point increase in adult earnings. Childhood scores also predict 1.1-1.5 additional years of schooling and 9.3-13.5 percentage points higher college or vocational attendance, as well as higher skills in adulthood. Interestingly, a linear-projection decomposition indicates that measured schooling and adult test scores explain between 18% (Peru) to 50-56% (India and Pakistan) of the FL-earnings gradient, suggesting that FL may raise earnings over and above the association with schooling and adult scores. Finally, FL can account for about 5-12 percent of the earnings gap between young Ethiopians and Indians in our sample, a number that could rise to 33 percent as returns to learning grow over the life cycle. We interpret these descriptive findings in light of recent causal evidence on the learning-to-earnings pipeline and discuss the implications for policy investments in FL.

04be1a0d28:dc36fc43da8feefd.title: Learn to Earn: The Long-Term Effects of Foundational Learning -- by Tahir Andrabi, Natalie Bau, Jishnu Das, Asim Ijaz Khwaja, Catherine Michaud-Leclerc
04be1a0d28:dc36fc43da8feefd.summary: Tracking Pakistani students over 15 years, we use two identification strategies to provide the first causal evidence linking learning in primary school to adult outcomes in a low-income country. Exposure to a school with higher test score value-added increases educational attainment and earnings 15 years later. A randomized information intervention that led to learning gains at the village level generated similar effects. Lifetime earnings gains across all students attending a 1sd better school total US$175,000, and for the information intervention, the marginal value of public funds is infinity for men. There is a strong economic case for investing in learning.

04be1a0d28:bf5dcaa75512ba06.title: A Blessing in Disguise: The Long-Term Effects of Childhood Exposure to the Boll Weevil on Old-Age Male Longevity -- by Hamid Noghanibehambari, Jason Fletcher
04be1a0d28:bf5dcaa75512ba06.summary: The infamous agricultural pest, the boll weevil, spread across southern US counties between 1892 and 1920. It had devastating impacts on cotton production, a highly child-labor-intensive crop. This study examines how the arrival of the boll weevil and the subsequent reductions in child labor affect later-life mortality outcomes. Using Social Security Administration death records linked with the 1940 census, we document that the staggered spread of the boll weevil improved the longevity of exposed male children. Full exposure to the boll weevil is associated with an intent-to-treat effect of 1-3 months of higher longevity. We show that the estimated effects are robust across a wide array of specifications, are not driven by sociodemographic and socioeconomic compositional change in the final sample, and are not associated with pre-existing trends in the outcome. Further, we find larger impacts among Blacks, children of lower educated mothers, whose fathers work in the farming industry, and those born in high cotton intensity counties. Moreover, the effects appear to be substantially larger among children in states with less restrictive child labor policies, implying the role of these policies in reducing the adverse effects of child labor in the absence of the boll weevil in cotton production counties. Affected children are more likely to migrate, and their destination counties are more likely to be urban and have higher socioeconomic scores. The 1940 census suggests that the exposed children attain higher levels of education and have higher socioeconomic scores. We discuss the policy implications of these results in relation to child labor and school attendance policies in developing countries.

04be1a0d28:8a9056cdf6b18aca.title: Clouds of Credit: Mapping the Financial Web Behind AI Compute -- by Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, Zijin Su
04be1a0d28:8a9056cdf6b18aca.summary: We map the financial network supporting the AI buildout. Substantial equity cushions protect creditors against large obligations outstanding in mid-2026, but concentrated exposures and interconnected claims create weak links. Our calibrated model supports a large compute expansion in the coming years. The equilibrium investment exceeds the social optimum because firms do not internalize their effects on competitors' revenues. Debt finances nearly 60% of the expansion, increasing leverage, while non-recourse borrowing leaves project lenders exposed despite equity buffers. In the low-productivity state, losses reach $16.8 trillion across shareholders and creditors, with 40% loss-given-default on debt. Suppressing contractual payment spillovers among the key firms reduces private losses by approximately 30%, revealing substantial network propagation.

04be1a0d28:8f503f559bca7744.title: Preconception Medicaid and Maternal and Infant Health: Evidence from Linked Administrative Data -- by Genna Campain, Sarah Miller, Petra Persson, Maya Rossin-Slater, Laura Wherry, Katlyn N. King
04be1a0d28:8f503f559bca7744.summary: Despite pregnancy-focused public insurance coverage in the U.S., low-income mothers and infants face persistent health disadvantages. Using linked birth, tax, and enrollment data, we examine the effects of preconception coverage from California's 2014 Medicaid expansion, comparing changes in outcomes for first-time mothers just below and above the income eligibility threshold. Expansion increased preconception Medicaid enrollment by 3.4 months (+23 percentage points in 12-month continuous coverage), first-month pregnancy enrollment by 24 percentage points, and adequate prenatal care and STI screening. Yet we find no improvements in maternal or infant health, suggesting preconception coverage alone cannot close health disparities.

04be1a0d28:1fa0d6631cf56aa6.title: The Recent and Impending Evolution of US Federal Support for State and Local Governments -- by Jeffrey Clemens, Anwita Mahajan
04be1a0d28:1fa0d6631cf56aa6.summary: In the US federal system, the federal government provides substantial fiscal support to state and local governments. In this paper, we describe how the landscape of intergovernmental grants, which exceeded $1.2 trillion in 2025, evolved during and in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic. We provide short-run evidence on how state and local government budgets have adapted as pandemic-era fiscal supports wound down. We further emphasize the pressures state and local budgets will face as several provisions of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), which are intended to restrain intergovernmental grants, go into effect over the coming years.

04be1a0d28:51c63d58005b4b02.title: Will AI Growth Reach the Developing World? -- by Daniel Björkegren, David Lagakos, Mitchell VanVuren
04be1a0d28:51c63d58005b4b02.summary: This paper explores how economic growth driven by AI will impact the developing world. Our analysis is based on a growth model of a developed and developing economy where AI services are traded on the world market, and may substitute for or complement different labor inputs in production. Preferences allow for the possibility that demand for services provided by AI has an upper bound. The model predicts that developing countries may not benefit as much from AI-driven growth. First, they may lack complementary skills needed to fully utilize AI domestically. Second, they may be priced out of world markets due to their relatively lower productivity. We use our model to simulate how growth and welfare are affected by making workers more complementary to AI, subsidizing compute, speeding technology diffusion, and providing cash transfers. Numerical simulations of the model suggest that the potential for developing countries to be left behind – or having some workers lose in absolute terms – is substantial enough that researchers should study the impacts of AI on developing countries in real time.

04be1a0d28:5469cfc06c072f69.title: How Does Capital Flow To Poor Countries? Evidence from Venture Capital and Private Equity -- by Emanuele Colonnelli, Marcio Cruz, Josh Lerner, Mariana Pereira-Lopez, Yuanchang Wei
04be1a0d28:5469cfc06c072f69.summary: Why does so little private capital flow to poor countries? We study how venture capital and private equity investors evaluate firms across countries, using an experimental survey of 1,485 investors in 108 countries who are incentivized to evaluate hypothetical investment opportunities with randomized firm characteristics, locations, and investment terms. Investors respond similarly to firm fundamentals, but otherwise comparable firms attract substantially less interest in poorer countries. This poor-country penalty is much smaller among investors specialized in emerging markets. Detailed survey data show that emerging market and developed market investors have largely similar investment practices, but differ in how they obtain country information, assess and manage country risks, and exit investments. Investors reporting active country-risk management apply smaller country penalties, even after accounting for market focus. Our findings suggest that investors' specialization and investment practices shape how country risk affects investment: the same firm can face drastically different financing prospects depending on where it is located and which investors evaluate it.

04be1a0d28:5cfa7b8214c8ee25.title: Target What? The Foundations of Poverty Targeting -- by Rema Hanna, Emily Breza, Benjamin A. Olken, Abhijit Banerjee, Arun G. Chandrasekhar, Gideon Moore
04be1a0d28:5cfa7b8214c8ee25.summary: Most government transfer programs aim to target the poor. Doing so implicitly assumes that the lowest-consumption households have the highest marginal social valuation, i.e., have the highest social welfare gain from an additional dollar. But this need not be the case. In 600 Indonesian villages, we ask over 5,500 villagers to rank other villagers on how well off they are and how much a modest cash transfer would help them, and compare these rankings to consumption and self-assessed welfare. Targeting consumption misses 77% of households with the highest marginal social valuation. Targeting self-assessed welfare misses 57%. Even targeting those the community ranks worst off in levels, not margins, misses 25%. Divergences between different notions of neediness are statistically predictable. In a randomized controlled trial, proxy means tests best target consumption, self-targeting ordeals capture self-assessed welfare levels, and community targeting comes closest to marginal social valuation. Targeting strategies inescapably embed normative stances.

04be1a0d28:ee90318fba1ffca5.title: Unconventional Monetary Policy and Deposit Retention -- by Philip Strahan, Tuo Yang
04be1a0d28:ee90318fba1ffca5.summary: The two dimensions of unconventional monetary policy — holding the short rate at the zero-lower bound (ZLB) and quantitative easing (QE) — shifted deposit composition toward more interest-sensitive customers. The ZLB drew these customers by creating rate compression, which limited the benefit of searching for high-yielding liquidity sources. QE also drew rate-sensitive, large depositors from the Federal Reserve’s purchases of bonds from non-banks. Once policy normalized, flow sensitivity and the deposit beta both increased with exposure to QE and the ZLB. We conclude that unconventional monetary policy made deposit retention costlier and riskier for banks.

04be1a0d28:4a6c094b462ab89d.title: Debiasing Law Enforcement Officers: Evidence from an Expressive Arts Intervention in India -- by Sofia Amaral, Girija Borker, Nishith Prakash, María Micaela Sviatschi
04be1a0d28:4a6c094b462ab89d.summary: Frontline state agents exercise substantial discretion over citizens’ access to public services, yet little is known about whether the attitudes and beliefs shaping this discretion can be changed among incumbent bureaucrats. Partnering with the Bihar Police - one of India’s largest states that operates under comparatively severe policing capacity constraints, we conduct a cluster randomized controlled trial across 417 police stations and roughly 2,500 active duty senior field police officers to evaluate a three-day expressive arts intervention, grounded in the Theatre of the Oppressed, designed to change police responses to gender-based violence (GBV). Approximately 7 months after baseline, treated officers exhibit more favorable attitudes toward GBV, greater empathy, and stronger legal knowledge. These changes translate into observed policing behavior: in standardized victim audits conducted one year later, officers in treated stations are 15 percentage points less likely to blame victims, dismiss fewer complaints, and provide more referrals, while administrative records show a 41 percent reduction in registration delays and, over a longer horizon, increased GBV reporting by citizens. Exploiting variation generated by officer transfers, we find suggestive evidence that these effects persist when treated officers relocate and diffuse to untreated officers working alongside treated colleagues. The effects also extend to the workplace: junior female officers working with treated senior officers report lower harassment and anxiety. These findings show that the attitudes shaping bureaucratic discretion are malleable and that changing how incumbent state agents exercise authority can improve both citizen-facing service delivery and the broader workplace environment.

04be1a0d28:15d97949f4ab4b94.title: TaskNet: Building Occupational Task Inventories from Worker Interviews at Scale -- by Jennifer Wang, Andreas Haupt, Isaac Robinson, Phil Lewis, Erik Brynjolfsson, Diyi Yang
04be1a0d28:15d97949f4ab4b94.summary: Understanding how AI is reshaping work requires an accurate account of the tasks workers perform. Workers are often the first to see how their jobs are changing, as new responsibilities and tools often appear in everyday work before these changes reach formal descriptions. Interviews with workers can help capture these emerging changes in job tasks. Yet existing methods support standardized ratings across workers, while open-ended conversations with workers remain costly to collect and synthesize at scale. We introduce the Stanford Task Network (TaskNet), an occupational taxonomy grounded directly in workers’ accounts of their everyday work. To construct TaskNet, we develop a mixed-initiative system that induces task inventories directly from workers. The system conducts interviews, standardizes reports into individual task lists, and aggregates these lists into occupational task inventories. Applied to six occupations spanning a range of education requirements and AI exposure, our system interviews 132 workers and produces 202 task statements from 2726 reports, all of which were accepted by O*NET Center analysts, compared to roughly 65%of workers’ write-in task suggestions collected through the current O*NET data collection process, a major alternative source for emerging tasks. Every statement is validated by 318 incumbents in 7923 ratings of relevance and importance. Relative to the task data from the O*NET 31.0 database for the sampled occupations, TaskNet covers 75% of the 118 published O*NET tasks and adds 79 tasks with no O*NET counterpart and 58 that refine existing statements. It covers 89% of tasks reported by held-out workers, compared with 79% for O*NET, and a larger share of the activities described in employer job postings (72.5% vs. 70.2%). Downstream, TaskNet changes AI exposure estimates in both directions, raising them for Software Developers and Lawyers, two occupations where AI’s effects are widely debated. Because such estimates guide…

04be1a0d28:1bc3a0ef5cb79204.title: The Hidden Sharpe Ratio -- by Mikhail Chernov, Bryan T. Kelly, Semyon Malamud, Johannes Schwab
04be1a0d28:1bc3a0ef5cb79204.summary: We estimate the maximal Sharpe ratio in large cross-sections of assets directly, without constructing the efficient portfolio. Covariance estimation in this setting requires regularization, which suppresses the contribution of small-eigenvalue directions. Our estimator progressively recovers this contribution, yielding tight upper and lower bounds with asymptotic confidence intervals. We further show that ridge-regularized Markowitz portfolios, the construction underlying many existing high-Sharpe benchmarks, deliver out-of-sample Sharpe ratios that fall short of the true maximum by an explicit, non-vanishing multiplicative factor. Applied to U.S. equities, the method delivers an estimated maximal annualized Sharpe ratio of approximately 7.4, or 5.0 once micro-cap stocks are excluded, substantially exceeding existing portfolio-based benchmarks of 1.0–4.0. Adding corporate bonds raises the maximum, though not by a statistically significant margin. Nonlinear portfolio weights dominate linear ones, and characteristics introduced after 2004 contribute little additional Sharpe ratio.

04be1a0d28:ee9518e448c2ded4.title: Clearing the Fog: Price Transparency, Market Churn, and Consumer Welfare in Short-Term Rentals -- by Ginger Zhe Jin, Liad Wagman, Jingyi Xing
04be1a0d28:ee9518e448c2ded4.summary: We study California's short-term lodging price transparency law (AB 537), which from July 1, 2024 required Airbnb and other providers to advertise fee-inclusive prices. Using Coarsened Exact Matching to compare Airbnb listings in San Diego and San Francisco with those in Seattle and Chicago, we find that all-in pricing made guests more price-sensitive relative to control cities; yet, contrary to the standard prediction that transparency lowers prices, average daily rates rose by 4.8 percent. We also observe significant market churn: relative to control cities, treated cities saw more exits and entries, listings reliant on cleaning-fee revenue disproportionately exited, higher-quality listings were more likely to stay, and entrants offered lower fees and lower quality than incumbents. A discrete-choice welfare analysis shows that the law removed a sizable “welfare illusion” created by obscured fees and, largely through market churn, raised realized consumer surplus. The net gains, after accounting for price increases, were positive on average but unevenly distributed across treated ZIP codes.

04be1a0d28:86aabf619c4f23ef.title: Financial Advisors and Retirees' Risk-taking -- by Allison T. Cole, Maarten Meeuwis, Alessandro Previtero, Noah Stoffman
04be1a0d28:86aabf619c4f23ef.summary: Advised retirees keep about two-thirds of their portfolios in equities well into old age—30 to 40 percentage points more than non-advised retirees, target-date funds, or common rules of thumb. These allocations reflect active choices rather than inertia, and they adjust gradually toward a new advisor’s investment style following advisor switches. Equity shares rise with relationship tenure, and advisor influence is strongest among clients with low financial knowledge or risk tolerance, consistent with trust facilitating risk-taking. Given retirees’ modest financial wealth relative to their safe pension income, we rationalize these portfolios in a standard life-cycle model with moderate risk aversion. Modeling advisors as “money doctors” who correct clients’ pessimistic beliefs about the equity premium, we find that, relative to a no-advice counterfactual, the welfare gains from higher risk-taking are of the same order of magnitude as the cost of advice.

04be1a0d28:938fa39fa6610cdb.title: Doing Better at Doing Good: Lessons from a Bayesian Meta-Analysis After 20 Years of Poverty Graduation Programs -- by Samantha Carter, Edward Jee, Dean Karlan, Patrick Premand
04be1a0d28:938fa39fa6610cdb.summary: Multifaceted poverty Graduation programs that aim to increase income generating activities for low-income households are being rapidly adopted and scaled by nonprofit organizations and governments. This paper conducts a Bayesian hierarchical meta-analysis of 49 studies (encompassing 81 treatment variations) on poverty Graduation programs, defined as containing at least three of five components: consumption support, savings facilitation, skills training, coaching, and a lumpsum transfer. The analysis finds large gains across economic and psychosocial outcomes: monthly consumption rises by 38 USD PPP (11 percent), income by 28 USD PPP (15 percent), alongside improvements in savings, assets, food security, mental health, and women’s empowerment. Beyond these average treatment effects, three results stand out. First, programs with large transfers (at least 400 USD PPP) have larger treatment effects but are not more cost-effective. Second, more expensive programs generate larger treatment effects, but the improvements are not commensurate with the cost increases; thus, lower cost programs tend to be more cost-effective. Third, programs implemented from 2016 onward perform considerably better than those implemented prior to 2016: benefit-cost ratios from 2016 onward are 5.39, compared to 2.89 through 2015. Neither changes in cost nor in high-level design (components) explain this upward trend. Considering other heavily studied interventions, the results show a similar upward trend for treatment effects on behavior change from financial education but not for unconditional cash transfers. The paper hypothesizes a mechanism of continuous sector-community learning and improved implementation quality.

04be1a0d28:0230fbc2e4a965c5.title: Policy Deterrence: Strategic Investment in U.S. Broadband -- by Karam Kang, Mo Xiao
04be1a0d28:0230fbc2e4a965c5.summary: Can firms influence policy through investment? Using 2010--2019 U.S. broadband deployment and state policy data, we find that large internet service providers expand capacity more in electorally competitive counties. Greater large-provider capacity in swing counties is associated with fewer subsequent entry- and investment-facilitating policies, especially rights-of-way accommodations that reduce deployment barriers faced by smaller providers. To interpret these patterns, we develop a model in which a large firm's capacity can reduce the policymaker's gain from intervention. In the model, policy deterrence raises the large firm's market share and can reduce total deployment.

04be1a0d28:39e15131b9607607.title: Peer Influence in College Applications -- by Ana M. Gazmuri, Elena Prager
04be1a0d28:39e15131b9607607.summary: This paper studies how exposure to peers affects college application behavior. We use neighbors who attend different high schools to mitigate concerns about common shocks. Using granular classroom-level data, we find that exposure to peers who have applied to a program increases application rates. Consistent with an information mechanism, there is no additional effect of peers who are admitted. In counterfactuals, the effect is large enough to close urban-rural gaps and gender gaps in applications to selective college programs. We make the (generally NP-hard) application portfolio choice problem tractable using a setting where admission probabilities are observable and conditionally independent.

04be1a0d28:98b4333a07b42644.title: The Impact of Climate Change on Fisheries -- by Fabio Cevenini, Christopher Costello, Carlo Fezzi
04be1a0d28:98b4333a07b42644.summary: This paper provides the first causal estimate of the effect of ocean temperature variations on fishing revenue. We develop a simple theoretical model underpinning an empirical specification estimated on 2.5 million spatially explicit observations of fishing revenue from all European vessels for 2013–2022. The identification strategy leverages a novel metric, Marine Degree Days, which quantifies species-specific temperature exposure relative to biologically established thermal tolerance intervals. Within this framework we address key identification challenges, including spatial selection and ecological interdependencies across species. We find that deviations from species’ thermal preferences lead to significant losses in fishing revenue, with heat exposure causing the most pronounced impacts. These effects are mediated by species’ vertical mobility and ecological characteristics. Projections across different climate scenarios point to widespread revenue declines by 2100, reaching €560 million annual losses in the warmest scenario, though impacts are highly spatially heterogeneous. Lower-income, equatorial areas are expected to suffer the most, while some colder regions experience gains.

04be1a0d28:c9b3c196072683cb.title: When Food Stamps Became Free: Impacts and Implications of Removing the Purchase Requirement -- by Amy Finkelstein, Matthew J. Notowidigdo, Charlie Rafkin
04be1a0d28:c9b3c196072683cb.summary: We analyze the food stamp program both as a potential investment in children’s health capital and as a redistributive tool by studying the 1979 reform that made food stamps free. We leverage geographic variation in exposure to the reform, which raised the program’s food subsidy from 65% to 100%. This raised enrollment by 1.85 percentage points (standard error = 0.15), or about 25%, with new enrollees substantially poorer than existing participants. From an investment perspective, we do not find evidence of improvement in infant health, and 95% confidence intervals rule out gains in birth weight from enrolling in food stamps exceeding 2%. From a redistribution perspective, the enrollment response implies that the average recipient of free food stamps acts as if they value them at 59 cents per dollar, with nonparametric bounds of 42–77 cents. Despite this substantial dissipation in transfer value relative to a frictionless cash transfer, under standard redistributive preferences the free food stamp program increases social welfare because of its targeting to very low-income households. The move to free stamps from a partially subsidized program improved targeting on social value but worsened targeting on private value.

04be1a0d28:f3157c2535879082.title: Beyond Overdose Prevention: Naloxone Coprescription Laws and the Path to Treatment -- by Shin-Yi Chou, Jiarun Li, Bingjin Xue
04be1a0d28:f3157c2535879082.summary: Over one-third of U.S. states have enacted naloxone coprescription laws, requiring physicians to prescribe or offer naloxone alongside high-risk opioids. Using Medicare Part D data, the Treatment Episode Data Set, and a difference-in-differences design, we study how these laws affect naloxone access, broader prescription behavior, and treatment engagement. Coprescription laws increased naloxone prescribing by 275%, with effects twice as large in states requiring prescriptions as in those requiring only offers. We find no evidence of increased opioid or benzodiazepine prescribing, countering moral hazard concerns that broader naloxone access might encourage riskier opioid use. Instead, we document significant increases in prescribing of medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD) and gains in opioid use disorder treatment admissions, primarily in deliberate treatment-seeking settings. These results suggest that coprescription laws may have broader benefits beyond overdose prevention.

04be1a0d28:89865f619d9a4dda.title: Sorting by Participation: A Field Experiment in a Stem-cell Registry -- by Michael Haylock, Patrick Kampkötter, Mario Macis, Susanne Seitz, Robert Slonim, Daniel Wiesen
04be1a0d28:89865f619d9a4dda.summary: Unavailability of stem-cell donors at the confirmatory typing (CT) stage, an operational milestone in the stem-cell donation process, reduces the effective supply of life-saving transplants for blood cancer patients worldwide. Although (potential) donors register voluntarily, requests may come much later, when circumstances and commitment have changed; keeping registered donors engaged and identifying who will follow through are therefore central managerial questions for registries. In a field experiment with a leading stem-cell registry, we randomize the framing of routine invitations to an engagement initiative. Relative to a business-as-usual letter, our experimental letters present the registry’s requests more saliently; two of them add identity framings inviting donors to join a “quickly available” or a “highly committed” donor team. The salience and identity framings significantly reduce initiative participation compared to the business-as-usual rate, yet intention-to-treat analyses show no detectable effect on average CT availability. Our central finding is that participation sorts donors by reliability: participants are unavailable in 12% of cases, versus 30% of non-participants. From a managerial perspective, opting in works as a reliability flag. Prioritizing participants in our experimental arms implies a relative increase of up to 7.5% more one-year survivors compared to not using this flag. Gains from flagging are likely to be larger for registries with lower availability.

04be1a0d28:3ddb126d1bcdc559.title: (In)Credible Development RCTs: False Discoveries, Low Power, and a Solution -- by Qingyuan Chai, Kevin Lang, Liang Zhong
04be1a0d28:3ddb126d1bcdc559.summary: We study the statistical credibility of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in development economics and the optimal allocation of resources to replication. Using 745 principal-hypothesis tests from 190 articles in leading economics journals, we find that actual t-statistics peak well below the theoretical benchmark of 2.8 expected under 80 percent power, though above values associated with p-hacking. This suggests many RCTs are underpowered. Estimating an empirical Bayes mixture model that accounts for selective publication, we find that approximately 30 percent of published rejections are false discoveries, with average directional power at only 40 percent. At conventional significance thresholds, the posterior probability of a false discovery reaches 66 percent. Doubling original sample sizes lowers the average false discovery rate by five percentage points, whereas tightening the significance threshold to 0.005 yields a larger reduction at the cost of total discoveries. Finally, we characterize a funder’s optimal replication policy under a fixed budget and an evidence standard. Under standard regularity conditions, replications concentrate in an intermediate interval of original test statistics, and the optimal replication sample size is single-peaked in the original t-statistic. Illustrative calibrations show that successful replications reduce aggregate false discovery rates to 1.8–7.8 percent, depending on the evidence standard.

04be1a0d28:2052393b6c6bd999.title: When More Prenatal Care Looks Like Less: Selection, Information and Maternal and Infant Health -- by Chien-Tzu Cheng, Shin-Yi Chou, Hsien-Ming Lien
04be1a0d28:2052393b6c6bd999.summary: We use Taiwan's 2003 SARS epidemic as a natural experiment, instrumenting prenatal care with gestational exposure to SARS-induced fear that reduced visits by over 20 percent. Adequate prenatal care reduces preventable maternal complications by 3.4 percentage points (26 percent), with no effect on infant outcomes. OLS estimates are perversely signed for maternal complications but overstate benefits for infant outcomes, consistent with competing patient- and provider-driven selection. Mechanism evidence points to prenatal care as a longitudinal information system: repeated contact facilitates detection of evolving risks and generates clinical information that informs delivery decisions, including delivery-mode routing and subsequent management at delivery.

04be1a0d28:7fe9fe310dfca511.title: Vigilance, Risk Vulnerability, and the Precautionary Augment -- by Miles S. Kimball, Vincent A. Mastantuno
04be1a0d28:7fe9fe310dfca511.summary: Risk raises the expected marginal utility of a prudent agent. We define this proportional change as the precautionary augment, which measures risk-induced changes in the marginal value of saving, the Lucas Tree risk-free rate, and asset prices in a derivative-saturated market where market-state securities provide incomplete coverage against idiosyncratic risk. One agent is more vigilant than another if their precautionary augment is larger for all unfair risks. We derive and compare conditions for greater vigilance, showing how to implement the Diffidence Theorem geometrically. Because risk vulnerability is equivalent to decreasing vigilance, classic results about risk vulnerability emerge as corollaries.

04be1a0d28:f03f66b98a78e90e.title: Knowledge Without Taxation? Experimental Evidence from a Tax Education Program -- by Anders Jensen, Nikhil Kumar, Konstantin Poensgen
04be1a0d28:f03f66b98a78e90e.summary: A property tax experiment in Ghana randomly provides tax education to property owners and frontline officials. The intervention raises tax knowledge, which spreads through social networks to untreated neighbors, but does not increase tax payments. Educated taxpayers and officials become more engaged in their interactions without developing more collaborative relationships. Taxpayers revise downward their beliefs about enforcement capacity and become more aware of legal ways to reduce their tax burden. Knowledge is a double-edged sword: it can stimulate citizens to engage with the tax system while exposing the state's limited capacity to enforce it.

04be1a0d28:06019537d7f4b1c9.title: AI as Shared Business Infrastructure: Firm Growth and the Distribution of Gains -- by Panle Jia Barwick, Lu Fang, Jinhan Liu, Huilan Xu, Zhe Yuan
04be1a0d28:06019537d7f4b1c9.summary: Generative AI improves performance on individual tasks, but whether those gains translate into firm growth, and for which firms, remains an open question.
