We study a leading Chinese e-commerce platform that in 2024 embedded a generative AI system in the operating software firms use to run their businesses, drawing on centrally developed models and platform-wide data to deliver ready-to-use applications to every firm. Complete records of each firm’s AI use, linked to its monthly operations and sales, let us trace adoption through changes in business capabilities, such as reaching customers and introducing new products, to sales growth. Using a matched difference-in-differences design and focusing on firms with annual sales below RMB 5 million, we find that adoption raises monthly sales by 51.6%, primarily through a 47.0% increase in the number of orders; instrumental-variable estimates confirm these results. Adopters reach more customers, update their product lines faster, and deliver better product and service quality, with the largest proportional gains for the smallest firms. Two mechanisms help explain the results. First, AI lowers the cost of routine work: adopters produce more product content and change listings more often while spending less staff time per order, and the gains are largest for firms that faced the highest costs relative to sales before adoption. Second, AI reduces information frictions: adopters post richer product information, and the gains are largest in markets where demand is hard to predict and matching quality is poor, especially for small firms. At the market level, product categories with greater pre-existing information frictions see more sales by existing firms, more entry, and more new products. AI expands markets rather than merely shifting sales from non-adopters to adopters.

04be1a0d28:a389899c8fa4f6dc.title: The Main Monetary Policy Shock -- by Christoph Boehm, Husang Kim, T. Niklas Kroner
04be1a0d28:a389899c8fa4f6dc.summary: We propose a novel procedure to identify a main monetary policy (MMP) shock as the linear combination of monetary policy surprises that best explains macroeconomic fluctuations. Implemented with two standard high-frequency yield-curve surprises and the Boehm and Kroner (2024) non-yield shock, the MMP shock explains nontrivial business-cycle variation over the last 30 years, in contrast with prior findings. Moreover, the MMP shock differs markedly from a textbook monetary policy shock: a contractionary shock leaves interest rates mostly unchanged but persistently lowers headline prices and appreciates the dollar, while temporarily tightening financial conditions and depressing industrial production.

04be1a0d28:854f80d57632c4c0.title: Policy Evaluation Beyond Significance Testing: Evidence from Chicago's ShotSpotter Contract -- by Terence Chau, Philip J. Cook, Javier Lopez, Jens Ludwig, Alejandro Roemer, Adam K. Soliman
04be1a0d28:854f80d57632c4c0.summary: Program impact estimates that are not statistically significant are often treated as providing little guidance for policy choice, even when economically important effects remain plausible. In such cases, the decision-relevant task is not simply to test whether the effect differs from zero, but to estimate the probability distribution of programmatic effects. The importance of going beyond hypothesis testing is especially clear when evaluations are underpowered relative to the effect needed for benefits to exceed costs. We illustrate this point using Chicago’s contract for ShotSpotter, an acoustical gunshot detection system that reduces police response times and may therefore have improved survival among shooting victims. Using a geographic RD design, we estimate that ShotSpotter reduced the shooting fatality rate by 2.5 percentage points, equivalent to roughly 49 fewer deaths per year. Although the estimate is not statistically significant, its implied benefit far exceeds the cost of the service. To have enough statistical power under the hypothesis testing approach to detect an effect of this size would require 87 years’ worth of Chicago shooting data. We instead implement a decision-relevant perspective using Bayesian analysis, treating the life-saving effect as a random variable. We find positive expected net benefits, with posterior probabilities that benefits exceed costs ranging from 70% under a flat prior and a $0.5 million value of statistical life to 99.6% under a no-harm prior and a $13.6 million value. The results illustrate how reliance on statistical significance can discard decision-relevant evidence when economically meaningful effects are difficult to detect precisely.

04be1a0d28:31cf5bdc4622b8cb.title: Can Home Visits Re-Engage Chronically Absent Students? Evidence from the LEAP Program -- by Eric Brunner, Shangyue Jiang, Stephen Ross
04be1a0d28:31cf5bdc4622b8cb.summary: Beginning in the summer of 2021, the state of Connecticut launched the Learner Engagement and Attendance Program (LEAP) where home visits by school personnel were conducted with students identified as chronically absent from Connecticut’s 15 most disadvantaged school districts. Home visits were designed to connect students and their families directly with teachers to foster strong connections. We use student-level data from 2021–22 through 2023-24 to estimate event studies of the effect of LEAP on student attendance, chronic absenteeism, disciplinary incidents, and student achievement. Utilizing models that address selection into treatment timing over student observable and unobservable attributes, we find that students who received the LEAP intervention experienced approximately a 4 to 5 percentage point increase in attendance rates, a 13 to 15 percentage point decline in chronic absenteeism, and a 3 to 5 percentage point decline in the number of disciplinary incidents. Notably, initial event studies indicated increasing treatment effects over time, but after correcting for selection on unobservables treatment effects appeared constant over time. These effects were broad based, with similar impacts by gender, race and ethnicity, and free or reduced-price lunch status. These attendance and discipline results provide suggest that the LEAP intervention increased student noncognitive skills.

04be1a0d28:506d5c2adf83e7ec.title: Unraveling the Cobweb of Global Imbalances: Drivers, Vulnerabilities and Adjustment Scenarios -- by Stefan Avdjiev, Kristin Forbes, Tsvetelina Nenova, Marjorie Santos
04be1a0d28:506d5c2adf83e7ec.summary: This paper analyses the evolution and drivers of the stock of global imbalances in order to assess associated vulnerabilities and potential adjustment scenarios. These imbalances have recently increased sharply, with a deterioration in the US net international investment position (NIIP) mirrored by NIIP improvements in most other major economies. We decompose these NIIP changes into their proximate drivers for a sample of 28 economies and find that financial factors (including valuation changes and investment income flows) are the primary drivers of global imbalances at both short and long horizons, while trade also plays a significant role (especially at long horizons). Valuation gains on international investment positions have supported economic growth in many countries since 2010, while also increasing their vulnerability to financial market adjustments. To assess the implications and potential risks, we simulate the spillovers through this cobweb of global imbalances from: (i) a sharp dollar depreciation, (ii) a repricing of equity markets, (iii) higher interest rates, and (iv) a halving of trade imbalances. These scenarios highlight the large international spillovers that would be associated with any reduction in global imbalances, the heterogeneous impact of various rebalancing mechanisms on individual countries and the limits of popular proposals for reducing these imbalances. The persistence of global imbalances underscores the importance of building resilience to the large spillovers that can occur through this cobweb of international exposures.

04be1a0d28:ccdd798fe0527c95.title: Affirmative Action, Faculty Productivity and Caste Interactions: Evidence from Engineering Colleges in India -- by Robert W. Fairlie, Saurabh Khanna, Prashant Loyalka, Gagandeep S. Sachdeva
04be1a0d28:ccdd798fe0527c95.summary: Affirmative action programs are often criticized because of concerns that they result in lower worker productivity and efficiency losses. We study the relative productivity of workers benefiting from an aggressive affirmative action policy in a setting where hiring constraints are mandated upon employers and are typically likely to bind. In India, colleges are required to reserve approximately 50 percent of faculty hires for individuals from disadvantaged caste and social class groups. We collect and analyze data from a nationally representative sample of 50 engineering and technology colleges in India, some of which randomly assign students to classrooms. We find that reservation category faculty have lower levels of education, lower professorial ranks and fewer years of experience in academia than general category faculty who are not hired through reservations. Yet, even with lower qualifications, we do not detect meaningful differences in instructional quality between reservation category faculty and general category faculty across a wide range of measures that include course grades, follow-on course grades, standardized test scores, dropout, attendance, graduate school plans, and graduation. In fact, we find that, at least for immediate effects on course grades, students taught by reservation category faculty perform slightly better than students taught by general category faculty. We also estimate “teacher-like-me” effects of reservation category faculty on the relative course performance and longer-term outcomes of reservation category students and cannot reject the hypothesis of null effects. Furthermore, even in the face of potential discrimination and resentment against faculty hiring quotas, general category students perform slightly better in classrooms taught by reservation category faculty than general category faculty. Finally, estimates of differences between reservation category and general category faculty in several measures of research…

04be1a0d28:fdd5bdcdef1a2313.title: Saving for the Machines -- by Jesús Fernández-Villaverde
04be1a0d28:fdd5bdcdef1a2313.summary: When machines can perform a growing share of tasks, growth depends on two margins: how the task structure affects the returns to accumulating machines, and how strongly capital accumulation responds to those returns. I argue that, in a standard task model, capital supply governs the size of the growth boom associated with automation, while the task structure sets the duration of this growth boom and the evolution of wages. I document how the same technology path that generates 11.7% annual growth when households choose their saving rate optimally delivers only 2.2% when the saving rate is fixed at the calibrated U.S. 2025 level of 23%. Therefore, slow growth might reflect too little capital accumulation instead of a technological bottleneck. Also, the saving rate rises mainly because automation raises the capital share, not because households become thriftier. Long yields price the growth boom: the ten-year real yield jumps from 5.1% to 13.6% on impact. In my benchmark calibration, hand-to-mouth households lose the equivalent of two-fifths to two-thirds of their consumption, while keeping them on trend temporarily costs at most a fifth of GDP.

04be1a0d28:b9a7707737bde578.title: Income Inequality and Intergenerational Mobility in Russia: Trends, Sources, and Measurement -- by Kristina Butaeva, Steven N. Durlauf, Dmitry Rudenko
04be1a0d28:b9a7707737bde578.summary: This chapter documents trends in income and inequality in Russia from the collapse of the Soviet Union through 2025, drawing on official statistics, the existing literature, and household survey microdata. It also reviews evidence on intergenerational mobility. While there is a consensus that inequality dramatically increased during the 1990s, its post-2000 trajectory is contested. Initial household survey studies usually found a decline, whereas official statistics reported a comparatively stable Gini coefficient. Our analysis of Russia's major household surveys, harmonized using common measurement conventions, aligns with the survey-based literature, indicating that the Gini coefficient generally fell from approximately 0.45–0.48 in the early 2000s to 0.29–0.38 in the early 2020s. We further find that most inequality arises within rather than between regions, urban and rural areas, and education and occupation groups. Household labor-market attachment, region, and household composition account for the largest shares of the explained variance in log income. The large literature on inequality is complemented by a small literature on intergenerational mobility. Here, the various studies on intergenerational dynamics in education, occupation, and income across post-Soviet cohorts conclude that, even against the background of dramatic structural changes, family background remains strongly associated with children’s outcomes.

04be1a0d28:8aa2ec613d606768.title: Public R&D and the Automation of Manufacturing: Evidence from the Space Race -- by Apoorva Babbar, Shawn Kantor, Alexander Whalley, Jingyuan Zeng
04be1a0d28:8aa2ec613d606768.summary: This paper examines how public research and development shaped the direction of technological change during the Cold War–era Space Race and its consequences for US manufacturing. While prior research has documented the effects of public R&D on innovation and economic growth, less is known about whether mission-oriented public investment directed innovation toward automation and how this affected labor markets. We exploit variation in exposure to NASA's Space Race investments across industries and locations to estimate the effects of public R&D on innovation and manufacturing outcomes from 1947 to 1992. Combining newly developed measures of automation in full-text patent data with historical evidence on government involvement in patenting, we show that NASA-sponsored patents are systematically more automation-intensive than non-NASA patents within the same technological classes. Industries and locations more exposed to Space Race activity experienced persistent declines in labor share, consistent with the diffusion of labor-saving technologies developed for space applications. In contrast, we find little evidence of systematic changes in skill composition. These findings show that mission-oriented public R&D can shape the direction of technological change and have lasting distributional consequences.

04be1a0d28:d9c50b84faabb32b.title: Aggregate-Surplus Maximizing Monetary Policy -- by David Baqaee, Ariel Burstein, Joao Guerreiro
04be1a0d28:d9c50b84faabb32b.summary: We study optimal monetary policy in a general heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian (HANK) economy. Instead of maximizing a social welfare function, the policymaker maximizes the joint surplus of all households, without taking a stance on how that surplus should be distributed. This is the policy that maximizes resources left over if winners from reform were to compensate losers. We derive the approximate optimal policy using linear-quadratic methods. The quadratic objective function nests the standard New Keynesian loss function and adds losses from incomplete markets and heterogeneous labor wedges. We show that optimal policy is the sum of time-dependent and state-contingent components. When labor wedges are homogeneous, monetary policy cannot improve household insurance: the time-dependent component is zero, and optimal policy coincides with the representative-agent New Keynesian (RANK) benchmark. Departures from RANK arise from heterogeneous labor wedges. In that case, the time-dependent component temporarily alleviates incomplete-market distortions but vanishes over time. The state-contingent component solves a dual-mandate problem, as in RANK, but with a higher weight on output-gap stabilization relative to inflation stabilization. In a calibrated model, heterogeneous labor wedges raise this weight by about 37 percent. We also find that a dual mandate with this higher weight achieves almost all of the aggregate-surplus gains from the full optimal policy and requires no compensatory transfers between winners and losers.

04be1a0d28:be2cb6766d1c270b.title: The Effects of Monetary Policy on Macroeconomic Expectations: High-Frequency Evidence from Prediction Markets -- by Eric T. Swanson, Wang Renxuan, Yanbin Wu
04be1a0d28:be2cb6766d1c270b.summary: When the Federal Reserve raises interest rates, standard macroeconomic models and VARs predict that output, employment, and inflation should fall over the next several quarters. However, monthly-frequency professional macroeconomic forecast revisions are sometimes positively correlated with Fed interest rate changes, leading to a debate about what could explain these puzzling correlations. We bring to bear new high-frequency data on this question from macroeconomic event contracts traded on Kalshi, a CFTC-licensed, U.S.-based event trading exchange and prediction market. These high-frequency event contracts allow us to isolate and estimate the effects of monetary policy and other announcements on Kalshi market-implied macroeconomic expectations. Our results are consistent with standard transmission channels from monetary policy to the macroeconomy, with little or no role for a “Fed Information Effect”.

4e96dc5201:4399dc08af6acb7b.author: Alex Mengden, Luis Zarka
4e96dc5201:4399dc08af6acb7b.summary: While there are many factors that affect a country's economic performance, taxes play an important role. A well-structured tax code is easy for taxpayers to comply with and can promote economic development while raising sufficient revenue for a government’s priorities.

4e96dc5201:239e6b8d4ed8ebac.title: Washington Voters Will Decide Whether to Keep or Reject an Income Tax on High Earners
4e96dc5201:239e6b8d4ed8ebac.author: Jared Walczak
4e96dc5201:239e6b8d4ed8ebac.summary: Washington’s new income tax on high earners doesn’t take effect until 2028, but it is already generating a lot of activity. A measure on the ballot this November, Initiative 645, would reverse the legislature’s decision, preventing the new tax from taking effect.

4e96dc5201:e4bd83d206d5ffb2.title: Spain’s Transformation After a Decade of Fiscal Competition
4e96dc5201:e4bd83d206d5ffb2.author: Cristina Enache
4e96dc5201:e4bd83d206d5ffb2.summary: The 2026 Spanish Regional Tax Competitiveness Index (RTCI) highlights a growing divergence between regions that have embraced tax reform and those whose tax systems have remained largely unchanged.

4e96dc5201:57c0f4b55261d9af.title: Why the US Needs a Fiscal Commission to Help Solve the Debt Crisis
4e96dc5201:57c0f4b55261d9af.author: William McBride
4e96dc5201:57c0f4b55261d9af.summary: The federal government’s debt burden and interest on the debt are near record levels and headed higher, raising legitimate concerns about an eventual debt crisis. Given the increasingly dysfunctional budget process, the most viable option on the table to stave off such a crisis is a statutory bipartisan fiscal commission with buy-in from leaders of both parties.

4e96dc5201:2dd4f3902e2222d6.title: Rental Cars Shouldn’t Face Another Layer of Tax
4e96dc5201:2dd4f3902e2222d6.author: Jared Walczak
4e96dc5201:2dd4f3902e2222d6.summary: Imposing sales taxes on rental car companies’ fleet purchases, in addition to the sales and rental car excise taxes levied when those cars are rented, yields double taxation and causes harmful tax pyramiding.

4e96dc5201:ce7995946a1eea1e.title: Estate and Inheritance Taxes by State, 2026
4e96dc5201:ce7995946a1eea1e.author: Nicole Fox
4e96dc5201:ce7995946a1eea1e.summary: In addition to the federal estate tax, which has a top marginal rate of 40 percent, 12 states and the District of Columbia impose estate taxes, while five states levy inheritance taxes.

4e96dc5201:56383b83d290b900.title: Combined State and Federal Corporate Income Tax Rates in 2026
4e96dc5201:56383b83d290b900.author: Garrett Watson, Alex Durante
4e96dc5201:56383b83d290b900.summary: Corporations in the United States pay federal corporate income taxes levied at a 21 percent rate. Forty-four states and D.C. also levy taxes on corporate income, with top marginal rates ranging from 2.5 percent in North Carolina to 11.5 percent in New Jersey.

4e96dc5201:ebad36d11d70ffb0.title: The 2026 Ballot Measures Shaping State Taxes
4e96dc5201:ebad36d11d70ffb0.author: Janelle Fritts, Erica York, Kyle Hulehan, Dan Carvajal
4e96dc5201:ebad36d11d70ffb0.summary: What happens when voters decide tax policy directly? This November, roughly 40 tax measures are on the ballot across 17 states. Some states want higher taxes on top earners, others want to write low rates into their constitutions, and Missouri voters will decide whether to start a fund that could one day replace every state tax.

4e96dc5201:f409e6466e319f34.title: A Small Value-Added Tax Could Pay for Tariff Repeal
4e96dc5201:f409e6466e319f34.author: Erica York
4e96dc5201:f409e6466e319f34.summary: Rather than continuing the Trump administration’s tariff policy, policymakers should explore new solutions that can raise sustainable revenue with fewer distortions, like replacing the tariffs with a value-added tax.

4e96dc5201:0f7e012116b1a0ae.title: Real Property Taxes in Europe, 2026
4e96dc5201:0f7e012116b1a0ae.author: Alex Mengden
4e96dc5201:0f7e012116b1a0ae.summary: High property taxes levied not only on land but also on buildings and structures can discourage investment in infrastructure, which businesses would have to pay additional tax on.

40c94f9b29:e085aa90a9924ead.title: The Wisdom of Montaigne (with Tyler Cowen)
40c94f9b29:e085aa90a9924ead.summary: Could a 16th-century Frenchman who spent two decades in a tower library be the first blogger? And could Tyler Cowen achieve immortality not through his books, but because AI has digested everything he’s ever said? Economist Tyler Cowen joins EconTalk’s Russ Roberts to explore the essays of Michel de Montaigne. They discuss what Montaigne got right about education (hire a tutor with a well-formed, not a well-filled, brain) and what he may have gotten wrong about material progress and growth. Along the way: Larry David, Torah study, kidney stones, Cowen’s odds of living to 120, why you should befriend people ten years younger, and Montaigne’s deceptively simple wisdom: when I dance, I dance. (0 COMMENTS)

40c94f9b29:b100efc723d36b59.title: Hubris, Humility, and the AI Revolution (with Walter Isaacson)
40c94f9b29:b100efc723d36b59.summary: The people building artificial intelligence worry there’s a real chance it could doom us all. So why do they keep building anyway? Walter Isaacson , biographer extraordinaire, talks with EconTalk’s Russ Roberts about why the AI innovators feel trapped in a race none of them can pause. Drawing on The Builders, a new podcast he’s launched, Isaacson explains why so many of these innovators see humility and empathy as handicaps rather than virtues, and why he worries they’re pouring their talent into autonomous agents that leave humans out of the loop. Isaacson traces today’s AI debate back to the rival visions of Alan Turing and Ada Lovelace, reveals why Elon Musk once told him his empathy was really vanity, and recalls Benjamin Franklin’s surprising lesson about faking humility. Plus: a Marie Curie story involving a secret affair and a second Nobel Prize. (1 COMMENTS)

40c94f9b29:150ea9598763b2ab.title: Revisiting the China Shock (with Joseph Francis)
40c94f9b29:150ea9598763b2ab.summary: What if the results of one of the most influential economics papers of the past 25 years are unreliable? The “China shock” narrative–that a surge of Chinese imports destroyed American manufacturing jobs and the communities that depended on them–became conventional wisdom in Washington and beyond. But economic historian Joseph Francis argues that the claim is much weaker than it looks. Listen as he tells EconTalk’s Russ Roberts how a 2022 correction to the paper’s research design cut its estimate of lost jobs in half and erased its findings on wages and living standards. He and Russ then look at what this affair reveals about economics as a field, including the incentives that reward dramatic results, and the problems with peer review. (0 COMMENTS)

40c94f9b29:132b72ffa2674c2c.title: The Fusion of Commercial Civilization
40c94f9b29:132b72ffa2674c2c.summary: In his new book The Civilization of Commerce ( Encounter Books, October 2026 ), American Institute for Economic Research president Samuel Gregg explores the requirements, benefits, and positive features of a commercial society, which isn’t merely trading and exchanging goods but a civilization of growth in knowledge, specialization, networks, and institutions that is built on tradition, virtue, and law. Moving beyond the usual arguments for free markets, Gregg doesn’t base his case on personal liberty, economic growth, efficiency, and technological sophistication. While these elements are present, Gregg grounds his case in the virtues, traditions, institutions, habits, and mindset of a commercial civilization. The book draws on the case made by Friedrich Hayek and Adam Smith for what they both called “the Great Society.” This commercial society is built on a certain approach to knowledge, dynamism, institutions, and virtue that drives individual and social improvement, all of which contributes to opulence, defined by Smith as “overcoming deprivation.” Such a trajectory also requires a steady adherence to, and a continued building of social and moral capital that no one rationally designed, but that many in the past and present have contributed to and shaped. In this argument, we can trace Hayek’s beliefs and his views as a central figure in the Austrian School of Economics , aspects of the American founding and the nineteenth-century republic, Tocqueville ’s musings on democratic society, and most significantly, the influence of the Scottish Enlightenment . Gregg observes that much of the case for understanding commercial civilization turns on what leading Scottish thinkers identified in their developing society in the eighteenth century: a new type of economic and social ordering that broke with a largely static and, in many cases, impoverished existence. He demonstrates how Friedrich Hayek and Adam Smith’s Great Society liberated people “from economic stagnation…

40c94f9b29:dab670eec04342c8.title: The Invisible Shackle: How Bureaucracy Stifles the Economy and Constrains Our Freedom
40c94f9b29:dab670eec04342c8.summary: For millions of entrepreneurs , the greatest barrier to generating wealth is no longer market competition but the relentless expansion of regulations and administrative procedures. While governance is ostensibly designed to ensure order, modern bureaucracy has morphed into a formidable “invisible shackle.” Rather than functioning as a neutral tool of oversight, excessive red tape treats a citizen’s inherent right to produce as a conditional concession granted by the state through endless, discretionary hurdles. The sixth edition of the Index of Bureaucracy 2026, developed at the Adam Smith Center for Economic Freedom at Florida International University, offers an empirical diagnosis of this administrative drain. Analyzing 27 countries—20 from Latin America and the Caribbean (Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Guyana, Honduras, Jamaica, Mexico, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Trinidad and Tobago, Uruguay, and Venezuela), representing 94.4% of regional GDP, and 7 from Europe (France, Germany, Italy, Portugal, Spain, Ukraine, and the United Kingdom), accounting for 59% of Europe’s GDP—the study maps the complete administrative burden cycle across three milestones of the business life cycle: opening, running, and closing. The findings offer an unvarnished look at how bureaucratic overload distorts economies, punishes small businesses, and destroys productive potential. The Relevance of Measuring Bureaucracy Quantifying bureaucracy is not a mere academic exercise; it is an urgent economic necessity. Historically, administrative complexity has been treated as an unavoidable cost of doing business. However, scholarly frameworks from public choice theory, institutional and neo-institutional economics, and modern studies of governance show that government rules and procedures tend to expand because of political incentives, institutional fragmentation, and the tendency of legislators to answer every social…

40c94f9b29:2702ebc51439ad37.title: How Your Situation Shapes You (with Angela Duckworth)
40c94f9b29:2702ebc51439ad37.summary: Sure, you can use willpower or grit to break bad habits and build new ones. But maybe the key to success is simpler: change your situation. Psychologist Angela Duckworth explains to EconTalk’s Russ Roberts why the people and places around us shape our behavior more than we realize–and why we’re hard-wired to resist that idea. Listen as they discuss the three-box framework for understanding human behavior, why creating friction to avoid temptation is itself an act of agency, and how the cultures we choose to join end up shaping who we become. (0 COMMENTS)

40c94f9b29:34e4107222a28b61.title: Sam’s Links: September Edition
40c94f9b29:34e4107222a28b61.summary: Sam Enright works on innovation policy at Progress Ireland , an independent policy think tank in Dublin, and runs a publication called The Fitzwilliam . Most relevant to us, on his personal blog , he writes a popular link roundup ; what follows is an abridged version of his Links for August. Within the first generation of settlement, British Australians were enjoying something like the living standards of Britain itself. Being a convicted criminal is apparently not enough to entirely exclude you from the benefits of legal occupational licensing: Before the arrival of solicitors who were also free settlers, legal representation was sometimes…

40c94f9b29:83e72c7055498ecf.title: Lives Wasted and Well-Lived: David Wolpe on The Death of Ivan Ilyich
40c94f9b29:83e72c7055498ecf.summary: What if you did everything right and discovered on your deathbed that you’ve wasted your life? Rabbi and author David Wolpe talks about Tolstoy’s “The Death of Ivan Ilyich” with EconTalk’s Russ Roberts . Weaving Rabbi Wolpe’s own brushes with mortality and his years at the bedsides of the dying into Tolstoy’s masterpiece, they talk about the lies we tell ourselves about death, our longing for honesty and human touch at the end, and the way that death forces us to take a clear-eyed look at life. They conclude by offering advice on how we can avoid Ivan’s regrets. (1 COMMENTS)

40c94f9b29:1f07dabd4e53cb32.title: The Liberty Fund Prize for Advancing Economic Liberty Presented by The Neal and Jane Freeman Foundation
40c94f9b29:1f07dabd4e53cb32.summary: Senator Phil Gramm and Professor Donald Boudreaux have been named the inaugural recipients of The Liberty Fund Prize for Advancing Economic Liberty, presented by The Neal and Jane Freeman Foundation. Through decades of teaching, writing, and public discourse, both honorees have deepened the public’s understanding of how competitive markets sustain a free society. The prize was presented during a ceremony at Liberty Fund headquarters in Carmel, Indiana, on Monday, October 12, 2026. Established to honor those who have illuminated the foundations of free markets and advanced them in the wider world, the prize reflects a principle long held by Liberty Fund and shared by Neal B. Freeman: That competitive markets are not merely instruments of material progress but expressions of human liberty itself, and that their defense requires both clarity of thought and steadfastness of purpose. Freeman, chairman of The Neal and Jane Freeman Foundation, served as Washington editor of National Review and was the founding producer of Firing Line . Across a long career in journalism and broadcasting, he has been a prominent voice in the public conversation about economic freedom and individual liberty. Together, the two recipients are honored for lifetimes of work that have shaped how the world understands economic liberty. Senator Phil Gramm began his career as an economist, spending more than a decade at Texas A&M University teaching and writing on monetary theory, private property, and the economics of natural resources. Over a long career in public service, he became a prominent advocate for fiscal restraint, competitive markets, and economic freedom while serving in the U.S. House of Representatives and the U.S. Senate. He continues to write and speak on economic policy as a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. Professor Donald Boudreaux has devoted his career to helping his students and the broader public better understand the principles of economics. Through…

40c94f9b29:0c24df0751808b58.title: A Nobel for Microfoundations
40c94f9b29:0c24df0751808b58.summary: This year, the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, colloquially called the Nobel Prize in Economics , went to Robert E. Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University for their work in “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization.” Those five words do not adequately describe their contributions. Hall and Woodford are macroeconomists whose major works emerged when macro was in crisis. Old school Keynesian economics had dominated economic policy discussions since the 1940s. Generally speaking, Keynesians advocated fiscal policy tools (specifically taxes and spending) to stabilize the economy. For about 20 years, those tools seemed to work. But starting in the late 1960s and through the 70s, the macroeconomic relationships broke down. A seemingly impossible confluence of rising inflation and high unemployment characterized this period. Keynesian spending policies were becoming impotent. Critics of Keynesianism rose, and macroeconomics called out for new theories. It was during this period that macroeconomics began to explore more microfoundations. That is, rather than treating the economy as a series of aggregates and their relations to one another, economists started to explore how aggregate macroeconomic factors were the results of individual behavior, institutions, and expectations. Stabilization policy could not be simply levers pulled or pushed by the policymaker. Rather, stabilization policy had to include theories on how people will react to such changes, as well as their expectations about the future. Models such as rational expectations, adaptive expectations, and the permanent income hypothesis were developed during this period as a means to explain why these Keynesian stabilization policies failed. One of the models that came out of this period was Milton Friedman’s Permanent Income Hypothesis. The basic idea is that people base their consumption decisions not just on current income…

40c94f9b29:a780bf86d4a4f4b9.title: The Great Fertility Collapse (with Jesus Fernandez-Villaverde)
40c94f9b29:a780bf86d4a4f4b9.summary: For the first time in human history, we’re not having enough children to keep the world’s population from falling. And fertility is collapsing fastest not in rich nations but in places like Colombia, Thailand, and Guatemala, upending decades of economic wisdom. Economist Jesus Fernandez-Villaverde tells EconTalk’s Russ Roberts that falling fertility has accelerated sharply over the past decade and defies easy explanation. Declining religiosity, smartphones and social media, soaring housing costs, and changing gender norms are popular, but unconfirmed, theories. Fernandez-Villaverde offers his own speculative answer, that modern life makes a third child costly and childlessness easy, but admits the puzzle is unsolved. What’s clearer is why it matters: as retirees become the dominant voting bloc, spending on pensions and health care crowds out roads, schools, and defense. Shrinking economies make public debt harder to service, and fewer births mean fewer scientists, artists, and inventors. (1 COMMENTS)

40c94f9b29:a54c6f82e5753273.title: Debt and Profit
40c94f9b29:a54c6f82e5753273.summary: An ordinary person can earn a paycheque, pay her taxes, cover living costs and mortgage payments, and perhaps even add to her savings — and at the end of the day she will still owe most of her mortgage. This is a normal state of affairs, and nobody finds it puzzling. Yet when a company reports profits alongside large amounts of debt, the reaction is often to question whether it’s really making money. After all, if a company is “truly” profitable, why is it in debt? The short answer is that debt is not the opposite of profit. Loss is the opposite of profit. This imagined contradiction is easier to resolve once we recognize that profit is a flow and debt is a stock. According to the SEC’s guide to financial statements, the income statement records revenues, expenses, and profit over a period, while the balance sheet records assets and liabilities — such as debt — at a point in time. In fact, debt and profit are entirely unrelated concepts. Imagine a firm borrows money to purchase a machine. When the loan arrives, the firm’s cash and debt rise by the same amount. When the purchase is made, the firm simply exchanges one asset (cash) for another (the machine). Neither transaction creates a profit or a loss. Over time, the machine may be used in productive activities that raise revenue. By the same token, depreciation in the machine’s value can lower profit over its useful life, and interest — the cost of managing debt — adds to expenditures for as long as the debt is outstanding. The best way to think about debt is as a contract that moves purchasing power across people and time. Savers give up control over their resources today, while borrowers promise principal and interest later in exchange for controlling those resources now. Banks and bond markets pool and match funds from many people, letting a single firm undertake a factory, railway, or phone network without first accumulating the cash itself. As Frédéric Bastiat put it, credit institutions “can make it easier…

26e942feef:5ac8ac602f6c2169.title: Severance pay reforms, worker flows, and labor market duality
26e942feef:5ac8ac602f6c2169.author: de Almeida Vilares, Hugo
26e942feef:5ac8ac602f6c2169.summary: This paper studies how cuts to statutory severance pay affect worker flows, contractual allocation, firm-level hiring composition, and wages in the Portuguese labor market. The analysis exploits the 2011-2013 reforms, which reduced the transfer component of dismissal protection for both fixed-term and open-ended contracts while leaving most procedural safeguards intact. Using matched employer-employee data for 2010?2019, we combine sharp legal-timing contrasts around the November 2011 and October 2013 cutoffs with an exposure-based IV/control-function design that leverages heterogeneity in admission cohort, tenure, contract type, and grandfathered rights. The results show that lower severance pay does not uniformly improve reallocation. Around the November 2011 cutoff, separations shift away from exits from private-sector employment toward job-to-job moves, whereas the October 2013 cutoff does not reproduce this pattern, instead displaying weaker job-to-job responses and a more uneven reduction in exits. In the broader exposure estimates, lower severance entitlements are associated with higher turnover, but the composition of that turnover varies across worker groups and contract types, combining selective conversion from fixed-term to open-ended jobs with increased reliance on temporary contracts. Within continuing worker-firm matches, wage-severance associations are economically small, providing little evidence that lower severance rights were offset by higher wages. Overall, the reforms reshaped turnover and contract use without delivering uniform improvements in labor-market reallocation, and temporary-permanent duality remains a central feature of the post-reform labor market.

26e942feef:ef6e72d6845e0735.title: An engine of (pay) growth? Productivity and wages in the UK auto industry
26e942feef:ef6e72d6845e0735.author: Van Reenen, John
26e942feef:ef6e72d6845e0735.summary: To what extent do identical workers in an industry benefit from productivity growth in the same industry? We study this question in the context of the UK auto industry which experienced a thirteen-fold increase in output per worker between 1980 and 2018. Over the same period, auto workers saw substantially stronger hourly wage growth than workers in other manufacturing industries. Controlling for unobserved worker heterogeneity, the auto wage premium over other manufacturing workers doubled from 8% in the 1980s to 17% in the 2010s, while the manufacturing premium over the rest of the economy remained roughly stable at 5%. Interpreted through the lens of a rent sharing model, we estimate that 63% of the increase in the raw firm-level auto wage premium can be accounted for by strong productivity growth. In contrast, differential bargaining power between auto workers cannot account for these changes.

26e942feef:e6a7e29f3d7e1ae7.title: Firm Size, Market Power, and Competition in a Frictional Market
26e942feef:e6a7e29f3d7e1ae7.author: Jan-Peter Siedlarek
26e942feef:e6a7e29f3d7e1ae7.summary: We study how firm size and market concentration drive price dispersion and margins in a market with information frictions. We start from the noisy-search framework and tie firm size to the number of establishments owned by a firm. Consumers sample establishments rather than firms, allowing multi-establishment firms to capture even informed consumers. This benefit comes at a cost to the firm, since establishments cannibalize each other's demand. We show that uniform pricing across a firm's establishments is optimal. The unique equilibrium involves price distributions with supports connected and nested by firm size: larger firms post prices over a wider support, but earn lower profit per establishment. Finally, mergers can increase concentration while reducing expected transaction prices and markups when the merger does not create a new market leader. When the merger creates a new largest firm, its effect can instead reverse, depending on the relative strength of the concentration and largest-firm channels. Thus, the effect of greater concentration depends critically on how ownership changes the firm size distribution.

26e942feef:8d1962f98ebcc65f.title: Earnings Dynamics under Firm Heterogeneity
26e942feef:8d1962f98ebcc65f.author: Timo Virtanen
26e942feef:8d1962f98ebcc65f.summary: We develop a permanent–transitory earnings process in which permanent shocks depend on a latent firm type and workers’ exposure to firm types is persistent. Persistence can substantially slow the finite-horizon attenuation of earnings skewness and excess kurtosis over the life cycle relative to an iid mixture benchmark. We estimate the model from matched employer-employee data, first grouping firms based on the distribution of residual earnings changes and then using worker transitions across groups to estimate persistence. Finnish data reveal heterogeneity in permanent-shock variances and persistent exposure to firm groups. Although skewness and excess kurtosis are not targeted in estimation, over ages 35–50 the extended model accounts for 49 percent of average empirical skewness and 39 percent of average excess kurtosis, compared with 4 percent and 3 percent under the iid benchmark. Quantitative exercises show that persistence increases the life-cycle cost of earnings risk and affects saving behavior.

26e942feef:fc419420556e8540.title: Rent Sharing under Innovation Tax Breaks
26e942feef:fc419420556e8540.author: Ana Popovici
26e942feef:fc419420556e8540.summary: We study whether firms share gains from innovation tax incentives with incumbent workers and whether such rent sharing is associated with increased worker retention. The Dutch innovation box reduces tax rates on profits from in-house innovation. Linking first-time beneficiaries to matched employer-employee data, we combine nearest-neighbour matching with staggered difference-in-differences. Part of the additional after-tax surplus is passed on to incumbent workers: wages rise by 3.27% on average, with increases of 2.05% for workers least involved in R&D and 4.14% for tertiary-educated STEM workers. Descriptively, treated non-R&D incumbents are 3.47 percentage points less likely to switch employers following treatment.

26e942feef:58acf291ef954ec1.title: Tariffs, Employment and the Balance of Trade
26e942feef:58acf291ef954ec1.author: Sweder van Wijnbergen
26e942feef:58acf291ef954ec1.summary: We study whether firms share gains from innovation tax incentives with incumbent workers and whether such rent sharing is associated with increased worker retention. The Dutch innovation box reduces tax rates on profits from in-house innovation. Linking first-time beneficiaries to matched employer-employee data, we combine nearest-neighbour matching with staggered difference-in-differences. Part of the additional after-tax surplus is passed on to incumbent workers: wages rise by 3.27% on average, with increases of 2.05% for workers least involved in R&D and 4.14% for tertiary-educated STEM workers. Descriptively, treated non-R&D incumbents are 3.47 percentage points less likely to switch employers following treatment.

26e942feef:7e521e588eaaccac.title: AI as Shared Business Infrastructure: Firm Growth and the Distribution of Gains
26e942feef:7e521e588eaaccac.author: Zhe Yuan
26e942feef:7e521e588eaaccac.summary: Generative AI improves performance on individual tasks, but whether those gains translate into firm growth, and for which firms, remains an open question. We study a leading Chinese e-commerce platform that in 2024 embedded a generative AI system in the operating software firms use to run their businesses, drawing on centrally developed models and platform-wide data to deliver ready-to-use applications to every firm. Complete records of each firm’s AI use, linked to its monthly operations and sales, let us trace adoption through changes in business capabilities, such as reaching customers and introducing new products, to sales growth. Using a matched difference-in-differences design and focusing on firms with annual sales below RMB 5 million, we find that adoption raises monthly sales by 51.6%, primarily through a 47.0% increase in the number of orders; instrumental-variable estimates confirm these results. Adopters reach more customers, update their product lines faster, and deliver better product and service quality, with the largest proportional gains for the smallest firms. Two mechanisms help explain the results. First, AI lowers the cost of routine work: adopters produce more product content and change listings more often while spending less staff time per order, and the gains are largest for firms that faced the highest costs relative to sales before adoption. Second, AI reduces information frictions: adopters post richer product information, and the gains are largest in markets where demand is hard to predict and matching quality is poor, especially for small firms. At the market level, product categories with greater pre-existing information frictions see more sales by existing firms, more entry, and more new products. AI expands markets rather than merely shifting sales from non-adopters to adopters.

26e942feef:49f8dd69ec7a2656.title: Migrant entrepreneurship, high-growth firms and cities
26e942feef:49f8dd69ec7a2656.author: Sivropoulos Valero, Anna
26e942feef:49f8dd69ec7a2656.summary: High-growth firms represent a small share of businesses in OECD countries, but disproportionately drive national economic activity. This paper examines migrants' role in founding high-growth firms, and the urban nature of high-growth entrepreneurship. Using novel founder- and company-level data on over 12, 000 UK companies and 15, 000 founders, we analyse the characteristics of migrant founders and the firms that they build. We establish six new facts. First, relative to the UK migrant population, migrant entrepreneurs are substantially over-represented among founders of high-growth potential firms. Second, compared to UKborn founders, migrant founders are positively selected on human capital, but negatively selected on entrepreneurial experience. Third, high-growth potential firms are highly urbanised, and those with a migrant (co-)founder display a distinctive urban geography. Fourth, firms with mixed native-migrant founding teams show faster employment and revenue growth than all-UK teams. All-migrant teams show weaker growth premia. Fifth, compared with UK-born founded firms, firms with mixed native-migrant founding teams have more distinctive strategic positioning, with fewer peers. Sixth, for co-founded firms, our results vary by birth countries, first language and urban location. Migrant-founded firms in London and conurbations exhibit the largest performance premia.

26e942feef:500832afa5a474d9.title: Policy Deterrence: Strategic Investment in U.S. Broadband
26e942feef:500832afa5a474d9.author: Mo Xiao
26e942feef:500832afa5a474d9.summary: Can firms influence policy through investment? Using 2010--2019 U.S. broadband deployment and state policy data, we find that large internet service providers expand capacity more in electorally competitive counties. Greater large-provider capacity in swing counties is associated with fewer subsequent entry- and investment-facilitating policies, especially rights-of-way accommodations that reduce deployment barriers faced by smaller providers. To interpret these patterns, we develop a model in which a large firm's capacity can reduce the policymaker's gain from intervention. In the model, policy deterrence raises the large firm's market share and can reduce total deployment.

26e942feef:598cd20e75ee58f7.title: Clearing the Fog: Price Transparency, Market Churn, and Consumer Welfare in Short-Term Rentals
26e942feef:598cd20e75ee58f7.author: Jingyi Xing
26e942feef:598cd20e75ee58f7.summary: We study California's short-term lodging price transparency law (AB 537), which from July 1, 2024 required Airbnb and other providers to advertise fee-inclusive prices. Using Coarsened Exact Matching to compare Airbnb listings in San Diego and San Francisco with those in Seattle and Chicago, we find that all-in pricing made guests more price-sensitive relative to control cities; yet, contrary to the standard prediction that transparency lowers prices, average daily rates rose by 4.8 percent. We also observe significant market churn: relative to control cities, treated cities saw more exits and entries, listings reliant on cleaning-fee revenue disproportionately exited, higher-quality listings were more likely to stay, and entrants offered lower fees and lower quality than incumbents. A discrete-choice welfare analysis shows that the law removed a sizable “welfare illusion” created by obscured fees and, largely through market churn, raised realized consumer surplus. The net gains, after accounting for price increases, were positive on average but unevenly distributed across treated ZIP codes.

26e942feef:6b561a81a4dbf40b.title: The real and financial effects of local corporate tax increases: evidence from linked firm–bank data
26e942feef:6b561a81a4dbf40b.author: S. Moura, Afonso
26e942feef:6b561a81a4dbf40b.summary: We study how local corporate tax increases affect firms’ financing and real activity. In Portugal, municipalities independently set a surtax on corporate income, generating plausibly exogenous variation across space and time. We link the universe of corporate balance sheets and profit-and-loss statements to loan-level data from the Bank of Portugal’s credit registry, allowing us to track firms’ liquidity, leverage, borrowing costs, and credit quality alongside revenues, employment, and productivity. We estimate local-projection difference-in-differences models that address staggered treatment timing and dynamic responses. Surtax hikes immediately tighten financing conditions: liquidity falls, implicit interest rates rise, debt increases at shorter maturities, and non-performing loans become more prevalent. These strains spill over into real outcomes: firms reduce sales and employment and experience persistent declines in total factor productivity. Effects are strongest among small firms, where leverage rises in response to liquidity losses. We also find higher exit and relocation probabilities, but no gains in neighboring output, pointing to inefficient reallocation. Our results highlight how local tax policy can transmit through both financial and real margins, with implications for fiscal design in decentralized settings. JEL Classification: E62, G38, H25, H32, H71

26e942feef:18ecca395efb763d.title: Heterogeneous Firms, Growth and the Long Shadows of Business Cycles
26e942feef:18ecca395efb763d.author: Adam Hal Spencer
26e942feef:18ecca395efb763d.summary: Do firms differ in their innovation response to business cycles? What economic forces shape this heterogeneity? And does it matter for aggregate propagation? We document substantial heterogeneity in firm-level R&D cyclicality, develop a theory to explain this fact, and validate its key mechanism in the data. In a tractable model of business cycles and innovation-driven growth, endogenous selection makes R&Dparticularly responsive to aggregate conditions for firms close to the exit mar gin. Consistent with this mechanism, firms closer to exit display more procyclical R&Din the data. Quantitatively, selection and endogenous growth interact power fully: selection generates heterogeneous R&D cyclicality, while endogenous growth translates these heterogeneous responses into persistent aggregate effects. Ignoring heterogeneous R&D cyclicality misses roughly half of the long-run output cost of a severe recession.

26e942feef:9e86f65dc1557311.title: The Transparency Tax : Discouraging Firm Ownership via Tax Havens
26e942feef:9e86f65dc1557311.author: Bajaña, Alex
26e942feef:9e86f65dc1557311.summary: Tax havens weaken tax enforcement by obscuring firm ownership and facilitating offshore evasion. This paper studies a reform in Ecuador that imposed a corporate tax surcharge on firms with owners in tax havens, using a newly available ownership registry. Comparing haven-owned firms to other foreign-owned firms, the analysis finds that the reform reduced haven ownership by 12 percentage points, largely through disclosure of non-haven individual owners. Exposed firms reduced transactions with tax havens and increased corporate tax payments, with no detectable effects on investment or firm size. The results suggest that ownership transparency can meaningfully improve tax compliance at limited efficiency cost, even through unilateral action.

26e942feef:59dc803835381515.title: Place-Based Federal Procurement and Resident Jobs: Lessons from the Historically Underutilized Business Zone Program
26e942feef:59dc803835381515.author: Craig Sylvera
26e942feef:59dc803835381515.summary: Unlike tax-based place policies that subsidize employment or investment, procurement-based approaches direct federal purchasing to businesses in distressed areas. I examine the HUBZone program, which targets federal contracts to firms in economically disadvantaged census tracts. I find that receiving an award increases jobs for residents of the census tract by 3.5 percent over five to seven years, with no corresponding increase in jobs within the census tract. Establishment-level analysis reveals no employment gains at recipient firms themselves, suggesting any employment effects occur outside the receiving firm. Housing markets respond positively with increased mortgage origination activity. Examining the variation in the size of awards does not reveal a relationship between award size and jobs gained. The findings demonstrate that procurement set-asides can improve local outcomes in distressed areas, though whether they create new jobs or redistribute existing opportunities remains an open question.

26e942feef:16426232dae6b9e2.title: Measuring Shipping Disruptions with Satellite Data
26e942feef:16426232dae6b9e2.author: Ricardo Marto
26e942feef:16426232dae6b9e2.summary: A new measure using satellite vessel-tracking data reveals how much potential U.S.-bound shipping capacity was reduced by disruptions such as port congestion, canal bottlenecks and rerouting.

26e942feef:aa9c38191ba05627.title: Which types of education raise firm productivity? Evidence for managers and workers in the UK
26e942feef:aa9c38191ba05627.author: Hall, Tessa
26e942feef:aa9c38191ba05627.summary: This paper estimates the firm productivity returns to degree field, institution quality, and degree level, and compares them with wage returns. I link a LinkedIn panel from Revelio Labs to Orbis financial accounts for over 20, 000 UK firms over 2015?2024. Within firms, a bachelor's degree raises a worker's productivity by around 20%; a top-20 institution adds a further 10% and a postgraduate qualification 6%. The returns differ by organisational role. A bachelor's degree raises productivity for managers and non-managers alike. Specialist credentials - a STEM field, an elite institution - raise productivity for non-managers but not for managers, whose premium loads instead on postgraduate qualifications, above all MBAs. Managers also contribute around 26% more than otherwise identical non-managers, a premium that education does not explain. Averaged over the workforce, wage premia are close to productivity premia for each type of degree. However, the average conceals two wedges of opposite sign: STEM-trained non-managers are paid below their relative productivity, and degree-holding managers above it. Finally, for a subset of firms matched to the World Management Survey, workforce education accounts for around a quarter the well-documented correlation between management practices and productivity.

26e942feef:d6ebf535151fd830.title: Business networks and the persistence of entrepreneurship: evidence from China
26e942feef:d6ebf535151fd830.author: Lee, Neil
26e942feef:d6ebf535151fd830.summary: This paper investigates the long run association between business networks and entrepreneurship and regional development in China. We focus on chambers of commerce, bodies which facilitated networking between businesses until private firms were banned by Mao. Our results suggest that the pre-Mao chamber system is associated with long-lasting patterns of business creation and economic output in China, with this influence surviving until the post-1978 return of the market economy. The associations are strongest in the early reform period but weaken over time. We show evidence that historic chambers density is correlated with later social capital, despite major political change.

26e942feef:800932119aa7f871.title: The Division of Labor: Productivity, Coordination, and Learning
26e942feef:800932119aa7f871.author: Xu, Yaling
26e942feef:800932119aa7f871.summary: The division of labor is fundamental to how firms organize production. Since Adam Smith, economists have recognized that dividing tasks more finely increases productivity through specialization but also raises coordination costs—a tradeoff formalized by Becker and Murphy (1992). Yet we have little systematic evidence on how this tradeoff operates within firms. Moreover, this classical perspective overlooks a second, dynamic tradeoff: firms not only produce output, but also develop a central input into future production—their workers’ human capital. A finer division of labor allows workers to develop greater expertise through repeated performance of narrowly defined tasks, but may also reduce opportunities to learn from coworkers by limiting interactions and knowledge exchange. We study both tradeoffs using population-wide Norwegian employer–employee records, linked workplace surveys, quasi-experimental variation in coworker availability, and randomized experiments with workers and managers. We find that more specialized firms exhibit higher productivity but also greater coordination costs. Their workers report more learning-by-doing but substantially less coworker learning, resulting in lower overall learning and slower wage growth. To establish the importance of coworker learning for human capital accumulation, we exploit extended coworker absences and show that losing access to colleagues reduces subsequent wage growth, particularly in occupations characterized by greater task overlap and coworker learning. To isolate the role of the division of labor from other workplace characteristics, we conduct randomized experiments that vary task allocation in otherwise identical workplaces. Workers and managers anticipate greater coordination demands, weaker coworker interactions, and lower skill accumulation under greater specialization. The experiments then ask workers to choose their preferred workplace and managers how they would organize production. Both favor…

26e942feef:33a508e98ad79509.title: What is an AI worker? Evidence from Matched Vacancy-Hires
26e942feef:33a508e98ad79509.author: Hellsten, Mark
26e942feef:33a508e98ad79509.summary: Despite growing policy interest in AI workforce development, surprisingly little is known about what defines these workers, or indeed if they differ from their occupational peers. Using a novel matched vacancy-hire dataset linking Swedish job postings to the individuals hired to fill them, drawn from register data on the entire Swedish population, I study the characteristics of workers who develop and apply AI. Observable traits including high cognitive ability, a tertiary degree in STEM subjects, and a recent migrant background largely explain occupational sorting. Of these, only higher education, prior AI experience, and a science degree set them apart within occupation. I then use earnings as a window onto unobservable differences: AI workers earn approximately 5% more than their peers, entirely explained by firm-level wages. However, AI workers with a doctorate degree stand out sharply in both traits and earnings, indicating that AI workers split into segments that differ by the complexity of their skills and tasks. Taken together, these results point to two distinct policy levers: the supply of average AI workers, termed AI integrators, can be expanded via STEM education participation, while the elite AI developers are supplied by researchers moving to the private sector.

26e942feef:e6c6f5dddcb85506.title: Tracking management practices over time: Response rates and survey design choices behind the UK Management and Expectations Survey
26e942feef:e6c6f5dddcb85506.author: Wickersham, Tom
26e942feef:e6c6f5dddcb85506.summary: This paper uses three waves of the ONS Management and Expectations Survey (2016, 2020 and 2023) to examine how management practices evolve over time and to understand response behaviour in a voluntary business survey. We track management scores for firms responding across multiple waves and assess the extent to which changes in management practices reflect genuine managerial improvements or responder biases captured by the responder’s occupation. Firms that responded in 2020 were 24.9 percentage points more likely to respond in 2023 when controlling for firm characteristics. Where the individual responding on behalf of the firm was a senior official, such as a director, the respondent provided faster and more consistent responses across waves than firms responding with junior staff. Firms responding in all three waves report higher and improving management practices on average, particularly in employment practices. However, this difference is associated with observable firm characteristics, such as firm size. These results highlight the importance of understanding response patterns when interpreting survey results. We recommend maintaining continuity by retaining firms that responded in all three waves, encouraging responses from senior staff, and applying longitudinal weights to address non-response. The findings support improved survey design for future MES waves and strengthen the use of management practices as a measure of organisational capital in productivity research.

26e942feef:0e817fa18a9b2d96.title: Crime and prices: thefts of expensive precious metals from cars
26e942feef:0e817fa18a9b2d96.author: Sandi, Matteo
26e942feef:0e817fa18a9b2d96.summary: Whether economic incentives matter for crime is studied in a novel way, from expensive precious metal thefts by thieves stealing catalytic converters from cars. Sharp and sizable variations in the prices of precious metals embedded in converters are combined with newly assembled U.S. crime data. Precipitously fast increases in precious metal prices generated a sizeable rise in auto-part thefts, while subsequent price declines and policy responses quickly reversed this pattern. The resulting boom-and bust dynamics provide clean evidence that prices affect crime, and for these crimes that local resale infrastructure and target availability shape both the magnitude of this effect and the effectiveness of policy response.

901dc0be66:09fe03837546f3a0.title: Earnings Instability*
901dc0be66:09fe03837546f3a0.summary: Abstract This paper uses high-frequency administrative data to show that most U.S. workers experience substantial month-to-month fluctuations in pay, even within ongoing employment relationships. Monthly earnings instability is pervasive but is masked in annual data. Moreover, this instability is unequally distributed: lower-income, hourly workers face more instability than higher-income, salaried workers. Firm-driven fluctuations in hours account for a large share of this instability. Monthly earnings instability, in turn, increases spending volatility and job separations. Short-term earnings risk is therefore a significant feature of the labor market and falls disproportionately on the most financially fragile workers.

901dc0be66:100290962a2d20d6.title: Labor Market Tightness and the Reversal of Inequality Trends in Germany1
901dc0be66:100290962a2d20d6.summary: Abstract Germany experienced a sharp rise in wage inequality over the two decades leading up to the Great Recession. However, a remarkable trend reversal occurred in 2010—well before the introduction of the minimum wage in 2015—when wages at the bottom of the distribution began to grow more rapidly than those higher up. This paper attributes the reversal to an increasingly tight labor market after the Great Recession, supported by strong domestic demand, and operating through several interrelated and mutually reinforcing channels. Consistent with this hypothesis, job-to-job transition rates and between-job wage growth rose markedly after the recession, especially for workers at the lower rungs of the job ladder. Concurrently, workers increasingly moved from low-paying to higher-paying firms, compressing the worker-weighted distribution of firm wage premia. Tighter labor markets also reduced assortative matching between workers and firms, lowered the skill premium, and weakened firms’ monopsony power.

901dc0be66:c821b678b270ddb9.title: When Insurers Exit: Climate Losses, Fragile Insurers, and Mortgage Markets*
901dc0be66:c821b678b270ddb9.summary: Abstract This paper uses a range of natural experiments to show how mispricing of climate risk in mortgages and property insurance creates large taxpayer exposures and leads to excess credit flows to risky areas. Our central finding is that the government-sponsored enterprises’ (GSEs) policies for evaluating property insurers are a crucial source of this mispricing. We assemble a comprehensive new dataset on both mortgages and insurance to analyze these dynamics in Florida from 2009-2018. We begin by documenting a breakdown in the quality of insurance provision, with new under-capitalized and under-diversified insurers dominating insurance markets. These fragile insurers have high rates of insolvency, which we show causally increases mortgage defaults after natural disasters. We find that the GSEs’ reliance on third-party ratings of insurers leads them to accept insurance from companies at high risk of insolvency without pricing for it. This creates large taxpayer exposures, with an estimated 25% of the GSEs’ expected losses in Florida coming from insurance fragility. Most starkly, we show that private lenders strategically respond to the GSE mispricing. Mortgage denial rates are sensitive to insurance quality in the jumbo segment where loans are retained, but not in the conforming segment where loans are offloaded to the GSEs. This suggests that, all else equal, fewer conforming mortgages would have been originated if lenders screened insurance fragility as they do in jumbos.

901dc0be66:43f09410481a8c5a.title: Channeled Attention and Stable Errors*
901dc0be66:43f09410481a8c5a.summary: Abstract People persist in mistaken beliefs even in settings with high stakes, abundant data, and repeated opportunities to learn—settings where standard arguments imply they should correct their errors. We develop an attention-based framework for understanding why errors persist. When a person channels his attention through the lens of his potentially misspecified model, exposure to data is not the same as tracking the statistics necessary to tell him his model is wrong. A model is attentionally stable when the data the person deems relevant will, in the long run, fail to make the model look implausible. Models that erroneously rule things out—e.g., beliefs that a variable doesn’t matter or that a distinction doesn’t exist—tend to be attentionally stable because they divert attention away from data that would refute the models. Conversely, models that erroneously rule things in are less likely to be stable. Whether an error is discovered depends on the structure of the decision problem but is not tightly linked to its level of harm; arbitrarily costly errors can persist while trivially inexpensive ones may be detected. Nevertheless, no error is robust both to changes in the decision environment and to shocks that expand attention: every channeled-attention error is vulnerable to some perturbation that would reveal it. We use the framework to analyze the stability of psychological biases and empirical misconceptions, as well as to explain why fresh eyes catch mistakes, why people use overly coarse rather than overly fine categorizations, and why people recognize errors in others that they miss in themselves.

901dc0be66:87624d0624dfeff6.title: Why Do Union Jobs Pay More? New Evidence from Matched Employer-Employee Data*
901dc0be66:87624d0624dfeff6.summary: Abstract We use Canadian matched employer-employee data to assess the sources of the union pay premium. After controlling for worker heterogeneity using the two-way fixed effects approach of Abowd, Kramarz, and Margolis (AKM), we find that unionized firms pay about 15 log points more than non-unionized firms. Forty percent of this gap is linked to productivity differences between unionized and non-unionized firms as measured by value added per worker. The remaining gap reflects unions’ ability to extract more rents for workers. Our estimates imply that unions raise pay among unionized workers by around 9 log points, with considerable heterogeneity by industry and firm birth cohorts. The union effect grows to about 11 log points in an extension of the AKM approach where unions also affect the returns to unobservable worker characteristics.

901dc0be66:7f4e1ec616e57a61.title: The Effects of School Phone Bans: National Evidence from Lockable Pouches*
901dc0be66:7f4e1ec616e57a61.summary: Abstract Schools across the U.S. have sharply restricted student use of phones during the school day. We evaluate one type of restriction—lockable phone pouches—using nationwide data combining a large-scale teacher survey, GPS pings, standardized test scores, and school administrative records, along with sales records from the largest pouch provider. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design, we find that pouch adoption substantially reduces phone use as measured by GPS pings and teacher reports. In the first year after adoption, disciplinary incidents increase, and we find suggestive evidence that student subjective well-being falls, consistent with short-term disruption. However, disciplinary effects fade, while the estimated effects on well-being appear to recover and become positive in later years. For academic achievement, average effects on test scores are consistently close to zero. High schools see modest positive effects, particularly in math, while middle schools see small negative effects. We find little evidence of effects on school attendance and no clear evidence of improvements in self-reported classroom attention or perceived online bullying.

901dc0be66:726c580558eff521.title: How New Products Enter Markets: Social Networks, Consumer Imports, and Retailer Learning*
901dc0be66:726c580558eff521.summary: Abstract This paper studies how new varieties enter markets and become locally available. We provide causal evidence of demand externalities that operate in two steps. First, information about new varieties diffuses directly through real-world social ties among consumers. Second, early purchases generate an indirect spillover to firms: local retailers learn from “pioneer” consumers which new varieties are most likely to succeed and adjust their product offerings accordingly. We study this process in the context of direct-to-consumer imports. Using customs records on individuals ’ purchases matched to population-wide social networks, international migrant links, and retailer catchment areas, we document economically meaningful demand externalities. Product-specific expenditure shocks abroad transmit through migrant networks and shift which varieties consumers purchase. Leveraging these shocks as a plausibly exogenous source of local demand variation, we show strong peer effects: prior purchases by close neighbors, coworkers, or friends increase an individual’s likelihood of purchasing the same variety, especially for premium and visible goods. We leverage this result to identify an indirect spillover from consumers to firms: retailers are more likely to add a variety to their assortment when it becomes popular among consumers in their catchment area. Combining the instrument with linked consumer–retailer data and a self-conducted retailer survey, we show that this response reflects learning about latent demand for varieties not yet stocked locally. Together, social diffusion and retailer learning generate demand multipliers that reshape local product availability and expand access to global variety.

901dc0be66:a03b417b94c31fd5.title: Optimal Flood Insurance in a Second-Best World: Fiscal Spillovers, Reclassification Risk, and Moral Hazard*
901dc0be66:a03b417b94c31fd5.summary: Abstract Intensifying climate change makes protection against natural disaster risk – either through ex ante insurance or ex post aid – a first-order public policy issue. Flood risk protection in the U.S. traditionally featured ex post aid through FEMA and heavily subsidized insurance through the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP). In an effort to correct subsidy-induced overbuilding and under-mitigation in flood-prone areas, the NFIP recently moved to actuarially fair insurance premiums. But this change has two unintended consequences: a fiscal spillover onto FEMA disaster aid as insurance coverage declines in flood-prone areas, and household exposure to uninsurable reclassification risk from uncertain climate projections. We develop a model of optimal flood insurance that incorporates the static and dynamic tradeoffs of subsidizing premiums. We then use a variety of identification strategies and data to estimate the five key parameters needed to implement this model. We find that the fiscal spillover and reclassification risk protection benefits significantly outweigh the moral hazard costs, and that the optimal subsidy to flood insurance is 51%, comparable to the level of subsidization before the recent reform.

Ordinary Jamaicans are fed up By Ben Ryder Howe A decade ago, while working for a travel magazine, I got into a conversation one day with a few colleagues about which countries, for moral reasons, we would never write about. I wouldn’t have said Jamaica back then; in fact, that year I visited Jamaica and wrote a short, positive piece about one of its hotels. fc4853f6ed:e43fac85e52bfb6e.summary: Ahead of the midterms, a new book of photographs by Jean-Pierre Laffont captures two decades of American defiance By Elena Clavarino P erhaps only a first-generation immigrant can truly understand America. “We are outsiders,” explains Eliane Laffont, wife of the French photographer Jean-Pierre Laffont. “Whether we like it or not. You know, we are not your typical Americans, so it’s very easy for us to see what’s good and what’s bad and what’s ugly …” Few have had a better vantage point than Jean-Pierre Laffont. Since his arrival in New York, in 1964, Laffont has photographed America at its most restless, rebellious, and unruly, capturing the civil-rights movement, anti–Vietnam War protesters, hippies turned Rajneeshees in Oregon, the gay-liberation movement, gangs in the Bronx, and the street culture that gave rise to hip-hop.
