ef78496c13:0a791fc2c22af02e.title: Rent Sharing under Innovation Tax Breaks
ef78496c13:0a791fc2c22af02e.author: Ana Popovici
ef78496c13:0a791fc2c22af02e.summary: We study whether firms share gains from innovation tax incentives with incumbent workers and whether such rent sharing is associated with increased worker retention. The Dutch innovation box reduces tax rates on profits from in-house innovation. Linking first-time beneficiaries to matched employer-employee data, we combine nearest-neighbour matching with staggered difference-in-differences. Part of the additional after-tax surplus is passed on to incumbent workers: wages rise by 3.27% on average, with increases of 2.05% for workers least involved in R&D and 4.14% for tertiary-educated STEM workers. Descriptively, treated non-R&D incumbents are 3.47 percentage points less likely to switch employers following treatment.

ef78496c13:98521d54d58b6699.title: The Transparency Tax : Discouraging Firm Ownership via Tax Havens
ef78496c13:98521d54d58b6699.author: Bajaña, Alex
ef78496c13:98521d54d58b6699.summary: Tax havens weaken tax enforcement by obscuring firm ownership and facilitating offshore evasion. This paper studies a reform in Ecuador that imposed a corporate tax surcharge on firms with owners in tax havens, using a newly available ownership registry. Comparing haven-owned firms to other foreign-owned firms, the analysis finds that the reform reduced haven ownership by 12 percentage points, largely through disclosure of non-haven individual owners. Exposed firms reduced transactions with tax havens and increased corporate tax payments, with no detectable effects on investment or firm size. The results suggest that ownership transparency can meaningfully improve tax compliance at limited efficiency cost, even through unilateral action.

ef78496c13:ccfd929afb3cc211.title: Partners on a Climb : Financial Sector Development and Tax Collections in Indonesia
ef78496c13:ccfd929afb3cc211.author: Polat, Beyza
ef78496c13:ccfd929afb3cc211.summary: Shallow financial markets may act as an important structural constraint on a country’s ability to mobilize tax revenues. This paper explores this hypothesis in the context of Indonesia, a middle-income country with persistently low tax collections and low financial sector depth. At the macro level, relating cross-country financial development to new estimates of tax gaps, it finds that a 1 percent increase in private credit as a share of GDP could reduce the tax gap by approximately 0.2 percent. At the micro level, analysis of publicly listed Indonesian companies suggests that a one-decile increase in financial constraints is associated with a 0.18 percentage point drop in cash effective tax rates, indicating that financially constrained firms may be using tax planning as a liquidity tool. The results suggest that tax collections are positively associated with financial sector deepening.

ef78496c13:f94c98ad2bfc0d23.title: Low fertility rates: A fiscal policy perspective
ef78496c13:f94c98ad2bfc0d23.author: Baur, Martin
ef78496c13:f94c98ad2bfc0d23.summary: Switzerland’s fertility rate fell below 1.3 children per woman in 2024 and has remained well below the replacement level for decades, reflecting a broader trend across advanced economies. This paper discusses the economic and fiscal implications of persistently low fertility, reviews its underlying causes and the extent to which family policy can influence fertility decisions, and presents policy options available for Switzerland. Low fertility slows growth of the domestic working-age population, accelerates population ageing, and reduces long-term economic growth potential. For public finances, it dampens tax revenues and social insurance contributions while increasing age-related expenditure, particularly on pensions and healthcare. The causes of low fertility are multifaceted, including the financial costs of having children, difficulties in reconciling work and family life, and broader changes in social norms and lifestyles. Evidence from OECD countries suggests that family policies can alleviate some constraints, but their effects on fertility are small and often temporary. Coherent and well-coordinated measures supporting families throughout the child-rearing years appear more promising than individual measures. As a sustained reversal of current fertility trends appears unlikely, economic and fiscal policy should focus on adapting to an ageing society by making better use of the domestic labour supply, facilitating labor-market-oriented immigration, and fostering productivity growth. Finally, reforms to strengthen the fiscal sustainability of pension and healthcare systems become even more important.

ef78496c13:0be26042a1eac5e4.title: The Fiscal Alibi: Hidden Spending Needs and Government Reputation
ef78496c13:0be26042a1eac5e4.author: Ly, Hengrina
ef78496c13:0be26042a1eac5e4.summary: A government may ask for a high tax because it faces a genuine expense. The same demand can also be made by a government that intends to keep the proceeds. We study this ambiguity in a two-period reputation model with privately observed spending needs and an endogenous tax base. The opportunist chooses between outright confiscation and levies that an honest government might impose. We characterize the three possible regimes through a single equilibrium equation. A mean-preserving spread of legitimate needs weakly raises the opportunist’s lifetime value, with a strict increase precisely when the spread changes the upper tail relevant for mimicry. We then give a necessary and sufficient curvature condition for this ordering to extend to a general reputational continuation prize. Verification reduces the value of concealment, but also changes how the opportunist extracts. In the benchmark economy, greater auditing weakly lowers current citizen welfare, even before audit costs, while improving the future allocation through better information. The welfare case for verification consequently depends on the balance between these two effects. Examples yield no auditing, an optimum within a regime, and an optimum at the boundary between regimes.

ef78496c13:1b25c4cb38967f26.title: Taxing Capital to Protect It
ef78496c13:1b25c4cb38967f26.author: Ly, Hengrina
ef78496c13:1b25c4cb38967f26.summary: This paper studies the composition of taxation when the government cannot fully commit to respecting private returns after investment. A fiscal authority must finance a given expenditure from labor and capital income. Ordinary tax receipts are protected, but an opportunistic executive can seize part of the remaining capital payment. We show that a revenue-neutral increase in the capital tax raises the probability of compliance whenever the labor tax is below its local, fixedwage revenue peak, provided the equilibrium remains on a regular mixing branch. This result does not depend on the elasticity of substitution between capital and labor. The same reform can raise investment: the gain in expected retention must outweigh the decline in the opportunist’s continuation gain as compliance becomes less informative. We also characterize the Ramsey allocation conditional on full compliance. Limited commitment then imposes a ceiling on sustainable capital payments, rather than a general lower bound on the statutory capital-tax rate. Finally, we distinguish a change in the authority’s concern for the future from an increase in both actors’ patience. The former favors more informative policies when continuation welfare is convex; the latter has no unconditional direction in the reduced-form policy problem.

ef78496c13:06732b4140d7f719.title: Tax Expenditure Reporting as a Commitment Device for Revenue Mobilization
ef78496c13:06732b4140d7f719.author: Gaël Tape
ef78496c13:06732b4140d7f719.summary: This note shows that publishing tax expenditure reports increases tax revenue mobilization over the medium term in emerging and developing countries. The results indicate that this effect emerges six to seven years after publication and is driven primarily by direct taxes. The effect is stronger when reports are published more frequently and on a regular basis. It is also more pronounced in low-income countries and in sub-Saharan Africa. Publishing tax expenditure reports acts as a commitment mechanism. By making tax exemptions visible, it raises the political cost of opaque exemptions and gradually strengthens the government's capacity to steer tax policy.

ef78496c13:15013f601580df67.title: The Strange and Curious Tax Treatment of Investment Expenses
ef78496c13:15013f601580df67.author: Morris, Mallory A.
ef78496c13:15013f601580df67.summary: To secure income, taxpayers often incur a wide range of expenses. At least theoretically, one might think that the Internal Revenue Code (“Code”) would accord all such expenses similar tax treatment, but (i) trade or business expenses and (ii) investment expenses endure the exact opposite tax treatment: the former are generally allowed, whereas the latter are commonly disallowed. The obvious question is why there is a difference in treatment between the two. This Article explores possible answers to that important question. It first traces the evolution of the Code’s dichotomous tax treatment of trade or business versus investment expenses. It then investigates possible justifications and their associated merits for the different handling of these two expense categories. With this background information in mind, to make the tax system more administrable, equitable, and efficient, this Article advocates for the deductibility of investment expenses and describes several beneficial implications associated with the institution of this proposed reform

ef78496c13:d93526d5ab31cb29.title: Workplace Transformation And Its Tax Compliance Implications
ef78496c13:d93526d5ab31cb29.author: Soled, Jay A.
ef78496c13:d93526d5ab31cb29.summary: Due to technological advances and the COVID-19 pandemic, taxpayers are increasingly utilizing their homes as a focal point from which to conduct their business affairs. On the one hand, the nation should applaud this workplace transformation insofar as it may enhance job performance and efficiency, reduce product cost and overhead, and improve work-life balance. On the other hand, this transformation process may open the door to rampant tax abuse as taxpayers alone or in collusion with their employers seek to transform home usage into a tax shelter refuge. This analysis delves directly into the income tax compliance concerns that the workplace transformation engenders. It does so by exposing the nature of the problem, its prevalence, what it might cost the nation annually in terms of lost revenue, and why current safeguards are failing to achieve their sought-after objectives. The good news is that if Congress proactively takes immediate remedial measures to address this nascent problem, such actions could help foster taxpayer compliance, defend the income tax base, and halt the depletion of the nation’s revenue coffers. However, if Congress dallies and is derelict in fulfilling its oversight duties, this problem is poised to go from bad to worse.

ef78496c13:2a829ab142f8603a.title: AI subsidies as a tool for redistribution
ef78496c13:2a829ab142f8603a.author: Lucas Parmentier
ef78496c13:2a829ab142f8603a.summary: I study the optimal taxation of artificial intelligence (AI). My analysis highlights a wage-compression effect that provides a rationale for subsidizing AI, as AI adoption may reduce rather than increase wage inequality. When this effect outweighs AI's social costs, AI should be subsidized instead of taxed. I treat AI as a productive input distinct from robots, as the two technologies perform different ranges of tasks. Using numerical simulations, I demonstrate that the optimal policy for AI may differ sharply from that for robots. Under the benchmark calibration, AI is subsidized, whereas robots are taxed. Therefore, the case for taxing AI is weaker than is commonly assumed. When AI lowers the skill premium, fiscal policy may need to encourage, rather than slow, adoption.

ef78496c13:d25c012959c8c987.title: Perverse Tax Incentives and the Destruction of Creative Works
ef78496c13:d25c012959c8c987.author: Maher, Luke
ef78496c13:d25c012959c8c987.summary: In late 2023, Warner Bros. Discovery announced that it would be permanently shelving Coyote vs. Acme, a complete and hotly anticipated film about popular Looney Tunes characters. This announcement was widely understood—and admitted by Warner Bros. Discovery in its Securities and Exchange Commission filings—to be motivated, at least in part, by a desire to “write off” the film’s costs for tax purposes. This Article is the first to (1) provide a full account for the tax rules that govern what constitutes a “loss” for purposes of unreleased creative works, (2) evaluate whether those rules make sense from both a technical and policy perspective (concluding that they do not), and (3) compare the relative merit of other approaches to allowing tax losses for unreleased creative works. In so doing, this Article makes two necessary contributions to current tax scholarship: first, it links the robust property scholarship on waste to tax policy, setting forth a framework through which critical reappraisals of long-entrenched tax laws and policies can be conducted, identifying ossified policies that no longer comport with our policy goals and revenue-raising needs and developing ways to improve them. Second, it also offers guidance in the ways that the law can think about the ownership, abandonment, and taxation of intangible assets.

b0a91b96f4:a484eaa198cae704.summary: In a month full of big stories, perhaps the biggest business story was the fall from grace of Jensen Huang and the consequences for Nvidia, investors, and the rest of the AI trade. The initial story, with its potent mix of personal fallibility and security concerns, related to Jensen’s affair with Alice Huang, who news stories labeled a Chinese spy, though the evidence on the ground is still thin. I had planned to write about the story then, but on the road in Asia and with teaching commitments, I put it off for a few days, and over those days, the story took a turn, with stories of dalliances with Nvidia employees. Last week culminated with Nvidia’s board asking Jensen to step down, and his agreeing, perhaps bringing to an end one of the more eventful and productive stints as a CEO in corporate history. I have no desire or standing to debate the moral aspects of this story, and I will let others take sides on whether the board should or should not have fired Jensen. In this post, I will focus on the question of what Jensen stepping down as CEO might mean for Nvidia’s value, and whether after the market correction over the last three weeks, the market has overreached. What does a CEO do? What does a CEO do for a business? Given the many tasks that go into creating, building, and running a business, it should come as no surprise that the list is long, but I will classify them broadly into groups: Storyteller: Every business is built around a story, and that story drives its valuation and sometimes its pricing. While that story is grounded in the company’s products and the markets that it seeks, it is the top manager’s job to craft and tell the story to investors, employees and to consumers. Clearly, the significance of this component of a CEO’s story will shift, depending on where the company is in its life cycle, with its importance being greatest at either end of the life cycle. b0a91b96f4:d6c6609f6ee2fd04.title: The Rocky Road from Aggregate to Per Share Value: Anthropic's IPO update
b0a91b96f4:d6c6609f6ee2fd04.author: Aswath Damodaran (noreply@blogger.com)
b0a91b96f4:d6c6609f6ee2fd04.summary: I valued Anthropic in a post on November 2, 2026, and while estimating a value of $1.475 trillion for the equity in the company, I noted that the share count was a placeholder, while we waited for bankers to make a final judgment on how many shares would be outstanding in the company. I promised that I would return to complete the per share valuation, when the details were made available, and an updated prospectus filed last week filled that gap. The world has not stayed still in the fifteen days since my original valuation, and both company-level and macro developments require an update to my valuation. The prospectus was updated to include third quarter numbers, and the midterm elections have potentially altered the economics of the AI business, as data centers may become more difficult and expensive to build and AI regulations may become more stringent. In this post, I will start with a general discussion of how share count is complicated by the existence of multiple classes of shares and stock-based compensation, and argue that the absence of standardization has made share count the Wild West in investing, with consequences for both intrinsic valuation and pricing. I will then update my valuation of Anthropic and assess the per share value, based on the prospectus that was just filed. The Elusive Share Count When I first started valuing companies, getting from aggregate value to equity value per share was a trivial exercise, where you divided the aggregate value by the number of shares outstanding. This was, of course, a period when almost every US company had only one class of shares and stock-based compensation was still in its nascent stages, and lightly used. b0a91b96f4:e32bca821dbdec7c.summary: When I posted my valuation of Anthropic a few days ago, I noted that turbulence lay ahead, both for the company and the market. I did not expect that turbulence to be this forceful and arrive this soon, but markets don't have an obligation to wait until it is convenient for investors, to adjust to new realities. With the election results on November 3 acting as a catalyst, investors initially responded positively with stocks up on Wednesday, but reversed course sharply on Thursday, with the NASDAQ down close to 6% and the S&P 500 declining 4%. This drop has again brought to the forefront questions about the AI trade and whether it has run its course. In this post, I will start by referring to my earlier note on AI as a business, and use the ideas in it to deconstruct the many players that are lumped together as AI companies, from those spending the money building the data centers (hyperscalers) to the firms benefiting from selling the builders the ingredients for these data centers (chip makers, electrical equipment, power and even real estate) to the companies that are spending considerable amounts , leasing these data centers for long periods (with the LLMs in the lead). I will argue that while all of these groups benefit, at least in general, from AI's success at creating large and profitable markets, we are at a point in the AI disruption, where their interests and payoffs will diverge, with implications for both the businesses and investors. I use last week's market carnage in technology and examine how the market treatment of these different groups may be a reflection of a more discerning market, less willing to mark up and mark down all AI companies, and more likely to treat them differently, as their business interests diverge. b0a91b96f4:7ec112c975bad06e.author: Aswath Damodaran (noreply@blogger.com)
b0a91b96f4:7ec112c975bad06e.summary: I was in San Francisco last week to talk to NYU Stern Alumni on October 15, and it was the day that Anthropic had a pre-IPO meeting with prospective investors. While I was not at the meeting, the focus of teh gathering was laying a foundation for its upcoming IPO, with the company reporting third-quarter revenue of $16.8 billion, which news reports described as surging 45% over the previous quarter's revenues, and positive profits, albeit on an adjusted basis. During the meeting, Anthropic also reported an annual revenue run rate (ARR) of $67 billion, a metric that those in the AI space have adopted with gusto, with an estimate that the ARR would exceed $100 billion by the end of the year. The nature of ARR, where choices on how revenue is calculated (gross versus net) and on annualization periods (daily, weekly or monthly) can make a significant difference, has led investors to be skeptical about comparing these numbers across time and companies. While I share some of that skepticism, it is worth remembering that young businesses are often priced on inventive metrics, some with more basis than others. In the late nineties, dot.com companies were priced not just on the number of visitors to their websites, but on eyeballs , where Mary Meeker argued that ad spending at these companies was correlated with time that these visitors spent on websites (eyeballs) rather than total visitors. In the last decade, you saw social media companies priced based upon the number of users and subscription-based companies on subscriber numbers. In this post, I will try to lay out the rationale for why pricing supplants valuation in young companies and why that pricing almost always has to be built around messy metrics like eyeballs, users and ARR, rather than more conventional metrics like earnings, book value or cash flows. 1aa97d921e:1bc106d2fe57d9bb.title: How George Stigler and the Chicago School Opened the Marketplace of Ideas to Business
1aa97d921e:1bc106d2fe57d9bb.author: Edward Nik-Khah
1aa97d921e:1bc106d2fe57d9bb.summary: Henry Simons, the “Crown Prince” of the Chicago School and a professor in the economics department and the law school prior to World War II, sought to develop a laissez faire economics program devoted to eliminating monopoly and pursuing egalitarian goals. George Stigler and the Chicago School abandoned Simons’s anti-monopoly and egalitarian program. The best market became one driven by the search for profits, and the best-functioning marketplace of ideas arose where winning ideas reflected the greater funding backing them, writes Edward Nik-Khah. 1aa97d921e:93e02838a27ed28b.title: The Chicago School Abandoned the Positive Freedom of Adam Smith and the Founding Fathers
1aa97d921e:93e02838a27ed28b.author: Maha Rafi Atal
1aa97d921e:93e02838a27ed28b.summary: Adam Smith’s theory of political economy did not begin with the isolated individual but rather the individual who operates to earn the respect of others. Wealth and freedom grew from these relationships and engaging with others to create a free society, or what 20th century philosopher Isaiah Berlin’s would call positive freedom. In the 1970s and ‘80s, the Chicago School abandoned this aspect of freedom in preference of the isolated individual, which in turn produced a weaker concept of freedom, morality, and society that has stifled the cultivation of all three in the United States, writes Maha Rafi Atal. Read it at ProMarket >>

1aa97d921e:8cf8fcb20f958484.title: Adam Smith’s Moral Philosophy Complicates Interpretations by the Chicago School and Its Critics
1aa97d921e:8cf8fcb20f958484.author: Sandra Peart and David Levy
1aa97d921e:8cf8fcb20f958484.summary: The connections between Adam Smith’s Wealth of Nations and Theory of Moral Sentiments reveal a much more complicated understanding of how markets work than developed in the common interpretation by the Chicago School of economics or that of its critics. Smith’s political economy based on commerce, sympathy, and competition produced social good but only when complemented and checked by other forces. When not checked, Smith worried about “factions” that produce bad outcomes, write Sandra J. Peart and David M. Levy. Read it at ProMarket >>

1aa97d921e:21d2bb63cb082313.title: Why Economics Forsook Democracy
1aa97d921e:21d2bb63cb082313.author: Robert Van Horn
1aa97d921e:21d2bb63cb082313.summary: The post-World War II Chicago School of Aaron Director and Milton Friedman reimagined a new (neo) liberalism that treated economic liberties and the free market as the greatest defense of political rights. The government, and democracy, were more often than not barriers to economic liberties. The United States continues to suffer from neoliberalism’s prescriptions, and addressing the concerns of today’s populist movements will mean rediscovering ideas of freedom that the Chicago School denigrated, writes Robert Van Horn. Read it at ProMarket >>

1aa97d921e:d2d33a26a587fd61.title: The University of Chicago Once Studied a Laissez-Faire Economics Compatible with Public Interest
1aa97d921e:d2d33a26a587fd61.author: David Mitch
1aa97d921e:d2d33a26a587fd61.summary: The Chicago School is often associated with laissez-faire economics that reads into Adam Smith’s philosophy of political economy justifications for self-interest and prudential motivations. However, a careful history of the University of Chicago’s early Economics Department and School of Commerce and Administration reveals a more complicated understanding of how economics and business were to interact with one another and society. The early University of Chicago pursued a program that emphasized that laissez-faire economics and a concern for the public interest were not antagonists but perfectly compatible, writes David Mitch. Read it at ProMarket >>

1aa97d921e:f1e2511bf4ba4c0f.title: America Became Rich Because of Liberalism
1aa97d921e:f1e2511bf4ba4c0f.author: Peter J. Boettke
1aa97d921e:f1e2511bf4ba4c0f.summary: Adam Smith and the Founding Fathers envisioned a society in which economic and political freedom, grouped together in the ideology of liberalism, would produce a wealthy, free, and peaceful society. Centuries later, this vision has come to fruition, and F. A. Hayek and Milton Friedman helped elaborate and advance that vision in their economic and philosophical works. The lesson for today’s populist moment is not to abandon these principles, but to continue to pursue them, as it is their imperfect realization, not their imperfect conceptualization, that burdens today’s society, writes Peter Boettke. Read it at ProMarket >>

1aa97d921e:c0503e070848a375.title: American Antitrust Has Yet To Figure Out Conglomerates
1aa97d921e:c0503e070848a375.author: Paul Friederiszick
1aa97d921e:c0503e070848a375.summary: The Neo-Brandeisians and Chicago School have employed different statistics to show respectively that markets are both concentrated and not concentrated, leaving Americans in the dark about who really holds corporate power. The evidence only looks contradictory due to the failure of American antitrust scholarship and regulation to understand how conglomerates collect market power across many neighboring markets, through what Paul Friederiszick calls “adjacent market takeovers.” This strategy can make firms more efficient, but it can also raise prices and weaken competition even as each individual market still looks competitive, he writes, drawing on his new paper, “The Conglomerate Power Puzzle.” Read it at ProMarket >>

1aa97d921e:ad66736fb16d41a6.author: Eli Orbach
1aa97d921e:ad66736fb16d41a6.summary: The transaction fees that businesses incur using credit and debit cards cost Americans billions of dollars each year. Despite the availability of alternative, cheaper account-to-account options that cut out the middleman, Americans have been slow to move away from card payment systems due to market mechanisms that hide the true costs of card transactions to consumers, writes Eli Orbach. 1aa97d921e:6ae56baa9c09d5f6.title: Two Questions Determine Whether a Pricing Algorithm Becomes Evidence of Price Fixing
1aa97d921e:6ae56baa9c09d5f6.author: Roger D. Blair and Javier D. Donna
1aa97d921e:6ae56baa9c09d5f6.summary: Two recent court rulings on casino-hotels using a shared software to fix prices reveal the importance of information exchanges as a super plus factor: an indicator of illegal conspiracy to limit trade. Donna discuss how these court cases and other recent lawsuits elucidate the role of the information exchange and the two vectors that determine its strength as a plus factor: data sensitivity and a give-to-get understanding among firms that if they shared their data, competitors would do the same.
