The court ordered Myanmar to investigate and punish those responsible, provide reparations to the Rohingya and allow refugees to return. Still, the ICJ has no direct way to enforce its ruling. What they're saying: "This judgment must now translate into real action," UN Human Rights Chief Volker Türk said in a statement . "The Court has made clear Myanmar's responsibilities. It sends a strong message to all States around the world that those responsible for genocide will be held to account." Myanmar's opposition National Unity Government welcomed the ruling, saying it would "carefully consider the Court's findings and any orders issued" and remained committed to holding perpetrators accountable and preventing further atrocities. Flashback: In 2022, the Biden administration formally declared that Myanmar's military committed genocide against the country's Rohingya minority and crimes against humanity. The ICJ in 2020 ordered Myanmar to protect Rohingya from genocide while the…

33e1d7779a:fa9bfba5949da6d4.title: Why the Senate energy permitting bill might become law
33e1d7779a:fa9bfba5949da6d4.author: Ben Geman
33e1d7779a:fa9bfba5949da6d4.summary: If the sweeping Senate permitting bill becomes law, it will reflect a rare convergence of political and market forces strong enough to trump the Beltway aversion to big, bipartisan deals. Why it matters: The bill could transform how America builds energy infrastructure, with major implications for everything from electricity costs to data centers. Getting rid of bureaucratic hurdles for energy projects is a top priority for the fossil fuels and renewables sectors. But critics argue the plan would unacceptably weaken environmental protections and the rights of Native American tribes. The latest: A vote on final passage of the White House-backed bill could occur Thursday after the Senate plows through some more amendments. The big picture: Many industries — pipelines, transmission, housing, you name it — call permitting a long bureaucratic and judicial maze that stymies projects. Yes, but: That, on its own, isn't nearly enough to get this far. Here are other reasons the bill has a path to becoming law after years of failed efforts to upend permitting. 🗳️ The cost-of-living election. The midterms were soaked in affordability politics at a time of rising energy bills. While critics can call the projected savings modest, cost is politically front and center. The Rhodium Group estimates that big provisions it analyzed would cut average residential power prices by 3%-4% in 2035. Third Way, a group that favors the bill, supported the research firm's work. 📈 Rising electricity demand. U.S. power thirst has been rising in the last few years after staying largely flat for decades, driven partly by AI and wider electrification of the economy. 🦋 A maturing clean energy industry. As sectors like renewables and storage become more mainstream, " more developers and companies are seeing the real-world challenges" of doing projects, clean energy lobbyist Jeff Navin notes via email. That puts them in agreement with utilities and oil and gas companies. "They all run into problems…

33e1d7779a:bc80716f0fe45a2e.title: New alarm over China controlling drug supply chains
33e1d7779a:bc80716f0fe45a2e.author: Adriel Bettelheim
33e1d7779a:bc80716f0fe45a2e.summary: China is intensifying efforts to control the entire drug supply chain, putting the U.S. at risk of being cut off from future lifesaving treatments, the National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology warns in a new analysis out Thursday. Why it matters: Western drug giants have invested huge sums in Chinese biotechs to boost their product pipelines. But sharing capital and expertise could give Beijing more control over critical pharmaceutical technologies. Concerns about the U.S. getting boxed out have intensified after the Chinese government proposed new restrictions last month on the export of certain technologies, including cell and gene therapy platforms. Driving the news: Western drug giants are increasingly entering into licensing agreements with Chinese firms that redirect U.S. capital away from U.S. innovation and toward the Chinese pharmaceutical industry, the commission found in its analysis of 57 deals from the beginning of 2023 through last month. The deals are being made earlier in the drug discovery process, allowing the Chinese partners to gain not just capital but know-how in developing and commercializing treatments. This kind of knowledge transfer in automobiles, semiconductors and industrial chemicals gave Chinese industry a competitive edge and leverage to control global markets for the products, according to the commission, which was established by Congress to examine how emerging biotech intersects with national security. "The end game is the same for the [Chinese Communist Party] in the pharmaceutical industry," the commission warns, saying the goal is increased U.S. dependence on Chinese innovation and enrichment of the Chinese pharmaceutical industry. Between the lines: Drugmakers including AstraZeneca, Bristol Myers Squibb and Pfizer have been drawn by China's surge of investment in the life sciences and the promise of faster clinical trials and product approvals. Typically a Chinese biotechnology company sells the license to…

33e1d7779a:68413ff474446dbc.title: Poll: Republicans in early 2028 primary states back Israel, not its critics
33e1d7779a:68413ff474446dbc.author: Marc Caputo
33e1d7779a:68413ff474446dbc.summary: Republican voters in four early 2028 primary states have favorable views of Israel by wide margins and have negative opinions of three leading right-wing critics of the Jewish state, according to a new poll by a national GOP consulting firm. Why it matters: The poll challenges the notion that Republican opinion toward Israel is fracturing significantly, and points to a potential disconnect between GOP voters' attitudes and the sentiments of those who often draw the most attention online. The survey, conducted by OnMessage Inc . for the Combat Antisemitism Movement 's political arm, essentially provides a roadmap for pro-Israel Republicans' messaging ahead of the 2028 presidential campaign. It seeks to cast the right's leading critics of Israel — Tucker Carlson, Candace Owens and Nick Fuentes — as liabilities in the GOP primary. Zoom in: After the midterms, Vice President Vance called on the U.S. and the GOP to "change our relationship to Israel," elevating the nations' longtime partnership as a 2028 campaign issue at a time when Vance is eyeing a presidential bid. Israel is supported by 68% of Republican voters in Iowa, New Hampshire, Nevada and South Carolina, according to the survey, a result similar to findings by Gallup and Pew . 17% disfavored Israel. 78% said the GOP's "relationship with Israel" makes them more likely to vote Republican. Large majorities also agreed with pro-Israel messages. In contrast , 53% of those surveyed said they disapprove of Carlson, and 30% approve. But among voters under 45 years old, Carlson's approval/disproval ratings were tied at 46%. 49% of the Republicans surveyed disapproved of Owens, while 23% approved. Fuentes, the least-known of the three media figures, was viewed unfavorably by 25% and favored by 13%. Among self-described MAGA Republicans, 22% approved and 23% disapproved of him, however. "The fringe messengers are underwater," says a slide deck for the poll, which was conducted ahead of the Combat Antisemitism…

33e1d7779a:6f70168f6a21bc7a.title: Putting cyber risk in perspective, from the experts (our own CTO)
33e1d7779a:6f70168f6a21bc7a.author: Dan Cox
33e1d7779a:6f70168f6a21bc7a.summary: Axios chief technology officer Dan Cox, who's spent 25 years at some of the world's biggest tech companies, puts the recent spate of high-profile failures in perspective: My parents, my siblings and plenty of other people are asking the same question: How worried should we be? The big picture: I've been in technology a long time. I take these threats seriously , but I'm not in panic mode. When something breaks, we need to understand what happened, how far it reaches and what we can do about it. A frightening headline doesn't answer those questions. Zoom out: The way I think about it, we've put powerful tools in more hands, and people are taking potshots to see what they can hit. Those shots can do real damage, and we need to protect ourselves. But hearing gunfire doesn't, by itself, mean an army is coming over the hill. We need to understand who's firing, what they can actually do and whether the threat is changing. Zoom in: Over the past few weeks, we've identified bad actors snooping around our own website, too. Our talented engineers have investigated threats and put mitigations in place. There may still be attempts on our site, but each incident gives us an opportunity to strengthen our systems. Between the lines: There are thousands of smart, resourceful and dedicated engineers working to protect the systems we all rely on. I see that commitment in our own team. I believe that if the threat grows, more people with those skills will step up. That's part of why I have confidence in our ability to respond, even as the threats evolve. The bottom line: Fred Rogers shared his mother's advice for frightening news: "Look for the helpers. You will always find people who are helping." I think about that here. There are a lot of capable people working on these problems. I have confidence in them, even while we have real work to do. I want people to feel informed enough to act, rather than frightened enough to assume the worst.

33e1d7779a:5ce699bc856d9e7f.title: Doomsday prepping goes mainstream
33e1d7779a:5ce699bc856d9e7f.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:5ce699bc856d9e7f.summary: The internet has caught the emergency preparation bug , fueled by fears of AI-led cyberattacks , power grid vulnerabilities, transportation standstills and international threats . The big picture: The "prepper" mindset is resonating with larger slices of society — who are packing emergency bags, stocking up on water and taking inventory of non-perishables. Michael Mills, a University of Greenwich senior lecturer who studies doomsday preparation, says some people are turning to "lightweight versions" of traditional prepping amid doubts about global stability. By the numbers: Sales at Survival Frog, a survival retailer that sells gear like emergency food and radios, saw sales jump 450% between Oct. 27 and Nov. 16, compared to prior weeks, CEO and founder Byron Walker tells Axios. Competitors saw similar trends, he says. And most recent buyers at Survival Frog were new customers. Food, including canned meats, leads demand, Walker says, followed by products like radios, solar generators, battery packs and water filters. State of play: Systems the world relies on for travel , communications , business , food, health care and more have been disrupted in recent weeks — whether because of tech shortfalls or malicious acts. While officials assure the incidents aren't broadly connected, fears of critical infrastructure failing are growing, and more people considering how to prepare for crises. "It does seem much more mainstream now," Walker says of preppers. "You can't turn on the news without hearing about a new cyber attack or a tech meltdown." Many of the emergency preparation skills people are using have long been observed in disaster-prone areas. And as many Americans learned during COVID, supply chain disruptions mean having extra water, radios and shelf-stable foods around the house isn't a bad thing. Krystal, known online as the "Queen of Doomsday," spends about five hours daily coaching new preppers and told Axios that recent online engagement with her content,…

33e1d7779a:f7d36e06473d502c.title: AI's great divergence: Machines accelerate as makers unravel
33e1d7779a:f7d36e06473d502c.author: Zachary Basu
33e1d7779a:f7d36e06473d502c.summary: Anthropic will make its Wall Street debut Thursday at a moment of profound contradiction in the history of AI: The humans are embattled — bogged down by scandal, financial turmoil and political revolt. But the machines are ascendant — accelerating toward an "intelligence explosion" they expect will transform civilization. Why it matters: The industry's recent chaos has obscured a breathtaking surge in technological progress, forcing some of the world's leading researchers to reconsider just how soon AI could surpass human intelligence. Zoom in: Inside Anthropic, soon to be valued north of $1 trillion, independent researchers at METR found that AI models are advancing at nearly twice their historical pace — largely fueled, they believe, by AI itself. Anthropic's own data shows Claude went from leading fewer than 1% of the company's AI research tasks in February to more than a quarter by August, with humans still supervising. METR found no clear obstacles to sustaining this pace over the next year, and reviewed confidential evidence suggesting the acceleration itself may be gathering speed. Zoom out: Across the frontier, leading companies are racing up what Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei calls "the exponential." OpenAI disclosed Tuesday that Astra 6.2 is its first publicly released model to reach the "High" threshold for AI self-improvement — equivalent, the company says, to giving every researcher another highly capable engineer. The advances span both software and silicon: OpenAI says its models helped AMD compress a year of chip-design progress into less than five months, while Google's Gemini is reducing weeks of chip-layout work to hours. The big picture: These breakthroughs are pushing some of AI's top forecasters to shorten their timelines for the fabled "intelligence explosion" — a runaway cascade of self-improving AI that could propel machine intelligence far beyond human comprehension. The influential AI Futures Project now expects machines to surpass the…

33e1d7779a:254b01190ebf6612.title: Exclusive: Bots amplified conspiracy theories and panic about recent tech outages
33e1d7779a:254b01190ebf6612.author: Sam Sabin
33e1d7779a:254b01190ebf6612.summary: Bot accounts have helped spread conspiracy theories about a wave of major tech outages over the last week, according to new research shared exclusively with Axios. Why it matters: Purveyors of disinformation appear to be exploiting public anxiety over the cyberattacks and fragile infrastructure, amplifying suspicions of coordinated cyberattacks and government cover-ups. While it's unclear who's behind these accounts, the pattern shows that when technology failures lack substantive explanations, bot networks will fill the void to manufacture panic. Catch up quick: Microsoft, Apple, JPMorgan Chase, United, Workday, the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Security Agency each faced outages over the last week. Then came the conspiracy theories: When the FAA grounded flights for four hours Friday, people were quick to assume it was tied to the rollout of an AI tool at the agency. Some also tried linking the widespread Microsoft outage to recent company layoffs. Yes, but : There's no publicly established evidence that these outages were part of a coordinated cyberattack, despite the theories circulating online. Several companies have attributed their disruptions to technical problems, rather than malicious activity, including efforts to patch vulnerabilities in order to make software more resilient. Downdetector data show that while the seven days through Monday saw the highest number of weekly outages in the last 12 months, longer-term patterns are far from unprecedented, as Axios previously reported . By the numbers: Suspected bots accounted for roughly 30% of posts promoting conspiracy theories about several recent tech outages, according to data from social media monitoring firm PeakMetrics. During Microsoft's outage, bots accounted for 26% of conspiratorial posts. Bots accounted for 34% of conspiracy-related posts during Friday's Workday outage, compared with 27% of other posts. Likely bot accounts also made up 31% of conspiracy-related posts about…

33e1d7779a:13a46f7720ed7db1.title: Republicans lost hope in Reconciliation 3.0
33e1d7779a:13a46f7720ed7db1.author: Kate Santaliz
33e1d7779a:13a46f7720ed7db1.summary: The Senate GOP's last-ditch effort to pass a defense-heavy, $350 billion reconciliation package is dead on arrival without accompanying spending cuts, House Republicans tell Axios. Why it matters: House Republicans have just 16 days left in session before Democrats take control in January. Many don't want to spend their final days in power adding to the national debt. "My concern is we squander these very few days we have left on something that won't get out of the House," outgoing House Budget Chair Jodey Arrington (R-Texas) told Axios of the Senate's emerging plan. Republicans have already passed two party-line reconciliation bills this Congress: The "one big, beautiful bill" in the summer of 2025, and nearly $70 billion for immigration enforcement in the summer of 2026. Zoom in: Finding spending offsets could reopen some of the most contentious fights from the GOP's first reconciliation package. Arrington told Axios that Senate Republicans worry that finding cost savings in health care spending could open the door to amendment votes that undo Medicaid cuts in the One Big, Beautiful Bill Act. But Arrington, who didn't run for reelection in 2026, told Axios he doesn't believe the Senate's proposal has the votes to pass the House without offsets. State of play: Arrington said he raised his concerns with Senate Budget Chair Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), and argued Republicans shouldn't let the risks deter them from pursuing additional spending cuts. "Some Republican members of the Senate might go rogue and might decide to, I don't know, repeal some of the reforms that we put in the 'big, beautiful bill.' Maybe they do it out of spite for President Trump," he said. "The midterms have passed us. We lost, but we still have this window to do what we think is right," he said. Between the lines: Senate Republicans haven't committed to moving forward with another reconciliation package. Leaving a Wednesday night meeting on reconciliation, Sen. Johnson told reporters the Senate…

33e1d7779a:a29e7d64fbf456aa.title: "There'll be no hostage-taking": The anti-Jeffries rebellion that failed to materialize
33e1d7779a:a29e7d64fbf456aa.author: Andrew Solender
33e1d7779a:a29e7d64fbf456aa.summary: The left's campaign to whip up a groundswell of opposition to House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) among his members failed in stunning fashion on Wednesday. Why it matters: Fewer than a dozen members voted against Jeffries' nomination for speaker. That bodes well for Jeffries' ability to manage the House going forward, his allies say. "There'll be no hostage taking," Rep. Troy Carter (D-La.) told Axios. Driving the news: Jeffries won a resounding victory Wednesday morning when House Democrats met behind closed doors to vote on their nominee for speaker of the House. Out of 264 Democratic House members and non-voting delegates, 251 voted to nominate him, 11 voted against and two did not vote. It was exactly the victory Jeffries' allies had hoped for after Tuesday's announcement that he planned to request a tallied vote rather than being nominated by acclamation. Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier (D-N.Y.), Adam Hamawy (D-N.J.), Melat Kiros (D-Colo.), Donavan McKinney (D-Mich.), Chris Rabb (D-Pa.) and Claire Valdez (D-N.Y.) put out a statement shortly after the vote confirming they voted against Jeffries. Rep.-elect Frederick Haynes III (D-Texas) also signed on to that statement, but a spokesperson said in a follow-up statement he "narrowly missed the vote" and that his "intended vote was no." Two other members-elect, Don Leonard (D-Ohio) and Angela Gonzales-Torres (D-Calif.), told Axios they also voted no. Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda (D-N.C.) missed the vote because he was in his district with family following the death of his father, but would have voted for Jeffries, a spokesperson told Axios. Zoom out: Many of the progressives who ultimately voted for Jeffries did so despite a torrent of phone calls and emails from constituents and grassroots activists urging them not to support him. Numerous high-profile progressives had said before the meeting they would vote for Jeffries, including Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.)…

33e1d7779a:9e95a87976f998d0.title: Anthropic valued at over $1 trillion in historic IPO
33e1d7779a:9e95a87976f998d0.author: Dan Primack
33e1d7779a:9e95a87976f998d0.summary: Anthropic on Wednesday raised over $81 billion in a long-awaited IPO that valued the Claude maker at over $1 trillion. Why it matters: Wall Street expects the AI boom to continue, despite some recent tumult. Zoom in: Anthropic priced at $83 per share, well above its planned range of $70 to $78 per share. It imputes an initial market cap of $1.08 trillion and a fully diluted value of around $1.5 trillion. Anthropic originally planned to sell 825 million shares, but increased it to 980 million shares. The company also could raise significantly more money if underwriters exercise their so-called "greenshoe" option, while Anthropic also will receive $26 billion via a concurrent private placement from tech giants like Nvidia, Google and Microsoft. Allocation decisions are expected to last several hours on Thursday evening. Context: Anthropic was valued at $965 billion in its most recent private round. The apples-to-apples comparison would be with the fully diluted value. SpaceX is the current IPO record-holder having raised $86.25 billion, although that included the greenshoe. What we're watching: Shares are expected to begin trading Thursday, Nov. 19, on the Nasdaq under the ticker "ANT."

33e1d7779a:558ecf00060ef09c.title: Mississippi senator-elect turns historic win into nationwide Nike offer
33e1d7779a:558ecf00060ef09c.author: Julianna Bragg
33e1d7779a:558ecf00060ef09c.summary: High school students across the U.S. have a new reason to vie for the top spot in their class: a custom pair of Nike Air Force 1 sneakers, thanks to a request from Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom . Why it matters: Colom is putting a fresh spin on academic achievement, turning his historic election into a nationwide incentive for students to hit the books — with a little help from Nike and no taxpayer dollars. What they're saying: Colom initially asked if Nike would celebrate the historic milestone by giving a custom-made version of his favorite sneakers to every Mississippi valedictorian for the 2026-2027 school year. "It would encourage MS students to hit the books the rest of the year! #justdoit," he wrote on X . Nike then upped the ante, extending the offer to valedictorians nationwide. "The athlete mindset makes things possible, including this idea," Nike said. Colom praised Nike for "stepping up to motivate students across the country in this historic moment," and suggested the design honor Hiram Revels, the first Black member of Congress who represented Mississippi. Context: There were more than 23,000 public high schools in the U.S. during the 2020-2021 school year and more than 3,600 private high schools during the 2019-2020 school year, according to the National Center for Education Statistics . A classic pair of Nike Air Force 1s retails for about $115 on Nike's website . Zoom in: In January, Colom will become Mississippi's first Democratic senator in nearly four decades and its first Black senator in almost 150 years. The senator-elect pulled off a stunning upset of Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the ruby-red state, which hadn't elected a Black senator since Reconstruction. His victory was fueled in part by voters in the Mississippi Delta, where Emmett Till was abducted, Fannie Lou Hamer fought for the ballot and the blues became an American art form. What we're watching: What Nike cooks up for the nation's brightest students.

33e1d7779a:37f18f007637b671.title: Islam will overtake Christianity as world's largest religion by 2035: Pew
33e1d7779a:37f18f007637b671.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:37f18f007637b671.summary: Data: Pew Research ; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Islam is expected to surpass Christianity as the world's largest religion by 2035, according to Pew Research Center projections released Wednesday. Why it matters: The shift has less to do with people converting to Islam and more to do with who's having more kiddos , a demographic trend poised to reshape the world's religious makeup as Christianity's center of gravity moves to Africa. By the numbers: Muslims are projected to gain 1.6 billion people through births exceeding deaths from 2020 to 2070, according to new Pew data released Wednesday. Christians are expected to gain 792 million people through natural population change. From 2020 to 2025, Muslim women had an average fertility rate of 3.1 children, compared with 2.5 for Christian women. For all other women, the average was 1.6. What they're saying: "These religious figures are driven by demographic change," David Voas, a University College London professor who researches secularization, tells Axios. He says the countries growing the fastest — in North Africa, the Middle East, Near East and South Asia — have a relatively high Muslim population, so naturally Islam would eventually be the most populous religion. Zoom in: The U.S. is expected to lose more Christians than any other country by 2070, even as Christianity grows globally. The U.S. had the world's largest Christian population in 2020, at 217 million. By 2070, that number is expected to drop to 174 million. Meanwhile, the Democratic Republic of the Congo is expected to have nearly 300 million Christians by 2070, far surpassing the U.S. By then, 54% of the world's Christians are projected to live in sub-Saharan Africa. "The center of gravity of Christianity has been shifting towards the global south," Voas says. "Traditionally, we tended to think of Christianity as being a kind of Western religion … but of course Christianity was taken to Africa and around the world, and Africa is now growing faster than…

33e1d7779a:c14b93582f14889b.title: Trust, but prepare: How to make sense of AI's age of upheaval
33e1d7779a:c14b93582f14889b.author: Mike Allen
33e1d7779a:c14b93582f14889b.summary: Most Americans are baffled and alarmed by the daily, if not hourly, explosion of technical glitches hitting air travel, banks and work products like Microsoft Outlook. The outages seem genuinely scary and related. So what the hell is going on? The most likely answer : This is the first true wave of unintended consequences of increasingly powerful artificial intelligence hitting us at once. The big picture: In short, AI is exceptionally good at building software, and therefore exceptionally good at spotting and exploiting bugs in large technical, software-based systems. The glitches come from a mix of sources — some innocuous, some scary, including: routine updates to aging infrastructure; humans scrambling to patch vulnerabilities discovered by AI; hackers exploiting existing weaknesses; and bad actors using swarms of AI agents to launch increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks. That's the new reality that government officials and AI experts believe we're entering. They expect this period of disruption and heightened vulnerability to persist for months, as powerful new AI tools expose weaknesses buried in decades-old systems. The catchphrase gaining currency : " Software Beirut " — a period of cascading failures, many of our own making, that could grow worse before things get better. What this means for YOU : Understand the different causes, detailed below, and resist the temptation to panic every time something goes haywire. It's easy to hop on social media and let the algorithm drag you into doomsday thinking. You should also prepare : Reset and protect your passwords . Keep more cash on hand if possible, in case your bank is down for a day or two. Buy some basic emergency supplies in case power or water do go out. Sadly, we believe this season of glitches and possible cyberattacks will persist. Better to be prepared. Here's a more detailed look at the different causes of these glitches or breakdowns: 1. Updates to old systems: The government says last Friday's…

33e1d7779a:9321f6ec53e0ba4a.title: The senators who could join Van Hollen's insurgency against Schumer
33e1d7779a:9321f6ec53e0ba4a.author: Herb Scribner
33e1d7779a:9321f6ec53e0ba4a.summary: Sen. Chris Van Hollen is picking up endorsements in his challenge to Chuck Schumer for Senate Democratic leader. Why it matters: The leadership fight exposes divisions within the Democratic Party days after its sweeping midterm victory , with some demanding a new direction and others crediting Schumer for the historic blue wave. Driving the news: Van Hollen (D-Md.), a senator since 2017, announced Thursday he's challenging Schumer because "we need new leadership." "This is not about any one person — it's about answering the call of the American people." The other side: Schumer has far more public endorsements than Van Hollen. "Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?" Sen. Angus King (I-Maine) said in a statement of support for Schumer. Van Hollen has disputed Schumer's claim to credit for the party's midterm performance, arguing that the wave was powered by voters rather than leaders in Washington. By the numbers: Schumer has public support from 14 senators, including himself, compared with five for Van Hollen. A candidate will need 28 or 29 votes to win, depending on the outcome of Alaska's Senate race, where votes are still being counted. Senators backing Van Hollen State of play: Van Hollen told MS NOW he has "more than 10" senators on his side, though only four have publicly endorsed him. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) endorsed Van Hollen on Thursday night, saying he will fight for working families. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) threw his support behind Van Hollen when he announced his challenge Thursday. Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) issued an endorsement for Van Hollen Friday afternoon. Incoming Sen. Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) endorsed Van Hollen Friday morning after previously calling for new leadership. Who wants new leadership? Some sitting senators have called for a leadership change without endorsing Van Hollen. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) has called for change but hasn't endorsed either candidate. Before Van Hollen…

33e1d7779a:849efd209ddc4df6.title: Trump to meet Putin in China amid renewed push to end Ukraine war
33e1d7779a:849efd209ddc4df6.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:849efd209ddc4df6.summary: President Trump will hold a one-on-one meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday during the trilateral summit in China, a U.S. official said. Why it matters: The meeting in Shenzhen will take place as Trump is making another push for a breakthrough on ending the war in Ukraine. Driving the news: Also on Thursday, Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will meet in Berlin with Ukrainian and European officials to work on security guarantees for Ukraine as well as a postwar Europe-Russia security architecture. They want to coordinate ahead of the next round of negotiations with Russia in Abu Dhabi planned for next week. The big picture: The Trump-Putin meeting will take place on the sidelines of the trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The summit wasn't intended to deal with Ukraine, but U.S. allies are bracing for Trump to make unexpected public statements that serve the interests of Russia and China. "We know that every time President Trump talks to or sees Putin, it translates into bad news for Ukraine and for Europe. We brace for anything," a European diplomat told Axios.

33e1d7779a:3222a09f8f628767.title: House Democrats formally nominate Hakeem Jeffries for speaker
33e1d7779a:3222a09f8f628767.author: Andrew Solender
33e1d7779a:3222a09f8f628767.summary: House Democrats voted at a closed-door caucus meeting Wednesday morning to nominate Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) as their candidate for speaker. Why it matters: It's a symbolic but significant step that suggests Jeffries has the votes he needs to be elected the first Black House speaker on Jan. 3. Jeffries won 251 of the 262 votes cast, putting him comfortably above the 218 votes he needs to win on the House floor in January. The vote was tallied at Jeffries' request . His allied had initially hoped he would be elected by acclamation, but the Democratic leader changed tack at the 11th hour and decided to call his detractors' bluff. Between the lines: Wednesday's caucus vote was a secret ballot. On Jan. 3, each House member will have to stand up during a televised proceeding and announce who they are voting for. That could be difficult for the members — particularly progressives — who have been flooded with calls and emails from constituents urging them not to vote for him. Only a handful of incoming House members, including Reps.-elect Angela Gonzales-Torres (D-Calif.) and Don Leonard (D-Ohio), have outright said they will oppose Jeffries thus far.

33e1d7779a:e35b8f4cb2d0f48d.title: U.S. drivers are just absorbing high gasoline prices
33e1d7779a:e35b8f4cb2d0f48d.author: Ben Geman
33e1d7779a:e35b8f4cb2d0f48d.summary: Pain at the pump may have changed some votes, but it's apparently not prompting big changes in how much Americans drive. Why it matters: Most driving isn't especially optional, so people are absorbing the cost. This year Americans have paid an additional $88 billion for gasoline relative to a no-war baseline, according to Brown University's Climate Solutions Lab. The Energy Policy Research Foundation finds that U.S. households paid between $300 and $730 more on gasoline in March-August compared to the prior year. State of play: Gasoline demand from the beginning of March, right after the Iran war started, through early November is very similar to the same stretch last year, per federal data. There's "no discernible evidence of a decline in gasoline consumption," UC-Berkeley energy economist Lucas Davis writes in a new post on the topic. That's despite gasoline prices being 31% higher since the war began compared to the same period last year. The intrigue: Davis points out that the stubborn demand comes despite polling that shows Americans say high prices are changing their habits. He flags an April Washington Post-ABC News survey that showed 44% of respondents saying they had cut back on driving. Multiple polls show some version of this. For instance, 57% of respondents in a June Gallup survey said high prices were causing them to drive less. How it works: Davis' post and the chart above rely on the federal Energy Information Administration's measure of gasoline product supplied. EIA calls it a proxy for demand, and measures gasoline leaving the supply chain, including refineries and bulk terminals. There's no perfect measurement. The Transportation Department tracks miles traveled, though there's a lag. The most recent data, for August, does not show a drop-off this year. The bottom line: "[T]his is a valuable reminder of the gap between what people say and what they do," Davis writes. "Drivers may talk about cutting back, but studies in the economics literature…

33e1d7779a:33381f78cd1e1fef.title: Jeffries nears historic speakership as power shifts in Congress
33e1d7779a:33381f78cd1e1fef.author: Russell Contreras
33e1d7779a:33381f78cd1e1fef.summary: Hakeem Jeffries could soon become America's first Black House speaker, even as Black lawmakers confront rising threats to their power in D.C. Why it matters: Proposed committee term limits and another round of redistricting could weaken Black lawmakers' influence they spent decades building. By the numbers: The number of Black lawmakers in the 120th Congress will be stable from the 119th, based on results so far. The House will likely seat 59 Black voting members, down from 61, according to the Joint Center for Political and Economic Studies . All four Black House Republicans are departing, while Black Democrats have gained two seats. Black membership in the U.S. Senate will rise from five to a record seven, including Sens.-elect Scott Colom of Mississippi and Juliana Stratton of Illinois . Zoom in: Democrats are in the middle of a sometimes messy generational power transfer, with younger lawmakers challenging more senior members for committee chairmanships. Those chairmanships have long helped Congressional Black Caucus members exercise power beyond their numbers. "For CBC members, the power is seniority," Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.) told Politico in 2014. "I've been around a while. ... Some wisdom, at least, is important to what we're going through right now," Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman, 81, (D-N.J.) told Axios in 2025. Sticking point: Democrats are considering a four-term limit for committee leaders , starting after the 2028 elections, that could eventually force three veteran Black Democrats to step aside as committee leaders. Bennie Thompson, 78, of Mississippi, leads Democrats on Homeland Security. Bobby Scott, 79, of Virginia, leads Democrats on Education and Workforce. He faces a challenge from Connecticut Rep. Jahana Hayes, 53. Maxine Waters, 88, of California, leads Democrats on Financial Services. She faces a challenge from Illinois Rep. Sean Casten, 54. Zoom out: A Democratic wave helped Black incumbents survive redistricting this year, but that level…

33e1d7779a:0fc19eca6657d86b.title: Xi Jinping breaks protocol to greet and hug Trump at China airport
33e1d7779a:0fc19eca6657d86b.author: Herb Scribner
33e1d7779a:0fc19eca6657d86b.summary: Chinese President Xi Jinping greeted President Trump in a surprise appearance on the tarmac in Shenzhen, China, Wednesday. Why it matters: Xi paid Trump a special honor by greeting him on the tarmac, reciprocating a gesture by Trump during Xi's state visit to Washington in September. The two are expected to hold a summit Thursday with Russian President Vladimir Putin, where the three are expected to talk about nuclear arms control, Iran, Ukraine, trade and AI chips. Driving the news: Trump arrived in China for the annual APEC conference just hours after spending time in the Philippines. Xi met Trump at the bottom of Air Force One's stairs. The two leaders shook hands and then embraced in a hug. Dozens of performers, waving pom-poms, stood on a red carpet outside the plane, chanting and cheering for Trump's arrival. Context: Xi's surprise appearance was an unusual diplomatic gesture, per multiple reports . The Chinese president did not personally greet Trump when he visited Beijing in May. Similarly, when Putin visited Shenzhen earlier today, he was greeted by Xi's chief of staff Cai Qi . Xi met former President Obama at the airport in 2009 when Xi was still vice-president. Flashback: In September 2025, Trump welcomed President Xi at Joint Base Andrews for the Chinese leader's state visit to Washington D.C.. U.S. presidents typically receive foreign leaders at the White House. Trump met Xi at the bottom of the stairs after Xi's jet landed at the U.S. military base. Go deeper: U.S. allies on edge as Trump heads to summit with Xi and Putin

33e1d7779a:49ab632d805ac6eb.title: House Dems prepare for broad Trump family probe
33e1d7779a:49ab632d805ac6eb.author: Mike Allen
33e1d7779a:49ab632d805ac6eb.summary: Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, is laying the groundwork for a wave of investigations into President Trump's inner circle. Why it matters: It's going to be a long two years in Washington, as Democrats emboldened by the blue wave step up their scrutiny of those closest to the president and the administration. Driving the news: Garcia is sending document-retention letters Wednesday to Vice President Vance , Don Jr. , Eric Trump , Jared Kushner , Kimberly Guilfoyle , Stephen Miller , Susie Wiles , Kristi Noem , Corey Lewandowski , Attorney General Todd Blanche and more. "This is just the beginning," Garcia said in a statement. What to watch: How the administration responds. Already, at least one U.S. Attorney is going after other Democrats who've promised oversight actions in the coming Congress. This is a developing story.

33e1d7779a:82d56757238fe34c.title: America's measles return leaves infants vulnerable
33e1d7779a:82d56757238fe34c.author: Caitlin Owens
33e1d7779a:82d56757238fe34c.summary: The loss of the United States' measles elimination status is a particularly worrisome sign for infants in hot spots who are too young to be vaccinated against the disease. Why it matters: Outbreaks still may be concentrated within certain parts of the country. But infants and other unvaccinated people are living with a continuous threat. Driving the news: The Pan American Health Organization announced on Tuesday that it revoked the U.S. status after 26 years, as expected . That's after state reports of 7,700 cases and 10 deaths since measles first began spreading in Texas early last year, according to the New York Times . (The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention currently reports only nine deaths.) Hundreds of people — often unvaccinated children — have been hospitalized. State of play: The measles-mumps-rubella vaccine is highly effective, meaning the vast majority of cases today occur in people who haven't received an immunization against the disease. Just over 1 in 10 of those infected this year were hospitalized, but that jumps to 17% among children under 5 years old, per the CDC . Between the lines: For most of the population, remaining unvaccinated against measles is a choice, albeit one parents make for their children. But for the youngest Americans, receiving a vaccine isn't an option for several months. The earliest an infant can receive an immunization against measles is at 6 months, with the official recommendation for most children being a first dose between 12 and 15 months. Though infants do receive protective antibodies against measles from their mothers, those gradually decline over their first months of life. What they're saying: "Most babies don't receive a first measles vaccine until age 1. With measles endemic again, parents can no longer assume grocery stores, airports, churches, or even pediatricians' offices are safe spaces," Jerome Adams, President Trump's first-term surgeon general, posted on X. "The community protection we took for…

33e1d7779a:ec035efde6d99951.title: The terrifying rise of AI hacking tools
33e1d7779a:ec035efde6d99951.author: Sam Sabin
33e1d7779a:ec035efde6d99951.summary: A new breed of widely available AI tools is helping hackers launch cyberattacks around the clock , breaching corporate networks in a matter of hours and overwhelming defenders. Why it matters: AI-enabled hacking is still in its infancy, but open-source tools — which are free to download — are fundamentally changing the economics of cybercrime. Hackers can launch self-adjusting attack plans, allowing agents to find vulnerabilities and steal credentials, sometimes before human defenders realize their systems are being probed. Driving the news: Recent cyberattacks involving publicly available "AI agent frameworks" are drawing warnings about how quickly hackers can infiltrate corporate networks. The FBI warned Friday that hackers have used an AI framework called Artex to attack organizations worldwide, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours. In a separate report Friday , Amazon said hackers used Artex to steal AI model credentials, then used those stolen resources to power additional attacks. Last week, developer platform Railway and blockchain infrastructure provider Chainstack also reported attacks involving Artex. Palo Alto Networks said Thursday that Chinese-speaking hackers used another open-source framework, Cairn, to conduct 25 operations against at least 19 organizations between August and September. In a separate report Monday, Google said hackers used Cairn during an intrusion into the U.S. aerospace sector. CrowdStrike also saw one group using Artex to target more than 200 organizations worldwide over 11 days last month. Reality check : Cyberattacks are still scary and tech resiliency is still built on a faulty internet foundation, making mishaps possible even without clear evidence of AI-assisted hacks. A litany of popular services — including Microsoft , Apple , Chase , United , Workday , the Federal Aviation Administration , the National Security Agency — have all reported outages in the last…

33e1d7779a:24690346eb13f9b8.title: Alaska Native strongholds push Peltola into Senate history
33e1d7779a:24690346eb13f9b8.author: Russell Contreras
33e1d7779a:24690346eb13f9b8.summary: Mary Peltola's path to Senate history ran through four Alaska Native strongholds that delivered more than half of her statewide first-choice lead. Why it matters: The Yup'ik Democrat is the nation's first Alaska Native U.S. senator, powered by communities that endured disenfranchisement, forced displacement and federal violence. The win amplifies their voice on tribal sovereignty and subsistence rights after decades of neglect and discrimination — much as Mississippi Delta Black voters powered Democrat Scott Colom to his surprising Senate victory. By the numbers: Peltola led Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by roughly 12,400 first-choice votes statewide in Alaska's Nov. 17 unofficial count . Four western and northern House districts delivered a combined margin of about 6,700 votes. In Bristol Bay/Aleutians , for example, Peltola led by roughly 1,150 votes. In Bethel/Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta and Western Alaska/Norton Sound , she led by roughly 2,300 votes. In North Slope/Northwest Arctic , she led by approximately 900 votes. Stunning stat: Those four districts accounted for just about 5% of Alaska's first-choice Senate votes, but roughly 55% of Peltola's statewide lead. Alaska's 2021 redistricting report identifies Districts 37–40 as Alaska Native-controlled. Alaska Natives, alone or in combination, accounted for 85.8% of the voting-age population in District 38, 85.1% in 39, 62% in 40 and 43.8% in 37, using 2020 census figures. About 22% of Alaska residents identified as American Indian or Alaska Native, alone or in combination with another race, according to the 2020 census . State of play: Peltola carried the 50% margin needed to avoid Alaska's ranked-choice tabulation , where lower-ranked preferences from other candidates' supporters could have tipped the race toward another candidate. Michelle Sparck of the nonpartisan Get Out the Native Vote effort told KNBA that Native groups mounted aggressive outreach, including in Native languages. Organizers saw gains in some…

33e1d7779a:f5e9ced9235ebbdb.title: Mary Peltola unseats Republican Dan Sullivan in Alaska, extending Democratic wave
33e1d7779a:f5e9ced9235ebbdb.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:f5e9ced9235ebbdb.summary: Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated two-term Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan , flipping another GOP-held seat in a state President Trump carried comfortably in 2024, the AP projects. Why it matters: Peltola becomes the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Alaska since 2008, extending a historic blue wave in a race marred by controversy. Her victory comes in a state Trump carried by 13 points in 2024, underscoring the extraordinary reach of the Democratic backlash against his second term. It also delivers another blow to Republicans after sweeping Democratic victories in states including Texas, Ohio, Iowa and South Carolina. State of play: The race drew scrutiny after The New York Times reported allegations that Democratic operatives recruited another candidate named Dan Sullivan to draw votes from the incumbent. Peltola's campaign denied involvement, but the reporting prompted Alaska's Republican governor, Mike Dunleavy, to order an investigation into whether state laws were broken. The Justice Department also launched a criminal investigation and subpoenaed people connected to the alleged effort. No one involved in the race has been charged with a crime. On the campaign trail, the candidates clashed over the cost of living, the Iran war and Alaska's energy industry, with Peltola challenging Sullivan's record in Washington. Peltola campaigned on her signature "fish, family and freedom" message, emphasizing affordability, protecting Alaska's fisheries and putting the state's interests ahead of party politics. Trump traveled to Alaska in October to rally support for Sullivan, whom he praised as one of Washington's most respected senators. Sullivan embraced the president's support , betting it would energize Republican voters despite their party's political headwinds. The big picture: Alaska has long leaned Republican, but Peltola's ability to win crossover support — including votes from Republicans who ranked her above former Gov. Sarah Palin in…

33e1d7779a:95f6450ce969fecf.title: House Dems can't stand the speaker vote drama anymore
33e1d7779a:95f6450ce969fecf.author: Andrew Solender
33e1d7779a:95f6450ce969fecf.summary: House Democrats aren't unanimous on whether House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) should be speaker, but they pretty much all agree on two things: He probably will be speaker, and they just want this to be over. Why it matters: Their phones and emails are still being blown up by constituents and grassroots activists urging them to do what they can to block Jeffries from securing the speaker gavel. There isn't much Jeffries' skeptics and detractors on Capitol Hill can do: He is set to easily win his caucus' nomination on Wednesday and then be formally elected to the role on Jan. 3. Rep.-elect Jake Johnson (D-Minn.), who told Axios last week he was undecided, said Tuesday he met with Jeffries and was "assured" votes on his two key issues: Ending the Trump administration's tariffs and the war in Iran. "I'll be voting for Leader Jeffries," Johnson told Axios. State of play: The movement to deny Jeffries the speakership has proliferated online and among the progressive grassroots but has struggled to gain a foothold on Capitol Hill. A handful of members of the progressive "Bloc" — and some other newly elected members in deeply red district — have voiced skepticism of Jeffries, but only in a few cases has that evolved into outright opposition. "As of now, I'm a 'no,'" Rep.-elect Angela Gonzales-Torres (D-Calif.) told Axios on Wednesday. "The people are saying we deserve better, and better is possible." Reality check: Nobody is challenging Jeffries. Some people floated as potential potential challengers, such as Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), have firmly ruled it out . Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.), the subject of an online petition urging her to seek the role, has privately told colleagues she is not running but been more equivocal in public. "I'm very humbled to even be in conversation," Pressley said at a town hall on Monday. She added that she was "making no declarations or announcements" at that event and does not "need to be the speaker of the House to speak…

33e1d7779a:d0d3c1b9bf0c2788.title: Scoop: White House drops Heidi Overton's FDA nomination
33e1d7779a:d0d3c1b9bf0c2788.author: Alex Isenstadt
33e1d7779a:d0d3c1b9bf0c2788.summary: The White House is dropping Heidi Overton 's nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration because of a lack of congressional support, Axios has learned. Why it matters: The decision means the Trump administration will have to find a new candidate to lead the FDA as HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. looks to advance his Make America Healthy Again agenda. "FDA nominee Heidi Overton lacks the support on the Hill to move forward with her confirmation," a senior administration official told Axios late Tuesday. Zoom in: Overton, a physician and deputy director of the White House Domestic Policy Council, was nominated by President Trump in August. She had drawn criticism from segments of the MAHA movement that saw her siding with health and agriculture interests and helping undermine Kennedy agenda. Antiabortion forces also questioned her commitment to tightening rules for prescribing the abortion pill mifepristone. The backstory: Her nomination faced opposition from Democrats and skepticism from some Republican senators, including Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), chair of the Senate's Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee. Cassidy said he had "strong concerns" about Overton's role in the administration's efforts to change childhood vaccine recommendations, which he called "almost disqualifying." What they're saying: "We need to go in a new direction at FDA, and everybody fully supports Secretary Kennedy's vision to Make America Healthy Again and get back to a more populist and common-sense approach to health in America," the senior administration official said. The White House had tried to shore up her nomination Monday, posting on social media an account from the former dean of the University of New Mexico School of Medicine supporting Overton's confirmation. What's next: The HELP committee had been scheduled to vote on Overton's nomination on Wednesday. The FDA has been led by acting Commissioner Kyle Diamantas since Marty Makary resigned in May.

33e1d7779a:21729ee21b74b75f.title: Exclusive: Donald Trump Jr. signals investors underestimated AI pushback
33e1d7779a:21729ee21b74b75f.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:21729ee21b74b75f.summary: Donald Trump Jr. signaled that investors underestimated the political pushback to the AI ecosystem in an interview at Axios' annual BFD summit in New York. The big picture: The 2026 midterms reflected deep distrust of the AI race, with voters approving dozens of moratoriums on data centers — which President Trump rallied around. Driving the news: Trump Jr. asserted that "a lot of" the pushback "is manufactured." But he added "that doesn't mean it's not real" in an interview with Axios Pro Rata author Dan Primack Tuesday. "I think some of the big founders of the biggest [AI] companies out there probably have not done themselves the best service as [a] marketing department," he said, adding that they're "probably not the best messengers when they basically say, 'AI is gonna rule the world, and you should be thrilled about it.'" Asked by Primack if investors, peers or the pair themselves underestimated the populist pushback to AI, Trump Jr. said, "I think we saw that very clearly." He likened AI to other "any great innovation," but said, "This is gonna be one of those things, but it is going to take some time for people to learn how to adapt that into their regular lives." State of play: Trump Jr. spoke with Primack alongside 1789 Capital co-founder Omeed Malik, whose venture Trump Jr. joined in 2024. The investment firm has since exploded from overseeing a few hundred million dollars to billions. Zoom in: Trump Jr. agreed that the rage toward data centers represents a broader concern over growing AI influence. That public anger is becoming key to candidates: Democrats in six early 2028 primary states expect their presidential nominee to prioritize AI regulations, according to new polling data first reported by Axios' Maria Curi. Ahead of the midterms, Republicans took note of the sagging views of the data centers needed to power the AI boom. While Trump has prioritized self-regulation for the industry, the November results raise questions about how Republicans will…

33e1d7779a:cd81011a0f9c024e.title: "We will remain thoughtful": Nvidia says it will continue to backstop AI ecosystem
33e1d7779a:cd81011a0f9c024e.author: Ina Fried
33e1d7779a:cd81011a0f9c024e.summary: Nvidia's interim CEO said Tuesday that the company will be "disciplined" as it decides how much to invest in neoclouds and other AI customers going forward. Why it matters: Nvidia isn't just the biggest chip partner for AI startups — it's a major source of capital . What they're saying: "Our momentum is real," interim CEO Colette Kress said on at the end of conference call with investors and analysts. "Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We've got this." She said the company would continue to use its balance sheet and support startups and the broader AI ecosystem, but she made clear it won't be a blank check. "As the market matures and additional sources of capital become available, we are rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees," she added. In particular, Kress said the company would continue to be "disciplined and selective in our support" for so-called neoclouds . Those companies provide additional computing capacity to big AI players as well as smaller and regional operators. "Our neoclouds have been so instrumental in terms of both supporting enterprises and supporting many of the different countries around the world." CoreWeave and Nebius, two such neoclouds, each ose by more than 10% in after-hours trading. Zoom in: Kress didn't name-check any other specific customers but said the company would offer capital to suppliers to help them move quickly. Nvidia will provide financing assistance or guarantees to some "very strong customers," she said. The chip-maker will "look very deeply" into whether guarantees are needed and conduct "a lot of work to understand if those are the right types of investments we need to make." Catch-up quick: Huang resigned last week after revelations that he had a relationship with a woman who allegedly had ties to Chinese intelligence. She was also a major Nvidia customer and helped Chinese AI companies gain access…

33e1d7779a:d638519e93ce118a.title: Nvidia posts strong earnings amid Jensen Huang exit, reported SEC probe
33e1d7779a:d638519e93ce118a.author: Nathan Bomey
33e1d7779a:d638519e93ce118a.summary: Nvidia posted a stronger-than-expected third quarter and a bullish outlook in its first earnings report after Jensen Huang was ousted as CEO in a scandal that has reportedly spawned an SEC investigation. Why it matters: Nvidia remains squarely at the center of the AI economy — and investors are anxious for guidance on the company's strategic roadmap following Huang's sudden exit. Zoom in: Nvidia recorded quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion and net income of $65.3 billion, both more than doubling its performance from a year earlier. S&P Capital IQ analysts had expected revenue of $108.7 billion and net income of $60.5 billion. The company's data center revenue — its largest segment — rose 110% from a year ago to $107.6 billion. The showing — which included a whopping gross profit margin of 74.8% — immediately calmed investors who have shaved more than $1 trillion off of Nvidia's market cap since the Huang scandal broke. The stock was up 2% in after-hours trading Tuesday. It marks the first moment for interim CEO Colette Kress — who is also still serving as CFO — to exert her leadership during the most tumultuous moment in the company's history. She didn't mention Huang on Tuesday in the earnings report but touted Nvidia's role as "an exceptional technology leader" and said sales of the company's new, advanced Vera Rubin chips are "off to an explosive start." "Our roadmap is on track and our ambition has never been greater," she said. What we're watching: Whether Nvidia discloses any additional details about its CEO search or other investigations on its earnings call. WSJ reported Tuesday afternoon that the SEC has opened a civil probe into the company. An SEC spokesperson declined to comment. Nvidia reps did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Huang posted a public letter Tuesday saying he'd be "honored" to return as CEO. Newly appointed Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones said on Tuesday afternoon's earnings call that the board unanimously accepted Huang's…

33e1d7779a:c130833e04673e07.title: Duffy's $50 billion request gets chilly reception from Senate GOP
33e1d7779a:c130833e04673e07.author: Kate Santaliz
33e1d7779a:c130833e04673e07.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's $50 billion request to overhaul the nation's air traffic control system is getting a chilly reception from Senate Republicans, who are balking at the hefty price tag. Why it matters: The pushback from within President Trump's own party casts doubt on the administration's ability to secure the full $50 billion, even after Friday's historic nationwide groundstop . Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) told reporters that Duffy "made a huge mistake" by originally requesting $30 billion for air traffic modernization, then later upping the ask to $50 billion following the groundstop. "Maybe he was taking orders, but he's smart enough to know better than to say, 'I need 30 billion. We have a catastrophe. I need 50 billion now.'" Kennedy said, adding, "We're not going to give them $50 billion." Both Duffy and Trump have urged Congress to move quickly on the funding, which the administration formally requested Tuesday. Driving the news: Duffy, along with FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford, pitched the funding — which include $10 billion specifically for air traffic equipment modernization — to Senate Republicans at their weekly lunch. "I don't think the full $50 billion will be funded. Some of that is not safety related," Commerce Chairman Ted Cruz (R-Texas) told reporters. Cruz floated using the fast-track reconciliation process to secure additional funding for upgrading the air traffic control system, but said the administration needs to show it can effectively spend the $12.5 billion Congress already provided in the " Big, Beautiful Bill " last year. "Demonstrate that you can actually modernize, and come back to Congress when you need additional funds," Cruz said. Zoom in: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) has also raised concerns about the unspent funds. "There's some explanations that have to be given as to why that number is where it is," Thune told reporters Monday. Thune poured cold water on using reconciliation to pass the…

33e1d7779a:7cd52d71e1a92af0.title: Why the world's biggest climate meeting (still) matters
33e1d7779a:7cd52d71e1a92af0.author: Amy Harder
33e1d7779a:7cd52d71e1a92af0.summary: Every year, tens of thousands of people gather to discuss nothing short of humanity's future on a hotter planet. Yet the world seems increasingly distracted by just about everything else. Why it matters: For all of their flaws, these annual gatherings remain one of the few places where the world collectively confronts a problem that no country can solve alone. "The fact that in these very disruptive times on trade and multilateralism, two wars going on, and inflation everywhere, countries can come together and actually prioritize this is a very important point," said Ani Dasgupta, head of the World Resources Institute. Driving the news: The annual United Nations climate summit enters its final stretch this week in Antalya, Turkey, with negotiators trying to bridge disagreements over fossil fuels, clean electricity and money to help poorer countries confront climate change. A first draft of a potential agreement released Monday includes proposals to accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels and electrify more of the global economy. But countries remain divided over what should make the final cut. Arab countries and Russia are pushing back against proposals on fossil fuels and electrification, while the European Union is backing the electrification goal but demanding substantial changes to the broader agreement, according to Climate Home News . If the past is prologue, we'll probably see some kind of deal emerge hours or a couple days after Friday's scheduled conclusion, given these meetings' habit of running overtime. The big picture: Climate diplomacy hasn't been futile. Nor has it been sufficient. The landmark Paris Climate Agreement in 2015, which aimed to limit global warming to well below 2 degrees Celsius, helped usher in an era of climate progress. Projected warming by 2100 has actually dropped from roughly 3.5 degrees to 2.7 degrees, according to Climate Action Tracker — still far above the Paris goal, but considerably less than previously feared.…

33e1d7779a:79c92c5d8e8b9c30.title: Why the internet suddenly broke all at once
33e1d7779a:79c92c5d8e8b9c30.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:79c92c5d8e8b9c30.summary: Americans were locked out of bank accounts, blocked from boarding flights and unable to check emails in rapid succession over the past week. Why it matters: The internet immediately pointed fingers toward an AI agent doomsday, sending people into a frenzy that the Big One™was about to happen. Reality check: Experts tell Axios these disruptions don't appear linked to hacking. To the extent they involve AI, the incidents may have just as much to do with widespread efforts to fix outdated code as they do with slop software. Downdetector data also show that while the seven days through Monday represent the highest number of weekly outages in the last 12 months, the pattern over longer periods such as 30 days is far from unprecedented. Driving the news: Some Americans struggled to access JPMorgan Chase banking services Monday. United Airlines briefly delayed departing flights later that day, days after the FAA executed the longest nationwide ground stop since 9/11. Microsoft Outlook's outage left users unable to access emails and other Microsoft 365 services. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin suggested Monday that AI systems capable of writing and changing code could be contributing to the outages. Yes, but: No evidence so far points to AI-assisted hacking. In most cases, the outages have been attributed to software patching and appear otherwise unrelated, even as small technical problems snowballed into big ones. Chase blamed an internal software bug that delayed transactions involving other banks. United cited a technology problem; the FAA said a flood of network traffic destabilized older, legacy equipment. Microsoft cited a months-old bug, increased traffic and reduced server capacity. Between the lines: There are ways AI may have played a role that have nothing to do with hacking. Institutions around the world are racing to update software in order to solidify systems, given that AI models are capable of finding and exploiting vulnerabilities with…

33e1d7779a:5df7d8f5f45d7774.title: What is a dirty bomb and how dangerous is the weapon
33e1d7779a:5df7d8f5f45d7774.author: Herb Scribner
33e1d7779a:5df7d8f5f45d7774.summary: President Trump warned Iran against orchestrating a "dirty bomb" attack in Washington, D.C., though the White House says there are no credible threats. The big picture: Unlike a nuclear weapon, a "dirty bomb" uses common explosives to scatter radioactive material, potentially contaminating surrounding areas, forcing evacuations and causing widespread disruption. Driving the news: Asked Tuesday about reports of a possible Iranian dirty bomb plot in Washington, Trump said, "We're looking into it." "We take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy," he added . Trump did not say an attack was imminent: "I hope it's not." Trump warned Iran would face unprecedented consequences if it carried out an attack. Catch up quick: Trump's comments came hours after CNN reported about the threat to D.C. CNN reported that unnamed officials described Iran's attack planning as "an effort to give itself options rather than an indicator of an imminent attack." "We remain vigilant monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland," says Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman. Iran has denied the allegations, with Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei calling them "baseless." Read more about dirty bombs below. What is a dirty bomb? How it works: A dirty bomb combines conventional explosives, like dynamite, with radioactive materials, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention . This is much different than a nuclear bomb. A nuclear bomb splits atoms and releases a huge blast of energy. Dirty bombs spread radioactive dust, smoke or other material that contaminate, the CDC says. How dangerous is a dirty bomb? The main danger stems from the explosion itself, which, like other explosive materials, can cause serious injuries and damage, according to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission . The scope of impact would depend on the size of the bomb, NRC says, as well as the type of radioactive material and weather…

33e1d7779a:1b11b29c4d2e966f.title: Scammers are sending fake emails to people worried about Nvidia's stock
33e1d7779a:1b11b29c4d2e966f.author: Sam Sabin
33e1d7779a:1b11b29c4d2e966f.summary: Scammers are already exploiting the scandal surrounding Nvidia to lure unsuspecting investors and business professionals into downloading malware. Why it matters: AI is making it easier for criminals to capitalize on the news cycle and tailor scams to specific audiences before people have time to recognize the threat. Driving the news: KnowBe4, the cybersecurity training platform, says it's seen scammer emails using the subject line "Invitation: Nvidia Executive Partnership Discussion" that purport to offer information about Nvidia's investment strategy. Inside the email, recipients see a clickable image appearing to show information about Nvidia's 2026 investment parameters. Clicking it could lead to malware being downloaded onto their devices. KnowBe4 started seeing signs of the scam Wednesday, just a few days after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife and a day before he resigned, triggering a crisis at the chip-maker. KnowBe4 CEO Bryan Palma told Axios that the campaign appears to be targeting people working in finance, transportation and government. It's unclear which group is behind the emails, he added. The big picture: The Nvidia lure is part of a growing trend in which hackers borrow a page from the marketing industry's playbook to turn breaking news into targeted phishing campaigns. Just like marketers, hackers can purchase detailed contact lists and use AI to sort potential victims by industry, profession and interests, Palma said. That allows them to tailor their scams to specific audiences rather than sending the same generic email to millions of people. AI is also speeding up their ability to develop and launch timely schemes, Palma said. By the numbers: Attackers are 5.4 times faster at responding to headlines in 2026 than in 2022, according to KnowBe4 data . In one case, following a major celebrity's death, scammers launched an email phishing campaign within 16 hours. Nearly 88% of phishing attacks tied to breaking news…

33e1d7779a:8082b8e3489a250e.title: FAA pauses tech upgrade linked to nationwide ground stop
33e1d7779a:8082b8e3489a250e.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:8082b8e3489a250e.summary: The FAA is halting the installation of new routers following Friday's nearly five-hour nationwide ground stop , the agency confirmed Tuesday.
