33e1d7779a:5d47aab2d4b87b6e.title: Jensen Huang agrees to face Congress over Nvidia scandal
33e1d7779a:5d47aab2d4b87b6e.author: Herb Scribner
33e1d7779a:5d47aab2d4b87b6e.summary: Jensen Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter will officially testify before Congress in early December, lawmakers announced Tuesday. Why it matters: Lawmakers want answers on whether Nvidia's powerful AI chips were compromised by Chinese intelligence and whether the company did enough to protect sensitive American technology. Huang and Teter will participate in transcribed, closed-door interviews with the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence and China select committees. Context: House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast (R-Fla.), House China committee Chairman John Moolenaar (R-Mich.) and House Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford (R-Ark.) sent letters to Huang, Teter and Commerce undersecretary Jeffrey Kessler on Nov. 12 , requesting they appear. The chairmen told Teter they were seeking information on alleged chip smuggling and the use of Nvidia products by U.S. adversaries, as well as the company's alleged export-control investigations. Kessler was expected to join a classified briefing with Commerce Chair Ted Cruz, but the meeting was postponed. What they're saying: "We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security," the three committee chairmen said in a release . A representative for Huang did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment Tuesday. What's next: Huang will appear before the committees on Dec. 1, and Teter will appear on Dec. 2. Catch up quick: Nvidia announced last week that Huang had stepped down as CEO over an alleged affair with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy and former executive of Nvidia customer Megaspeed International. Huang's resignation ignited requests from Congress to investigate his relationship with Megaspeed , a Singapore-based data center company that gained access to Nvidia's AI chips. Megaspeed faces its own investigations for allegedly smuggling chips into China, which the company denies. The big picture: Huang ties to President Trump and…

33e1d7779a:70054ab4672706c2.title: Jensen Huang says he'd be "honored" to return as Nvidia CEO
33e1d7779a:70054ab4672706c2.author: Herb Scribner
33e1d7779a:70054ab4672706c2.summary: Jensen Huang acknowledged in a statement to the Wall Street Journal that he'd be willing to return to Nvidia as CEO. Why it matters: A push to reinstate Huang began almost as soon as he exited the company, but Nvidia's board isn't currently considering reinstating the former CEO, according to multiple reports. What they're saying: "Since my departure, I've seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO," Huang's statement said. "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO." State of play: A slew of candidates have been mentioned across multiple analyses and reports about the Nvidia successor. President Trump suggested former Apple CEO Tim Cook for the role. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has urged Nvidia to look for outside candidates. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress is currently serving as the company's acting interim CEO. Editor's note: This is a breaking story and will be updated.

33e1d7779a:af8ebd3cedf11692.title: Tech leaders tell Fed chairman Warsh how AI could transform the economy
33e1d7779a:af8ebd3cedf11692.author: Courtenay Brown
33e1d7779a:af8ebd3cedf11692.summary: Just maybe, both the extreme techno-optimists and AI doom-and-gloomers are wrong about the economic impact of the technology. That's the argument that venture capitalist Marc Andreessen — who is co-leading a Federal Reserve task force on the topic — made in a high-profile panel Monday. Why it matters: The argument could help shape how the Fed assesses AI's economic consequences, with major implications for its outlook on growth, inflation and interest rates. Andreessen's argument offered an early glimpse of the thinking that will underpin his recommendations to the central bank's leaders. What they're saying: "My line has been both utopians and the doomers are going to be disappointed, specifically disappointed by the scope and magnitude of the real-world impact, and specifically the economic impact," Andreessen said at the San Francisco Fed. Andreessen, a co-leader of Fed chairman Kevin Warsh's Jobs and Productivity Task Force, spoke alongside former Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo at a hearing in the Bay Area, where Warsh studied at Stanford and later spent 15 years teaching and conducting research. (Fellow task force member Chad Jones, a Stanford economist on leave for Anthropic, was in the audience but did not speak because the company is preparing to go public, Andreessen said.) Zoom in: Andreessen previewed his contribution to the task force's report, arguing that the economy is divided into two groups: Fast-changing industries, such as technology and media, where innovation drives productivity gains and lower prices. Slower-changing industries, including health care, education and housing, where regulations, limited competition and other barriers make technological progress harder. The intrigue: These slower-changing sectors account for some of Americans' biggest expenses. Those sectors of the economy "are not legally allowed to have rapid change," Andreessen said. Andreessen argued that regulations and other barriers could prevent AI from transforming…

33e1d7779a:dd86484486845238.title: Hakeem Jeffries shifts tactics ahead of House Democrats' internal speaker vote
33e1d7779a:dd86484486845238.author: Andrew Solender
33e1d7779a:dd86484486845238.summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) plans to force his members to take a tallied vote this week on whether to nominate him as speaker of the House, according to two sources familiar with the matter. Why it matters: The plan represents a shift in tactics — his allies had previously hoped to nominate him by acclamation — that would help reveal whether he has the votes to become speaker on Jan. 3. If he loses more than 40 votes, he may be in trouble. If not, he likely sails through even if some of his members ultimately oppose him on the House floor. Jeffries and his allies are confident he has more than enough support to get the 218 votes needed to become speaker even as some of his freshman members express skepticism or even outright opposition to him. "Jeffries will win," a senior House Democrat told Axios. Jeffries' plans were first reported by Punchbowl News. Between the lines: This new strategy would exploit the fact that, as of Tuesday, no other House Democrat has announced their candidacy for speaker. Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), who is often floated as a possible alternative in constituent phone calls to lawmakers urging them not to back Jeffries, told Axios he is not running for speaker. Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.), who has become the focus of a recent draft movement, has also told allies she is not interested in the role, as Axios previously reported. Pressley, asked about running for speaker at a town hall event in her district on Monday, told attendees : "I do not need to be the speaker of the House to speak for the people." State of play: House Democrats are set to meet behind closed doors starting Wednesday morning to elect their leadership team for the 120th Congress. In addition to nominating a candidate for speaker, they are set to vote on electing a House majority leader and whip, an assistant speaker, and a Democratic caucus chair and vice chair, among other leadership positions. Most of the candidates for those senior roles are…

33e1d7779a:8402278f32eb9f02.title: Nvidia's earnings mark start of post-Jensen era
33e1d7779a:8402278f32eb9f02.author: Matt Phillips
33e1d7779a:8402278f32eb9f02.summary: Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios Nvidia's post-Jensen Huang era begins in earnest with the release of its third-quarter results after the close of trading Tuesday. Why it matters: Investors and analysts will be reading tea leaves and listening for hints about near-term changes the company is making (or expecting the government to make) as a result of Huang's resignation last week and the circumstances that led to it. The big picture: Besides selling the world's most sought-after AI processors, Nvidia is a giant source of financial backing to the AI ecosystem — buying equity, making co-investments and backstopping debt in companies ranging from neoclouds like CoreWeave to fiber-optic cable providers like Lumentum. Nvidia is also a major partner of the two AI labs at the heart of the boom, striking a deal to provide a backstop for an OpenAI data center in Ohio and planning to invest about $10 billion into Anthropic following its IPO later this week, according to its prospectus. Huang could make these unorthodox deals — some call them circular finance — because of his position as a co-founder and sole CEO of Nvidia. Now that he's gone, investors will be listening closely for any indication that Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress, plans to step back from Huang's strategy of using Nvidia's resources to bolster the AI sector. What they're saying: Analysts will also be tuning in to Nvidia's conference call for hints about how the circumstances of Huang's ejection from the corner office — after reports of multiple affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset — could shift global sales patterns over time. "Our biggest concern now is new scrutiny that may restrict some of its sales into certain geographies such as Singapore/Malaysia. In a worst case, we estimate this could cut up to ~10% out of revenue," wrote UBS analysts. "Greater scrutiny of NVDA Asia shipments that indirectly (via cloud) service China customers, or more…

33e1d7779a:b16d704e72abfd3d.title: U.S. gets another D+ on premature births
33e1d7779a:b16d704e72abfd3d.author: Carly Mallenbaum
33e1d7779a:b16d704e72abfd3d.summary: Data: National Center for Health Statistics via March of Dimes; Map: Carly Mallenbaum/Axios The U.S. earned a D+ for its preterm birth rate yet again , according to the latest March of Dimes report card . Why it matters: Babies born before 37 weeks of pregnancy face greater risks of serious health complications, hospitalization and death in their first year of life. By the numbers: The national preterm birth rate remained at 10.4% in 2025 for the fourth year in a row. It marked the fifth consecutive year at D+ (which March of Dimes considers 10.4% to 10.7%). Zoom in: Mississippi had the highest rate at 14.9%. Vermont had the lowest at 8%. Rates improved in 23 states and jurisdictions, including D.C. and Puerto Rico, per the report that relies on CDC data. But only Idaho, South Dakota and Puerto Rico recorded statistically significant declines. Between the lines: Rising rates of chronic health conditions before pregnancy are one reason the nation's preterm birth rate remains stubbornly high, Michael Warren, chief medical and health officer of March of Dimes, tells Axios. High blood pressure and diabetes became more common among women giving birth in 2025. Both conditions increase the risk of pregnancy complications and premature birth. What they're saying: "It's not just about improving care during labor and delivery," Warren says. "It's really about improving their health across the life course." That means addressing chronic conditions even before pregnancy. What we're watching: Whether strategies including expanding access to doula care and encouraging low-dose aspirin use among pregnant women at risk for preeclampsia can help bring down preterm birth rates.

33e1d7779a:93bdc8eb0df6e1c4.title: Behind the Curtain: If competence were cool
33e1d7779a:93bdc8eb0df6e1c4.author: Mike Allen
33e1d7779a:93bdc8eb0df6e1c4.summary: So many government problems, like last week's nationwide aviation meltdown , are foreseeable ... and foreseen. Why it matters: Again and again, we choose to do nothing until a crisis hits. A big reason: These are huge, tedious, complex, unsexy, antiquated systems that require persistence and competence to fix. A big new problem: These systems are deeply intertwined with our daily lives, and highly susceptible to malfunctions, mishaps and AI-enhanced cyberattacks. They're boring until they're vital. The big picture: We have federal agencies and congressional committees designed explicitly to monitor, protect and improve these complex systems. But they've atrophied as power has been centralized in the presidency and congressional leadership, where daily political warfare rarely includes sober discussion of competence and essential interconnected systems. Here are a few of the foreseeable (and foreseen) crises that have been staring at us, many for literally decades: The skies: We've known for years that the air-traffic system relies on copper wire and floppy disks . We've seen and known the vulnerabilities through Democratic and Republican administrations. We've known the fix is expensive: $31.5 billion, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told lawmakers last year. At Friday night's briefing at the White House, Duffy said: "I want $50 billion ." The grid: We've known for a long time that our electricity is delivered through an aging patchwork system vulnerable to accidents or attacks. The nonprofit power authority NERC (North American Electric Reliability Corp.) warned this spring that the system is so strained by rising energy needs from AI and humans that it could jam up or break. The water: Drinking and wastewater systems are old and in dangerous disrepair — a huge risk to hospitals, in particular. In July , cyberattacks hit over 30 municipal water systems in Minnesota, with Iran as a likely culprit . The government's computers: Washington spends over $100…

33e1d7779a:6b256a6ce0839fc0.title: Push to reinstate Jensen Huang tests superstar tech CEO accountability
33e1d7779a:6b256a6ce0839fc0.author: Ina Fried
33e1d7779a:6b256a6ce0839fc0.summary: The push to reinstate Jensen Huang is set to test whether America's most powerful CEOs can still be held accountable — or if extraordinary success and political alliances have made them untouchable. Why it matters: Silicon Valley has long treated its most successful founders as indispensable. But a new class of tech billionaires, led by figures like Elon Musk, has amplified that culture while swatting away efforts to curtail their power. Their immense wealth and growing political clout raise a fundamental question: Can corporate boards, regulators, Congress or the courts actually rein in a superstar CEO anymore? Huang's potential return — or the Nvidia board's refusal to entertain it — could signal whether that balance of power is changing. "Power corrupts, and people start to think they are invincible," Anne Wojcicki, the founder of 23andMe and ex-wife of Google co-founder Sergei Brin, told Bloomberg . "We are all complicit in making these people think they are gods. And people do stupid things when they think they are untouchable." Driving the news: A growing campaign to reinstate Huang has attracted more than 180,000 signatures, including thousands of people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees, following his departure after revelations of intimate relationships involving subordinates and an alleged Chinese spy. President Trump said Monday he wouldn't mind seeing Huang return. Elon Musk has also backed the effort. Other supporters include Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan , Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney , Replit CEO Amjad Masad and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke. Prominent investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker have separately urged the board not to rule out Huang's return. Some pushing for a reexamination of the issue have focused on what they see as a lack of proof that Alice Huang, the executive with whom he had an affair, was a Chinese intelligence asset. That claim has been attributed in media reports to U.S. intelligence officials, although other stories have…

33e1d7779a:e20dd7a20ce30e4d.title: Democrats' squishy definition of Medicare expansion
33e1d7779a:e20dd7a20ce30e4d.author: Caitlin Owens
33e1d7779a:e20dd7a20ce30e4d.summary: Democrats marching into a debate over expanding Medicare are about to confront difficult questions about how far to go — including for seniors who are already in the program. Why it matters: Holes in traditional Medicare leave seniors exposed to out-of-pocket costs and affordability struggles, but making the program's benefits more generous may be prohibitively expensive. The big picture: Democrats scored overwhelming gains in the midterms after making health care affordability a major priority for the next Congress. Though the election results reinvigorated progressives' push for Medicare for All, there are also less sweeping options for what expanded coverage should look like. How far to go — and what to call the plan — will become critical heading into the 2028 presidential cycle and likely determine whether Democrats can attract any Republican support. Driving the news: Lowering the Medicare eligibility age is emerging as an early front-runner for what Democrats may try to pass and defy President Trump to veto. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) called on Democrats to lower the eligibility age to 55 soon after the election, framing it as an "immediate first step" toward his long-sought goal of Medicare for All. Sanders also wants to add vision, dental and hearing benefits and strengthen children's coverage. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York on Friday threw his support behind that kind of package, as well as strengthening children's coverage, Stat reported . And groups of Democrats in both chambers have recently introduced legislation lowering the Medicare eligibility age to 50. What they're saying: " Medicare for All is unlikely to be enacted in the near future, but the political push for it could prompt a debate about the services Medicare itself does not cover and the high costs current Medicare beneficiaries can incur," KFF executive vice president Larry Levitt wrote last month in JAMA Forum . State of play: Some Democrats are looking at other…

33e1d7779a:8f9f0823954db4d4.title: Trump's biggest project is running out of time
33e1d7779a:8f9f0823954db4d4.author: Brittany Gibson
33e1d7779a:8f9f0823954db4d4.summary: Look past the White House renovations , the proposed arch and the golf course : President Trump's border wall project is hundreds of miles behind pace. Why it matters: " Build that wall " helped build MAGA. But with two years to go, tough terrain and mounting political resistance threaten to leave Trump's signature promise unfinished. State of play: At the current pace, the main wall won't be finished until late 2029, while Trump will leave office in January 2029. There are about 619 miles of primary wall left to build, according to data from Customs and Border Protection as of November 10. The Trump administration has picked up the pace — from 2.6 miles a week earlier this year to 3.9 miles a week between mid-June and earlier this month — according to an Axios review of the agency data. But much of the remaining mileage is in Texas, where local landowners are fighting back and Trump's biggest allies were swept out of power in the midterms. Zoom in: The Big Bend sector — home to the state and national parks, multi-generational family ranches and numerous ecotourism businesses — has become a hot spot of resistance to construction, galvanizing political leaders across the spectrum to speak out against any physical intervention. "Just about every Democrat running statewide came to the Big Bend," said Susan Hays, who was just elected to be a Presidio County Commissioner. "all of them care about the border, the Big Bend, and they're going to fight for our public lands." Friction point: Texas Land Commissioner-elect Benjamin Flores, who opposes wall construction plans in West Texas and Big Bend, says his office could leverage state-owned land to advocate for surveillance technology to monitor for illegal crossings, which would be less invasive on the land, instead of a physical border wall there. The state owns 31 linear miles of land along the border. "The federal government is gonna need cooperation from us to get other areas that they may want done [and] that would…

33e1d7779a:84ce1146103b038d.title: Florida stayed red in a blue wave. But look at what happened in Hispanic precincts.
33e1d7779a:84ce1146103b038d.author: Sommer Brugal
33e1d7779a:84ce1146103b038d.summary: Some Democrats see Angie Nixon's Senate loss in Florida as a warning about running too far left. But her results with Hispanic voters challenge that idea, an Axios analysis found. Hispanic-majority precincts that some feared would reject her politics swung more than 21 points toward Democrats from 2024 and gave her a slight edge over moderate gubernatorial candidate David Jolly. Why it matters: Democrats gained more ground in Florida than in most states this year despite falling short in the two biggest races. Whether they can finish climbing out of their hole will shape the party's 2028 chances in a state seen as a Republican stronghold. " There definitely was a broad blue shift, it just wasn't deep enough," Daniel Smith, a University of Florida political science professor, tells Axios. "But you don't get to these close numbers without non-party affiliates and Republicans voting Democrat." The big picture: Florida swung further toward Democrats than Georgia's gubernatorial race or Ohio's Senate race, yet Florida Democrats had a bigger hole to climb out of. Governor: Democratic nominee David Jolly improved on the 2022 margin by more than 18 points, nearly 6 points above the median gain across 36 states, and 2 points more than neighboring Georgia, where Democrats took the office for the first time in decades. Senate: Nixon improved on the 2022 margin by nearly 14 points, more than a point above the national median, and 2.5 points above Ohio's Democratic gains. State of play: Florida's five statewide Democratic nominees finished within 1.6 points of one another in two-party margin, the least ticket splitting out of the 23 states with both a governor's race and a U.S. Senate race. Nixon's margin improved in Hispanic-majority precincts by 22 points over Val Demings in 2022 and 21 points better than Kamala Harris in 2024. The shift showed up regardless of where Hispanic voters came from, in mostly Cuban precincts (R+34 to R+14), mostly Puerto Rican ones (D+16 to D+35)…

33e1d7779a:ff99fa484e81b09b.title: U.S. allies on edge as Trump heads to summit with Xi and Putin
33e1d7779a:ff99fa484e81b09b.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:ff99fa484e81b09b.summary: President Trump's trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin has the makings of an unpredictable spectacle — and that's exactly what has U.S. allies anxious. Why it matters: Trump's stated goal for the first-ever summit between the nations' three leaders is to start a discussion on nuclear disarmament. But the fear is that he could go off script and take positions on Ukraine or Taiwan that undermine their interests or appear to side with their chief adversaries, according to several European officials and Western diplomats. "We know that every time President Trump talks to or sees Putin, it translates into bad news for Ukraine and for Europe. We brace for anything," a European diplomat told Axios. Substance aside, Western diplomats worry about the optics of Trump appearing alongside two emboldened strongmen. On Monday, Trump also floated a possible meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Driving the news: Before leaving for the Philippines on Monday, Trump reiterated that his goal for the summit is to talk about denuclearization — a "tough subject," he said, "because it's very hard for any of us to say we'll get rid of our nukes, right?" But other topics will get attention, too, Trump went on to say. "We'll talk about Iran. We have Iran in very good shape, but we'll talk about Iran a little bit," he said. The president also said "we'll talk about my favorite subject, Ukraine." His comments came after U.S. officials stressed in a call with reporters on Friday that the summit would not deal with the war in Ukraine. Chinese officials said the same thing. Context: Neither China nor Russia was enthusiastic about discussing denuclearization. But China agreed after Russian lobbying. And Putin saw the summit as a chance to lobby Trump on Ukraine. Behind the scenes: The Trump-Xi-Putin summit was a topic of closed-door talks among European leaders at a meeting in Dublin last week, according to a European diplomat. Some of…

33e1d7779a:ced3d5cccecfc0ba.title: Top Trump aides to meet with Europeans, Ukrainians on peace plan
33e1d7779a:ced3d5cccecfc0ba.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:ced3d5cccecfc0ba.summary: President Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are planning to meet with Ukrainian and European officials this week to work on security guarantees and a postwar economic recovery plan for Ukraine, a U.S. official said. Why it matters: The Thursday meeting in Berlin comes a week after Witkoff and Kushner urged Russia to propose a postwar security framework for Europe — a parallel effort they hope will help bring the war to a close. On the same day, Trump will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in China. Trump said on Monday that he expects to talk about the war in Ukraine. Zoom in: The aim of the Berlin meeting is to develop security guarantees to deter future Russian attacks on Ukraine as well as plans to rebuild its economy, the official said. The Trump aides have been in regular contact with Ukrainian and European officials as they engage Russia simultaneously, the person said. The U.S. official described the Berlin meeting and Trump's visit to China as a coordinated diplomatic effort. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller — who are joining Trump in China — have been briefed on the Ukraine negotiations, the person said. Zoom out: Witkoff and Kushner met with Putin in Moscow last Thursday. They also spoke Monday with his foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov about the next steps in the war talks. Axios reported last week that the U.S. asked Russia for a European security proposal that includes steps by Moscow to ease tensions. Many European governments, however, are highly skeptical that Russia would honor any agreement. Earlier this month, Axios reported that the U.S. hoped easing Russian diesel sanctions would win concessions, but Putin still rejected a ceasefire. The big picture: One overarching question is whether Europe will participate directly with Russia in negotiations to resolve the war. Witkoff and Kushner said Russia agreed that…

33e1d7779a:3c7fccd5ae28a517.title: Jordan inherits House GOP fight over punishing rebels
33e1d7779a:3c7fccd5ae28a517.author: Kate Santaliz
33e1d7779a:3c7fccd5ae28a517.summary: One of House GOP Minority Leader-elect Jim Jordan's first challenges will be navigating a push by Republicans to punish members who buck party leadership. Why it matters: Jordan, a founding member of the House Freedom Caucus, is now tasked with leading a conference where lawmakers are seeking to rein in the very tactics his conservative allies have long used to challenge GOP leadership. The conference will consider a number of amendments and rules when it organizes in a few weeks. Discussions are ongoing, a source familiar with Jordan's thinking tells Axios. Driving the news: Rep. Mike Flood (R-Neb.) and members of the Republican Main Street Caucus want to punish members who vote against the party on procedural rule votes , a technical vote that conservatives have repeatedly used as a hostage-taking tactic. Main Street's proposal would empower the Steering Committee to impose penalties ranging from loss of committee seniority to "more serious" consequences. Leadership or the chair of the relevant committee would then implement Steering's decision. Flood told Axios that Main Street members developed the proposal collectively over several months, including through a survey and multiple meetings. Flood and other Republicans pushing accountability measures have been in contact with Jordan's team as they work to finalize their proposals. The big picture: House Republicans' razor-thin majority gave every member outsized leverage over GOP leaders this Congress. One consequence has been repeated defeats on procedural votes that used to be automatic for the party. That has derailed GOP priorities and, on must-pass bills, left GOP speakers dependent on Democratic votes instead of legislation supported by their conference. Main Street's proposal would restore a small piece of that leverage by letting Steering leaders punish members who block those votes. "This has nothing to do with telling a member how to vote on an issue," Flood said of the proposal. Zoom in: House…

33e1d7779a:b81275929fb927ab.title: United Airlines resolves "widespread system outage" that delayed flights
33e1d7779a:b81275929fb927ab.author: Donica Phifer
33e1d7779a:b81275929fb927ab.summary: United Airlines said Monday that it resolved what it called a "widespread system outage" that delayed departing flights for about 90 minutes. Why it matters: It was a quick resolution to yet another issue affecting the U.S.' beleaguered airspace, which spent days digging itself out of thousands of flight delays and cancellations following Friday's hours-long ground stop . What they're saying: "We sincerely apologize for the inconvenience. We're aware of the widespread system outage, and our teams are working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible," United Airlines wrote on X in reply to a customer. "We appreciate your patience while we work through this. Please check back with us for updates, and keep an eye on your flight status through the United app or at http://united.com . Thanks for bearing with us!" The customer said the issue stemmed from planes being unable to determine weight limits, though United did not confirm that was the problem. United Airlines told Axios that the company is "troubleshooting a technology issue affecting departing flights." "There is no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights. There is no indication that this is a cybersecurity-related issue," they said. About an hour and fifteen minutes after United posted its apology, the company tweeted again to say the issue was resolved and encouraged passengers to check their flight status at the company's website. United gave no additional information about what caused the outage, and it's unclear how many flights were impacted. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information.

ecbefe1924:a1112539a5399e7d.title: An engine of (pay) growth? Productivity and wages in the UK auto industry
ecbefe1924:a1112539a5399e7d.author: Van Reenen, John
ecbefe1924:a1112539a5399e7d.summary: To what extent do identical workers in an industry benefit from productivity growth in the same industry? We study this question in the context of the UK auto industry which experienced a thirteen-fold increase in output per worker between 1980 and 2018. Over the same period, auto workers saw substantially stronger hourly wage growth than workers in other manufacturing industries. Controlling for unobserved worker heterogeneity, the auto wage premium over other manufacturing workers doubled from 8% in the 1980s to 17% in the 2010s, while the manufacturing premium over the rest of the economy remained roughly stable at 5%. Interpreted through the lens of a rent sharing model, we estimate that 63% of the increase in the raw firm-level auto wage premium can be accounted for by strong productivity growth. In contrast, differential bargaining power between auto workers cannot account for these changes.

ecbefe1924:48aaa5128f75aff6.title: The Division of Labor: Productivity, Coordination, and Learning
ecbefe1924:48aaa5128f75aff6.author: Xu, Yaling
ecbefe1924:48aaa5128f75aff6.summary: The division of labor is fundamental to how firms organize production. Since Adam Smith, economists have recognized that dividing tasks more finely increases productivity through specialization but also raises coordination costs—a tradeoff formalized by Becker and Murphy (1992). Yet we have little systematic evidence on how this tradeoff operates within firms. Moreover, this classical perspective overlooks a second, dynamic tradeoff: firms not only produce output, but also develop a central input into future production—their workers’ human capital. A finer division of labor allows workers to develop greater expertise through repeated performance of narrowly defined tasks, but may also reduce opportunities to learn from coworkers by limiting interactions and knowledge exchange. We study both tradeoffs using population-wide Norwegian employer–employee records, linked workplace surveys, quasi-experimental variation in coworker availability, and randomized experiments with workers and managers. We find that more specialized firms exhibit higher productivity but also greater coordination costs. Their workers report more learning-by-doing but substantially less coworker learning, resulting in lower overall learning and slower wage growth. To establish the importance of coworker learning for human capital accumulation, we exploit extended coworker absences and show that losing access to colleagues reduces subsequent wage growth, particularly in occupations characterized by greater task overlap and coworker learning. To isolate the role of the division of labor from other workplace characteristics, we conduct randomized experiments that vary task allocation in otherwise identical workplaces. Workers and managers anticipate greater coordination demands, weaker coworker interactions, and lower skill accumulation under greater specialization. The experiments then ask workers to choose their preferred workplace and managers how they would organize production. Both favor…

ecbefe1924:b243d5e5a333b044.title: AI Adoption and Employment Expectations: Evidence from a Survey of Small Business Owners
ecbefe1924:b243d5e5a333b044.author: Asani Sarkar
ecbefe1924:b243d5e5a333b044.summary: There is little consensus on the effect of AI adoption on employment. Economy-wide measures of pay and headcount have moved little even as AI adoption has spread rapidly, yet narrower measures document declining hiring for workers at the start of their careers or in AI-exposed occupations. In this post, we revisit this topic for U.S. small businesses. We use data from the 2025 Small Business Credit Survey (SBCS) to examine the twelve-month-forward employment and revenue expectations of AI users. We find that firms currently using AI are significantly more likely than non-users to expect increased employment and revenues over the next year, even after accounting for firm and owner characteristics and location. Revenue expectations are most optimistic for AI users that report facing operational challenges in utilizing technology.

ecbefe1924:f2a4557243c634ca.title: Beliefs Over Contracts
ecbefe1924:f2a4557243c634ca.author: Collin B. Raymond
ecbefe1924:f2a4557243c634ca.summary: We study how firms choose among incentive contracts and how accurately managers predict their effects. Using a survey of managerial beliefs and a large-scale field experiment, we randomly assign agents at the market level to several widely used, expenditure-equivalent incentive schemes. In the field, the best-performing contract increases agent output and firm revenue by over 20% relative to the status quo, despite being ranked lower by managers, whereas the worst-performing contract performs as predicted. Managers correctly identify underperforming contracts but systematically underestimate top- performing ones. We document the sources of performance di!erences—labor supply responses rather than selection or pricing and the determinants of managerial predictability: contract complexity and managerial hierarchy. Our results highlight the importance of contract design for firm performance and reveal systematic limits to managerial cognition in shaping incentives.

ecbefe1924:cc19a494a9782497.title: Asymmetric Information in Wage Contracts: Experimental Evidence and Welfare Implications
ecbefe1924:cc19a494a9782497.author: Daniel Herbst
ecbefe1924:cc19a494a9782497.summary: Compared to self-employment or performance-based pay, fixed wages reduce earnings uncertainty but are prone to market distortions through moral hazard and adverse selection. Using a model of wage contracts under asymmetric information, I show that these distortions map to marginal treatment response functions in a marginal treatment effects (MTE) framework. I apply this framework to a field experiment in which data-entry workers choose between a randomized fixed wage and a piece rate. I find evidence of both moral hazard and adverse selection: Fixed wages reduce worker productivity by an estimated 8.74 percent relative to the mean. Meanwhile, a 10 percent increase in the wage offer attracts a marginal worker whose productivity is higher by 1.90 percent of the mean. Using semi-parametric MTE estimation, I calculate the welfare loss associated with asymmetric information and the marginal values of public funds (MVPFs) for policies aimed at recovering this loss. I find that a tax on piece rates can mitigate adverse selection into fixed wages, generating tax revenue at social costs as low as $0.88 per dollar.

b3ea4f41ab:7c080b908a305ced.title: Productivity review of the Netherlands: Supporting business dynamism to revive productivity growth
b3ea4f41ab:7c080b908a305ced.author: OECD
b3ea4f41ab:7c080b908a305ced.summary: The Netherlands has one of the highest levels of labour productivity in the OECD, but growth has slowed over the past decade. The slowdown partly mirrors global trends but has been accentuated by weak investment and declining business dynamism. Against this background, this paper provides a cross-country comparative analysis of the role of firm entry, exit, growth and resource reallocation across firms, in shaping recent Dutch productivity performance. A set of policy simulations suggests that, even though the country performs well on a wide range of policy indicators, some reforms could boost business creation and job reallocation, thereby lifting productivity. The most promising measures include streamlining labour legislation, upgrading education and training, reducing the administrative burden on start-ups, refining the insolvency regime and further encouraging R&D and venture capital investment.

b3ea4f41ab:5832b279f95538ba.title: Transforming Textile Waste into Circular Value: Innovation, Community Participation and Sustainable Entrepreneurship in Micro and Small Enterprises
b3ea4f41ab:5832b279f95538ba.author: Sweta Patnaik
b3ea4f41ab:5832b279f95538ba.summary: In an era marked by economic uncertainty and environmental urgency, entrepreneurs are increasingly turning to sustainable innovation as a pathway to resilience and growth. This paper examines how the transformation of textile off-cut waste into functional and marketable products serves as both an entrepreneurial response to material scarcity and a strategic contribution to the circular economy. In contrast to high-capital technological innovation, this form of resource-based creativity offers accessible, low-cost solutions for emerging enterprises, particularly in the fashion and textile sectors. Drawing on examples of micro and small businesses navigating uncertain economic terrain, the study highlights how such innovations can generate value, reduce waste, and meet growing consumer demand for sustainability. While many entrepreneurs falter in the face of early challenges, those who reframe problems as opportunities particularly through material reuse are better positioned to survive and scale. This paper argues that innovation rooted in environmental consciousness and adaptability is not only viable during times of uncertainty but essential for long-term entrepreneurial success and inclusive economic recovery.

b3ea4f41ab:399cb4b09b29ab56.title: Current state and development prospects of franchising in the Republic of Uzbekistan: From an emerging market to a systemic driver of economic growth
b3ea4f41ab:399cb4b09b29ab56.author: Malika Azimova
b3ea4f41ab:399cb4b09b29ab56.summary: This article examines the institutional and economic conditions shaping the development of franchising in the Republic of Uzbekistan. Drawing on an analy-sis of the legal and regulatory framework, industry statistics, field research, and comparisons with selected international markets, the study identifies the main fac-tors limiting the sector's growth and proposes a phased model for its institutional development. Particular attention is given to regional disparities, the sectoral composition of the market, and the potential of locally developed franchise sys-tems to support entrepreneurship and expand employment opportunities. The empirical evidence covers the period 2024?2025 and includes an analysis of commercial concession agreements as well as expert interviews with market par-ticipants from eight regions of Uzbekistan.

b3ea4f41ab:6a6cf025f7cc45bd.title: Heterogeneous Firms, Growth and the Long Shadows of Business Cycles
b3ea4f41ab:6a6cf025f7cc45bd.author: Adam Hal Spencer
b3ea4f41ab:6a6cf025f7cc45bd.summary: Do ï¬ rms differ in their innovation response to business cycles? What economic forces shape this heterogeneity? And does it matter for aggregate propagation? We document substantial heterogeneity in ï¬ rm-level R&D cyclicality, develop a theory to explain this fact, and validate its key mechanism in the data. In a tractable model of business cycles and innovation-driven growth, endogenous selection makes R&D particularly responsive to aggregate conditions for ï¬ rms close to the exit margin. Consistent with this mechanism, ï¬ rms closer to exit display more procyclical R&D in the data. Quantitatively, selection and endogenous growth interact powerfully: selection generates heterogeneous R&D cyclicality, while endogenous growth translates these heterogeneous responses into persistent aggregate effects. Ignoring heterogeneous R&D cyclicality misses roughly half of the long-run output cost of a severe recession.

b3ea4f41ab:47c0143a0dd77ed0.title: Women Artisans in Economic and Social Development: A Systematic Literature Review on Entrepreneurship, Cultural Heritage, and Empowerment
b3ea4f41ab:47c0143a0dd77ed0.author: Yingying Zhang Zhang
b3ea4f41ab:47c0143a0dd77ed0.summary: Introduction: Women artisans play a crucial role at the intersection of cultural heritage, entrepreneurship, and rural development, acting as preservers of age-old traditions and catalysts for community economic growth, although the scientific literature on this phenomenon remains fragmented. Objective: To synthesize and analyze existing evidence regarding women artisans, focusing on their roles as agents of economic development, preservers of cultural heritage, and drivers of social empowerment initiatives. Method: A systematic review was conducted following the PRISMA methodology, involving searches in the Scopus and Web of Science databases. Following a screening process, 30 studies were analyzed using both bibliometric and hermeneutic approaches. Results: Systemic barriers-such as limited access to finance and sociocultural restrictions-were identified alongside effective facilitators, such as cooperatives that generate income growth. Conclusions: Women's artisan entrepreneurship constitutes an integrated model of sustainable development that links personal empowerment, cultural preservation, and economic growth. Women artisans act as agents of social transformation, creating impacts that extend beyond their own lives to benefit entire communities.

b3ea4f41ab:82a934767f3d67c7.title: Sorting into entrepreneurial teams
b3ea4f41ab:82a934767f3d67c7.author: Marta Morazzoni
b3ea4f41ab:82a934767f3d67c7.summary: This paper studies how entrepreneurs sort into founding teams and how team composition shapes the firm distribution. We develop a theory of career choice and team formation in which skill complementarities make team entrepreneurship attractive for agents with unbalanced skill profiles, while talent similarity makes teaming preferable to other career options. Using matched employer-employee and balance-sheet data from Portugal, we show that teams combining similar talent with diverse specializations create larger, more productive, and longer-lived firms; yet founders with dissimilar skills are less likely to start firms together. We calibrate the model to reproduce these patterns and use it to quantify the cost of imperfect founder matching. Counterfactuals show that reducing founders’ biased exposure reallocates activity from low-productivity solo firms toward more productive teams. An optimal-assignment benchmark reveals that even unbiased random search leaves substantial gains unrealized because high-surplus matches fail to form.

b3ea4f41ab:daeafea108d23544.title: AI Adoption and Employment Expectations: Evidence from a Survey of Small Business Owners
b3ea4f41ab:daeafea108d23544.author: Asani Sarkar
b3ea4f41ab:daeafea108d23544.summary: There is little consensus on the effect of AI adoption on employment. Economy-wide measures of pay and headcount have moved little even as AI adoption has spread rapidly, yet narrower measures document declining hiring for workers at the start of their careers or in AI-exposed occupations. In this post, we revisit this topic for U.S. small businesses. We use data from the 2025 Small Business Credit Survey (SBCS) to examine the twelve-month-forward employment and revenue expectations of AI users. We find that firms currently using AI are significantly more likely than non-users to expect increased employment and revenues over the next year, even after accounting for firm and owner characteristics and location. Revenue expectations are most optimistic for AI users that report facing operational challenges in utilizing technology.

b3ea4f41ab:6735834859328ccf.title: Breaking into Supply Chains : Experimental Evidence on Procurement Training for Women-Owned SMEs
b3ea4f41ab:6735834859328ccf.author: Neelamraju, Kalyan N.
b3ea4f41ab:6735834859328ccf.summary: Women-owned-or-led small and medium-sized enterprises (WSMEs) are underrepresented in public and corporate supply chains worldwide. There is growing interest in promoting SMEs’ and WSMEs’ integration into value chains, but limited causal evidence whether interventions to support their participation in procurement are effective. This paper conducts a phased randomized controlled trial to estimate the impacts of corporate procurement training for WSMEs in Colombia. The program increases procurement knowledge and readiness, resulting in a ten percentage point increase in registrations to corporate portals, and an eight percentage point increase in the likelihood of submitting a bid. Impacts on winning bids are concentrated in WSMEs with prior procurement knowledge or experience, whose probability of winning a contract increases by eight to nine percentage points. These impacts are approximately twenty percent of the control means. More broadly, the paper illustrates how complier-weighted treatment effects can be used to evaluate programs delivered through a funnel-shaped participation process, common in private sector development interventions.

18d1edb9f2:ce90462aa69c2379.title: Anchor or sinker – Large firms, anchoring capacity and regional development
18d1edb9f2:ce90462aa69c2379.author: Nilsson, Magnus
18d1edb9f2:ce90462aa69c2379.summary: This paper ties together two literatures which explain regional anchoring from different perspectives. One is based on the role of large organizations in anchoring an industry in a region, the other is systemic and deals with anchoring processes that circulate and embed knowledge. Each leaves implicit what the other explains. The aim is to understand how anchor effects and regional anchoring capacity interact across different regional contexts. Illustrative cases from three Swedish regions show how the two both diverge from and reinforce each other, anchor without anchoring and anchoring without an anchor, depending on regional configuration and anchor control.

18d1edb9f2:f67930276d86a5c4.title: University as catalyst of public R&D expenditures? An empirical assessment on EU NUTS 3 regions
18d1edb9f2:f67930276d86a5c4.author: Saverio Barabuffi
18d1edb9f2:f67930276d86a5c4.summary: This study examines whether universities shape the regional innovation effects of public R&D expenditure and whether this role varies across regional development trajectories. We analyse a panel of 1166 EU NUTS 3 regions over the period 2007-2020, combining data on European public R&D funding, patenting performance, university presence and regional development traps. Toa ddress the endogeneity of public R&D expenditure, we employ a control function aproach. The results show that public r&D expendirue positively affects patenting performance in both university and non-university, but the difference between them is not statistically significant. University presence therefore does not sistematically amplify the returns to public R&D. However, its moderating role becomes more pronounced in regions exposed to development trap risk and in regions experiencing persistent stagnation, while evidence is weaker for trap intensity. These fundings suggest that universities act as contingent rather than unviersal catalyst of public R&D. Their contribution appears particularly relevant in vulnerable and persistently stagnant regional trajectories, but less able to offset sever structural constraints. The study contributes to debates on the geography of public R&D and regional development traps by showing that the effectiveness of research funding depends not only on institutional presence, bu also on the development rajectory in which that institutional capacity is embedded.

18d1edb9f2:c83ad7175e77dfed.title: Place-based multi-system innovation: the case of the twin transition technologies in European regions
18d1edb9f2:c83ad7175e77dfed.author: Ron Boschma
18d1edb9f2:c83ad7175e77dfed.summary: There is increasing interest in studying how multi-system innovation (MSI) emerge across regions. Understanding it requires attention to the co-evolutionary dynamics among systems and to their spatial co-location. Integrating insights from the Sustainability Transition and Evolutionary Economic Geography literatures, a framework is proposed to study the critical emergence of innovation at the intersection of digital and green technologies, as outlined in the European twin transition agenda. Despite numerous studies, it remains unclear how specific components and capabilities recombine within regions to support the emergence of twin technologies. This framework is explored empirically in a study of 271 European NUTS-2 regions, using a random forest classification model to identify which configurations of regional technological trajectories most strongly support the emergence of twin technologies during the period 2000-2021. Using patent data, the results show that digital and green follow different trajectories into twin regional specialisation. Digital technologies contribute primarily through relatedness among themselves, while green technologies contribute when co-located with digital ones, with Artificial Intelligence being the most consistent interaction. These findings inform place-based regional innovation strategies by showing that the emergence of twin technologies depends not only on the accumulation of digital and green knowledge bases, but also on the specific configurations through which regions enter the twin technological space.

18d1edb9f2:43e63914665bf0ef.title: Foreign Giants' Broad Shoulders: The Causal Effect of Foreign Ideas on U.S. Innovation
18d1edb9f2:43e63914665bf0ef.author: Juan Cruz Lopez Del Valle
18d1edb9f2:43e63914665bf0ef.summary: We study the role of foreign ideas in U.S. innovation by constructing a directed “genealogy” of technologies from the full text of 13 million patents filed between 1887 and 2024. By tracing which earlier technologies appear in the founding patents of new ones, we recover a large-scale input–output network of technological recombination that identifies the foreign technologies that serve as inputs into innovation in the United States. We report four main findings. First, foreign ideas are pervasive: 54% of U.S. technologies build on at least one foreign input, and the most fertile U.S. technologies rely on foreign inputs most heavily. Second, foreign ideas have large causal effects on U.S. innovation. Using the historical settlement of migrants as a source of exogenous variation in local ancestry, we show that U.S. counties more exposed to knowledge from a given foreign country absorb substantially more technologies from that country and, in turn, invent significantly more U.S. technologies building on them. Third, foreign ideas shape not only the level but also the direction of technical change: U.S. counties are far more likely to pioneer the specific technologies whose foreign inputs are already in their local idea stock, and the changing origins of foreign ideas accompany the shift of American innovation from its historical heartland toward the coasts. Fourth, these effects leave a lasting imprint on local labor markets: decades later, counties that absorbed more of an origin’s ideas host more jobs working with those ideas, and even more work with the U.S. technologies descended from them.

18d1edb9f2:539ee550d8e511a5.title: From research & innovation to deployment - Tapping into the R&I policy potential to transform knowledge into products
18d1edb9f2:539ee550d8e511a5.author: Igor CZERMAINSKI DE OLIVEIRA
18d1edb9f2:539ee550d8e511a5.summary: This paper analyses how EU Research & Innovation policy can support the transition from knowledge generation to deployment and industrial scaling in strategic technologies. It uses RADAR, a policy simulation model, to test what emergence-oriented and industrial-scaling oriented policies can most effectively foster the translation of R&I outcomes into products that can successfully be commercialised and adopted. Results suggest that these two policy logics affect different outcomes and operate on different timelines. Early emergence support is especially relevant for product development outcomes, while scaling support becomes more important for installed capacity, employment and market capture once an upstream base exists. The results should be read as exploratory scenario evidence rather than as forecasts or optimal policy prescriptions. Their policy value lies in clarifying bottlenecks, sequencing issues and monitoring needs across different technology domains.

fd826003ba:97d3780fdbff4a98.title: Episode 108: Tom Schwantje on Choosing Middle Managers and Delegating Power in Multi-Ethnic Countries
fd826003ba:97d3780fdbff4a98.author: Jordi Blanes i Vidal | The Visible Hand
fd826003ba:97d3780fdbff4a98.summary: Organisations face a trade-off when appointing and delegating power to middle managers. On the one hand, the manager may take decisions that are not beneficial to the organisation. On the other hand, the manager may have better local information. In multi-ethnic countries this trade-off shapes whether the organisation may want to appoint a manager co-ethnic to the market served or co-ethnic to the organisation itself. This is studied in the context of Ethiopia, where an unexpected civil war increased the salience of ethnicity.

fd826003ba:10eb88327ee6e17c.title: Episode 107: Cristobal Otero on the Effect of Managers on Public Hospital Performance
fd826003ba:10eb88327ee6e17c.author: Jordi Blanes i Vidal | The Visible Hand
fd826003ba:10eb88327ee6e17c.summary: This paper studies the effect of managers for the performance of public hospitals, specifically following a reform in Chile that changed their recruitment process. The main findings are that the reform decreased mortality, likely through the mechanism of improving the quality of managers (e.g., replacing managers without management degrees with managers with management degrees).

fd826003ba:6efc59758fb1d8a7.title: Episode 106: Alexia Delfino and Miguel Espinosa on Value Dissonance at Work
fd826003ba:6efc59758fb1d8a7.author: Jordi Blanes i Vidal | The Visible Hand
fd826003ba:6efc59758fb1d8a7.summary: This paper studies what happens when a worker has a different set of values than (a) their boss, or (b) their colleagues. Productivity is lower workers with such value dissonance, and the mechanism appears to be worse worker morale and worse communication between worker and manager.

fd826003ba:9e3018f394a3b4a7.title: Episode 105: Michael Frakes on Doctor Diversity and Racial Health Differences
fd826003ba:9e3018f394a3b4a7.author: Jordi Blanes i Vidal | The Visible Hand
fd826003ba:9e3018f394a3b4a7.summary: This paper studies whether the racial diversity of medical providers (mostly doctors) in the hospital, affects the health outcomes of minority patients. There is a big effect and, most importantly, it does not only operate through the concordance between individual patient and individual doctor: having more diverse doctors in the hospital generates positive externalities that go beyond the patient-doctor relation.

fd826003ba:999aee89b4154734.title: Episode 104: Victoria Angelova on the Comparison between Algorithms and Humans Making Decisions
fd826003ba:999aee89b4154734.author: Jordi Blanes i Vidal | The Visible Hand
fd826003ba:999aee89b4154734.summary: This paper studies whether human decision-makers can improve on algorithmic recommendations, in the setting of bail decisions in the criminal justice system. Bail judges receive recommendations from predictive algorithms and can choose to confirm or override them. The paper finds that most judges do not add value beyond the algorithm, although a minority do.

f3fd1ffa24:dbf4ff0e1e4b1a71.title: Does the Stock Market Stigmatize Banks that Borrow from the Fed?
f3fd1ffa24:dbf4ff0e1e4b1a71.summary: Banks may resist borrowing from the Federal Reserve during a panic if such borrowing is stigmatized (that is, viewed by the market as a sign of financial weakness), thus hampering the Fed’s ability to resolve the crisis. The problem may be particularly acute for publicly traded banks since their stock prices immediately reflect the market's opinion of them. In this post, based on a recent paper , we track what happened to stock investors' perceptions of a bank's risk level right after it first borrowed from Fed facilities in the first month of the bank run of 2023 . We find that, after a first trip to the Fed's Discount Window (DW), investors became more sensitive to that bank's weaknesses. In contrast, investors did not evince such concern when the bank took a first loan from a new facility, the Bank Term Funding Program (BTFP).

f3fd1ffa24:4a93cf67344f3221.title: Can Workers Predict Job Finding and Job Loss?
f3fd1ffa24:4a93cf67344f3221.summary: Workers’ perceptions of the labor market may differ from aggregate labor market statistics. Individuals might be overly optimistic about their chance of finding a job, or too pessimistic about the odds of losing their current position. In this post, we compare subjective beliefs of future job-finding and job-loss from the New York Fed’s Survey of Consumer Expectations (SCE) with their realized counterparts in the Current Population Survey (CPS). We then investigate how closely aggregate perceptions of job-finding and job-loss prospects align with realized rates.

f3fd1ffa24:1fa93dbff6be7665.title: Banking System Vulnerability: 2026 Update
f3fd1ffa24:1fa93dbff6be7665.summary: As in previous years, we provide in this post an update on the vulnerability of the U.S. banking system based on four analytical models that capture different aspects of this vulnerability. We use data through 2026:Q2 to update our analysis and discuss how the vulnerability measures have changed since our last update one year ago .

f3fd1ffa24:1754a7c07a755517.title: A Look at the Wider Divide in Credit Card Delinquency by Income
f3fd1ffa24:1754a7c07a755517.summary: Credit card delinquency rose sharply between 2022 and 2024, and the increase was steepest among borrowers in lower-income neighborhoods. Here, we check in on credit card performance by neighborhood income and trace when the borrowers who are now struggling with their payments were issued cards. We find that during the pandemic, an increasing share of new credit cards went to borrowers with lower incomes and credit scores, and those accounts are now showing higher levels of distress.

f3fd1ffa24:f15416153b845e47.title: Has U.S. Monetary Policy Really Improved? A 150‑Year Perspective
f3fd1ffa24:f15416153b845e47.summary: Has U.S. monetary policy actually improved over time? Or was the apparent success of the modern Federal Reserve mostly the result of more favorable economic conditions and better luck? In this post, we summarize our paper , * which develops a framework for comparing monetary policy across different economic environments. Our approach asks how close policy came to the best response given the economic conditions and shocks policymakers faced. Applying this framework to 150 years of U.S. monetary history, we find that meaningful improvements in monetary policy occurred only in the last thirty years. Most of the gains reflect, among other developments, substantially better responses to financial shocks and supply shocks.

f3fd1ffa24:8c142c33b72c8379.title: The U.S. Oil Sector’s Role in Restraining Prices
f3fd1ffa24:8c142c33b72c8379.author: Thomas Klitgaard
f3fd1ffa24:8c142c33b72c8379.summary: The start of the Middle East conflict in early 2026 caused an unprecedented drop in global petroleum supply. In response, oil prices jumped—but not to unprecedentedly high levels. The U.S. oil sector was a key factor in moderating the shock. For one, its steady increases in drilling helped create a large oversupply in the global market before the conflict, making it less of a challenge to offset the drop in Middle East oil output. In addition, U.S. commercial and government inventories were rapidly drawn down, filling half the gap between global supply and demand in the second quarter by some estimates. Inventories, though, are a limited resource and U.S. stockpiles stopped falling in July. As a consequence, the continued shortfall in global production has been managed by running down inventories in the rest of the world.

f3fd1ffa24:f264753704ee9bc6.title: How Market Position Shapes Credit Card Interest Rates
f3fd1ffa24:f264753704ee9bc6.author: Kyle Herkenhoff and Juan M. Morelli
f3fd1ffa24:f264753704ee9bc6.summary: Why is it that two borrowers who look much alike can be offered very different rates when applying for a credit card? In a recent paper , we address this question by examining how the rate offered changes when the lender’s funding cost falls. Data on 14 million newly issued cards show that when a lender's funding costs decline, the lender passes less of that decline on to the offer rate when it holds a large market share. That is, two borrowers with similar credit scores and incomes borrowing from the same lender can see noticeably different interest rates on the credit card they are applying for.

f3fd1ffa24:c48a20582dc18d57.title: How Do Banking Supervisors Deal with Failing Banks?
f3fd1ffa24:c48a20582dc18d57.author: Sergio Correia, Stephan Luck, and Emil Verner
f3fd1ffa24:c48a20582dc18d57.summary: In this post, we discuss insights from a recent staff report on the role of banking supervision in identifying and disciplining failing banks. We show that bank failures typically result from supervisory closure decisions based on hard information about book equity. Yet hard information is itself partly produced by supervision, as our evidence suggests that supervisors require troubled banks to recognize potential losses. We argue that supervision faces a trade-off: Stricter supervision can reduce the costs of resolving failing banks, but it can also lead to tighter regulatory capital constraints and hold back credit supply.

f3fd1ffa24:a4402c9f2991db79.title: Evaluating New LinkedIn Labor Market Tightness Indicators
f3fd1ffa24:a4402c9f2991db79.summary: Measures of labor market tightness (LMT) describe how difficult it is for firms to find workers. The labor market is considered tight if there are few job seekers available relative to job openings, implying stronger wage pressures as employers compete for scarce job seekers. Thus, good measures of LMT are important for predicting wage inflation and calibrating monetary policy. Recently, the hiring platform LinkedIn began producing three innovative LMT measures based on its user data. In this post, we use public data from the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) and the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) to evaluate the ability of these novel measures to predict wage and price inflation relative to existing LMT measures, finding that one stands out as particularly useful and timely.

f3fd1ffa24:42008bb79cf11289.title: Revenue per Worker Is Up. Are Firms Getting a Larger Share?
f3fd1ffa24:42008bb79cf11289.summary: From the Great Recession until 2019, U.S. labor productivity growth disappointed. Nonfarm-business output per hour grew about 1 percent a year from 2010 to 2019, down from 3 percent in the late 1990s. This slowdown was especially pronounced in manufacturing, and it coincided with a slowdown in the growth of revenue per worker among public firms. However, since 2019, growth has picked up to twice the 2010s rate, around 2 percent. In this post, I use data from firms’ 10-K filings to unpack this recent acceleration. I first show that the acceleration appears in public firms’ revenue per worker, then document how the gains went into profit margins, and finally, what firm characteristics predicted significant profit margin increases. The increase in profit margins is consistent with ongoing declines in the labor share of output .

f3fd1ffa24:22a1cb8ad31be2ec.title: Has the AI Boom Impacted the U.S. Current Account?
f3fd1ffa24:22a1cb8ad31be2ec.author: Julian di Giovanni
f3fd1ffa24:22a1cb8ad31be2ec.summary: The AI boom is showing up in different corners of the U.S. economy, including international trade. Imports of semiconductors, servers, and computing equipment have climbed sharply yet the U.S. current account deficit has been largely unchanged. To better understand how the AI boom has not substantially affected the trade balance, consider that the current account is dictated by the gap between domestic saving and investment spending. It turns out that aggregate saving and investment spending have not changed much during the AI boom. Aggregate investment has not risen due to weakness outside the AI sector and business saving has remained robust.

f3fd1ffa24:45d0a3bff02d5db0.title: Prices, Prices, Prices: Overall Inflation and the Costs You Care About
f3fd1ffa24:45d0a3bff02d5db0.summary: As fall starts to show itself in cooler weather, I want to discuss a topic that usually raises temperatures: inflation. Like a budget-conscious consumer, the Federal Reserve is highly attuned to changes in the price of goods and services; minimizing such swings is one of the Fed’s primary duties, after all. But how does the Fed’s view of prices differ from that of a consumer? And how does the Fed go about stabilizing prices writ large when it lacks the ability to set prices directly? In this post, I explore that apparent paradox from the perspective of a central banker (though I remain a budget-conscious consumer when off duty).

f3fd1ffa24:2fd0334d84f65de0.title: AI Adoption and Employment Expectations: Evidence from a Survey of Small Business Owners
f3fd1ffa24:2fd0334d84f65de0.summary: There is little consensus on the effect of AI adoption on employment. Economy-wide measures of pay and headcount have moved little even as AI adoption has spread rapidly, yet narrower measures document declining hiring for workers at the start of their careers or in AI-exposed occupations . In this post, we revisit this topic for U.S. small businesses. We use data from the 2025 Small Business Credit Survey (SBCS) to examine the twelve-month-forward employment and revenue expectations of AI users. We find that firms currently using AI are significantly more likely than non-users to expect increased employment and revenues over the next year, even after accounting for firm and owner characteristics and location. Revenue expectations are most optimistic for AI users that report facing operational challenges in utilizing technology.

f3fd1ffa24:00bc17cbb1a550c2.title: Firm Heterogeneity and the Response of Investment to Monetary Policy
f3fd1ffa24:00bc17cbb1a550c2.summary: It is well known that monetary policy affects firms’ investment decisions. But which firms are the most responsive to changes in interest rates? And does this responsiveness vary over time? The literature has given diverse answers to this question, focusing on characteristics such as firm size, age, and financial position, and mostly studying these traits in isolation. In this post based on a recent Staff Report , we explore how investment responsiveness to monetary policy changes across firms and over time. We find that investment by most firms in most time periods responds little to monetary policy. For some firms in some periods, however, investment is very responsive to changes in interest rates. While these instances of strong sensitivity correlate with several firm traits, there is substantial variation that cannot easily be linked to specific characteristics of firms. Our findings therefore underscore the importance of considering the entire distribution of investment responses rather than focusing on the average effect.

f3fd1ffa24:60233756dac81b20.title: How Fast Do Tariffs Pass Through into Consumer Prices?
f3fd1ffa24:60233756dac81b20.author: Mary Amiti, Sebastian Heise, and David E. Weinstein
f3fd1ffa24:60233756dac81b20.summary: There has been a lot of interest in how tariffs affect consumer prices (for example, Cavallo et al. 2021 , 2025 ). In this post, we present results from our new research paper that estimates the effects of the 2025-26 tariffs on retail consumer prices. We find that for every percentage point increase in average tariffs, consumer goods prices increase by about a quarter of a percent after one year. Roughly two-thirds of the effect arises because tariffs raise the prices of imported consumer goods. The remaining third arises indirectly: tariffs increase the prices of goods made in the U.S. because producers pay more for imported parts and materials, and because producers raise their markups when competing imports cost more. The effects differ in their timing. Prices of imported goods respond quickly to tariffs, while prices of U.S.-made goods adjust over six to twelve months as higher costs move through the supply chain.
